agr-rice.title: Rice farming and the uses of rice
agr-rice.objective: Explain rice classification and the differences between unhusked, brown and white rice.

paragraphs.agr-rice-p1: Rice farming means growing rice plants to produce rice. Distinguish the living plant from the harvested grain used for food and other purposes.
paragraphs.agr-rice-p2: Cultivated rice includes Asian rice and African rice. Asian rice is broadly divided into indica and japonica; japonica is the main type grown in Japan.
paragraphs.agr-rice-p3: Removing the husk from harvested unhusked rice produces brown rice. Further milling produces white rice, which is commonly eaten. Threshing and removing the husk are different operations.
paragraphs.agr-rice-p4: Rice is not only cooked and eaten as grain. Some rice is grown for livestock feed, while some is processed into products such as rice flour. Organize these uses into separate categories.
paragraphs.agr-rice-p5: Consider ploughing, transplanting, harvesting, threshing and preparation as connected stages in the annual farming cycle. These operations have become increasingly mechanized.
paragraphs.agr-rice-p6: Explain the difference between brown and white rice in processing order. Then identify the main rice type grown in Japan and two uses other than eating cooked rice.

agr-rice.activity: Draw “unhusked rice → brown rice → white rice” and label each processing step. Sort the uses into food, feed and processing, then compare your notes with the rice classification diagram.

paragraphTitles.agr-rice-p3: From unhusked rice to brown rice
paragraphTitles.agr-rice-p4: Uses other than eating cooked rice

agr-organs.title: Plant organs and two types of growth
agr-organs.objective: Classify leaves, stems and roots separately from flowers and fruit by their roles, and explain vegetative and reproductive growth.

paragraphs.agr-organs-p1: A plant consists of parts such as leaves, stems, roots, flowers and fruit. Besides recognizing their shapes and positions, organize what each part does.
paragraphs.agr-organs-p2: Leaves, stems and roots are organs that support plant growth. Together they are called vegetative organs. The term refers to parts of the plant, not to fertilizer itself.
paragraphs.agr-organs-p3: Flowers and fruit have roles in producing the next generation and are called reproductive organs. Their distinction from vegetative organs is based on the roles discussed here, rather than their size.
paragraphs.agr-organs-p4: Growth in which leaves, stems and roots become larger is vegetative growth. For example, relate an increase in leaves or the lengthening of a stem to the organ that is changing.
paragraphs.agr-organs-p5: Reproductive growth involves forming flowers and fruit and leads to the formation of fruit and seeds. Plant growth should therefore be understood as more than just an increase in height.
paragraphs.agr-organs-p6: The conditions for moving from vegetative to reproductive growth, and the way this happens, differ by crop. Do not assume all crops make the transition after the same number of days or at the same size.

agr-organs.activity: Make five cards for leaf, stem, root, flower and fruit, then group them by role. Match “the stem lengthens” and “fruit forms” to the two types of growth and explain why.

agr-vegetables.title: Vegetable parts used and places of cultivation
agr-vegetables.objective: Distinguish the parts of vegetables that are used and open-field cultivation from cultivation in protected structures.

paragraphs.agr-vegetables-p1: When grouping vegetables, consider which part is harvested and used. Root vegetables use roots or underground stems, leafy vegetables use leaves, and fruit vegetables use the fruit.
paragraphs.agr-vegetables-p2: The term “root vegetables” classifies vegetables by the part eaten. “Open-field cultivation” and “protected cultivation” classify them by the growing place or facilities. These are different classification criteria.
paragraphs.agr-vegetables-p3: Vegetables are grown in outdoor fields as well as in structures such as greenhouses. When recording information, distinguish the use of a structure from the type of crop itself.
paragraphs.agr-vegetables-p4: Year-round cultivation means producing the same kind of vegetable throughout the year by using environmental control equipment, covering materials and similar resources. It does not simply mean repeatedly growing the same crop in the same place.
paragraphs.agr-vegetables-p5: A production-area relay supplies vegetables throughout the year by shifting production between areas, taking advantage of differences in climate and elevation. This mechanism differs from year-round cultivation.
paragraphs.agr-vegetables-p6: Organize vegetable classifications under three headings: the part used, the growing place, and the method of year-round supply. Descriptions based on these different criteria can be combined for a single vegetable.

agr-vegetables.activity: Make a table with three columns and record the part used, growing place and annual supply mechanism separately. Explain what changes in year-round cultivation and in a production-area relay.

agr-fruit.title: Evergreen and deciduous fruit trees
agr-fruit.objective: Group the fruit trees listed in the material as evergreen or deciduous and explain typical regional growing patterns.

paragraphs.agr-fruit-p1: Fruit trees include evergreen and deciduous types. Rather than classifying them only by fruit color or sweetness, focus on the characteristics of their leaves.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-p2: Citrus trees, including satsuma mandarin, are evergreen fruit trees. Loquat is also an evergreen fruit tree. Learn the names together with their classification, rather than memorizing the names alone.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-p3: Apple, grape, pear, peach and persimmon are examples of deciduous fruit trees. Even for fruit you often eat, check the classification of the tree separately.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-p4: Apples are widely grown in colder regions and satsuma mandarins in warmer regions. These are typical patterns, not a claim that they can never be grown outside those regions.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-p5: Evergreen and deciduous describe the classification of fruit trees; cold and warm describe the climate of their growing areas. Keeping these as separate information helps avoid confusion.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-p6: Group the seven examples into evergreen and deciduous types, then explain the typical growing areas of apples and satsuma mandarins. Do not replace “widely grown there” with “grown only there.”

agr-fruit.activity: Write fruit-tree names on cards, divide them into two groups, and explain the classification aloud. For apple and satsuma mandarin, add the typical regional climate in a separate column.

agr-climate.title: Japan’s climate and regional differences in agriculture
agr-climate.objective: Organize north–south differences, the four seasons and regional winter differences without treating the material as one nationwide set of conditions.

paragraphs.agr-climate-p1: Japan’s climate cannot be explained by a single set of conditions. The material shows the north–south contrast between subtropical Okinawa and subarctic Hokkaido.
paragraphs.agr-climate-p2: Temperatures rise in spring and plants begin growing. The rainy season brings prolonged rain, followed by a hot, humid summer. Relate the seasons to the condition of crops.
paragraphs.agr-climate-p3: In winter, snow is more likely on the Sea of Japan side, while dry, clear weather tends to persist on the Pacific side. Confusing the two sides reverses the regional explanation.
paragraphs.agr-climate-p4: The material also discusses localized heavy rain and bands of rain-producing clouds. Distinguish short-duration rain from rain that lasts over a wide area; do not reduce all of these patterns to “a lot of rain.”
paragraphs.agr-climate-p5: Rice is grown in paddy fields. Upland fields are used for field crops, vegetables, fruit trees, flowers and other crops. Understand land categories together with the crop examples.
paragraphs.agr-climate-p6: Compare Okinawa with Hokkaido, and winter on the Sea of Japan side with winter on the Pacific side. The descriptions are regional tendencies, not a weather forecast for deciding whether work can be done on a particular day.

paragraphTitles.agr-climate-p2: The progression of the four seasons

agr-climate.activity: On a simple outline map of Japan, mark the north–south climate differences and regional winter differences. Add the progression of the four seasons and explain regional and seasonal differences separately.

agr-statistics.title: Reading years and proportions in agricultural statistics
agr-statistics.objective: Check the year, units, subject and denominator of proportions, and avoid mixing different statistics.

paragraphs.agr-statistics-p1: The agricultural statistics include figures for 2019 and floriculture statistics for Heisei 30. Do not present the values in the material as if they were current figures.
paragraphs.agr-statistics-p2: The explanation of agricultural output value in 2019 gives vegetables as 24%, rice as 20%, fruit as 9% and flowers as 4%. These are different from shares of cultivated area or shares by weight.
paragraphs.agr-statistics-p3: The same amount of money is displayed differently when expressed in yen, hundreds of millions of yen or trillions of yen. Check the table title and units before comparing figures, and do not add numbers in different units without conversion.
paragraphs.agr-statistics-p4: The material contains a calorie-based explanation and a weight-based table for 2019. Since the indicators differ, they cannot simply be compared as percentages with the same denominator.
paragraphs.agr-statistics-p5: The share of cut flowers and similar categories within the total value of floriculture differs from floriculture’s share of all agriculture. State what total is being treated as 100%.
paragraphs.agr-statistics-p6: Record the year, units, subject and denominator first. Put figures from different years in separate columns, and do not conclude that the material is wrong merely because the numbers differ.

paragraphTitles.agr-statistics-p5: The breakdown of floriculture and the overall total

agr-statistics.activity: Using the 2019 explanation, create fields for year, units, subject and denominator. Explain why proportions within floriculture do not mean the same thing as floriculture’s share of all agriculture.

agr-flowers.title: Flower production and forms of use
agr-flowers.objective: Understand the meaning of floriculture and the use categories in its statistics, and distinguish cut flowers from potted plants.

paragraphs.agr-flowers-p1: Flowers produced, grown and sold are treated as floricultural products. Organize floriculture as a field of agricultural production rather than grouping it with edible vegetables and fruit.
paragraphs.agr-flowers-p2: The source statistics include a cut-flower category. Read crop names such as chrysanthemums and roses together with the form in which they are sold or used.
paragraphs.agr-flowers-p3: Potted plants such as cyclamen and cultivated orchids are also shown. Cut flowers and potted plants belong to floriculture, but their forms of use differ.
paragraphs.agr-flowers-p4: The flower charts and tables carry reference years such as Heisei 30. Do not confuse the production composition or growing areas described for that period with current market trends.
paragraphs.agr-flowers-p5: The material also shows flower production value by prefecture. When discussing rankings, state the reference year and monetary unit, and do not describe those rankings as fixed into the future.
paragraphs.agr-flowers-p6: Summarize separately the field of floriculture, its cut-flower and potted-plant categories, and the reference year of the statistics. Detailed cultivation work is studied separately in the Level 2 chapter on flower cultivation.

agr-flowers.activity: Group the examples of chrysanthemums and roses, and cyclamen and cultivated orchids, by their form of use. Record the statistical year separately and distinguish it from explanations of cultivation techniques.

agr-plant-balance.title: Photosynthesis, respiration, transpiration and uptake
agr-plant-balance.objective: Distinguish the processes that produce and consume carbohydrates, and the routes through which water enters and leaves the plant.

paragraphs.agr-plant-balance-p1: Plants need light, carbon dioxide and water for photosynthesis. When reading a diagram or explanation, distinguish light from materials and check that all three requirements are included.
paragraphs.agr-plant-balance-p2: Photosynthesis produces carbohydrates. Taking in water or carbon dioxide is not the same as synthesizing carbohydrates; distinguish the inputs from the products.
paragraphs.agr-plant-balance-p3: Plants carry out respiration as well as photosynthesis. The material explains that respiration becomes more active during vigorous growth or at high temperatures. Do not confuse respiration with photosynthesis, which produces carbohydrates.
paragraphs.agr-plant-balance-p4: High night temperatures increase consumption through respiration, leaving less of the carbohydrates produced during the day stored in the plant. This alone does not establish one optimal temperature for every crop.
paragraphs.agr-plant-balance-p5: Transpiration is the release of water vapour through stomata in leaves. It differs from roots absorbing soil water in both location and the direction of water movement.
paragraphs.agr-plant-balance-p6: Plants absorb water and nutrients from soil through their roots. Separating the route into the roots from the route out through the leaves helps you diagram the relationship between uptake and transpiration.

paragraphTitles.agr-plant-balance-p6: Water and nutrients entering through roots

agr-plant-balance.activity: Make four columns for photosynthesis, respiration, transpiration, and water-and-nutrient uptake. Record only what the text confirms about requirements, where each process occurs, and how water or carbohydrates move.

agr-flowering.title: Flower-bud differentiation, day length and low temperature
agr-flowering.objective: Organize the triggers for flower-bud differentiation without confusing short-day and long-day responses with the length of darkness.

paragraphs.agr-flowering-p1: Flower-bud differentiation is the stage when flower buds form after vegetative growth has progressed to some extent. Distinguish the formation of buds from flowers already being open when observing plants.
paragraphs.agr-flowering-p2: Tomato is an example of a crop that differentiates flower buds regularly after reaching a certain stage of growth. Understand this separately from types triggered by changes in the environment.
paragraphs.agr-flowering-p3: In some types, environmental conditions such as temperature and day length affect flower-bud differentiation. Rather than judging from the crop name alone, check which condition is being explained.
paragraphs.agr-flowering-p4: Strawberry and chrysanthemum are examples of short-day plants. Focus on darkness lasting longer than a certain duration, or, in other words, a shorter light period. This explanation does not establish a specific number of hours common to all types.
paragraphs.agr-flowering-p5: Spinach is an example of a long-day plant. In contrast to short-day plants, focus on darkness lasting less than a certain duration. Always check whether “long” refers to darkness or to light.
paragraphs.agr-flowering-p6: Examples of crops whose flower-bud differentiation is induced by exposure to low temperature include daikon, cabbage and broccoli. Day length and low temperature are different conditions, so do not replace every explanation with just one condition.

agr-flowering.activity: Make a comparison table for short-day, long-day and low-temperature responses. Separately explain the length of darkness, the crop examples in the text, and the fact that no specific hours are given.

agr-crop-plan.title: Cropping systems, cultivation patterns and harvest timing
agr-crop-plan.objective: Distinguish a plan for the sequence of crops from a cultivation pattern, and explain earlier and delayed production relative to conventional cultivation.

paragraphs.agr-crop-plan-p1: When considering a cropping system, organize which crops to grow and in what order. It is important to think about how successive crops connect, rather than simply listing crop names.
paragraphs.agr-crop-plan-p2: Understand a cultivation pattern as a combination of variety selection, plans and techniques from sowing through harvest, suited to seasonal and regional conditions. It does not refer only to the day of sowing.
paragraphs.agr-crop-plan-p3: Crops such as cabbage and daikon have spring-, summer- and autumn-sown cultivation patterns. The sowing season and the harvest season are separate information, so record how the two correspond.
paragraphs.agr-crop-plan-p4: In protected cultivation of crops such as tomatoes and cucumbers, advancing growth or harvest compared with conventional open-field cultivation is earlier or forcing cultivation. Explain what the timing is earlier than.
paragraphs.agr-crop-plan-p5: Delayed cultivation postpones growth or harvest relative to conventional cultivation. Do not confuse its name or the direction of the timing arrow with earlier cultivation, which advances them.
paragraphs.agr-crop-plan-p6: In a cultivation-pattern diagram, read the sowing symbols, greenhouse-use span and harvest period separately. Do not treat the example months as a fixed work schedule common to every region and variety in Japan.

paragraphTitles.agr-crop-plan-p1: What to grow and in what order

agr-crop-plan.activity: Use the conventional harvest period as a reference and place earlier and delayed cultivation on opposite sides. Then draw your own explanatory diagram using different symbols for sowing, protected cultivation and harvest.

agr-germination.title: Sowing and the conditions for germination
agr-germination.objective: Distinguish the three conditions for germination, responses to light, direct sowing and thinning.

paragraphs.agr-germination-p1: Sowing means placing seeds in the soil; germination means a seed starts to sprout. Keep the record of the work performed separate from the observed result that sprouts have emerged.
paragraphs.agr-germination-p2: The three conditions needed for germination are water, temperature and oxygen. Seeds also differ in their response to light, but light must not replace oxygen in the list of these three conditions.
paragraphs.agr-germination-p3: Covering seeds with soil after sowing is called soil covering. Understand it as a way to provide germination conditions, and do not assume all seeds should receive the same depth of covering.
paragraphs.agr-germination-p4: Seeds that germinate more readily with light are light-favoured seeds; those that germinate less readily with light are light-inhibited seeds. The material describes thinner covering for the former and thicker covering for the latter. It does not prescribe one fixed depth.
paragraphs.agr-germination-p5: Direct sowing means sowing seeds straight into the field, as with daikon and carrots. Distinguish this from raising seedlings elsewhere before planting them out.
paragraphs.agr-germination-p6: In direct-sown crops, thinning removes surplus seedlings and those affected by pests, disease or abnormal shape, to adjust spacing. It does not mean removing all large seedlings without considering their condition.

agr-germination.activity: Write the three germination conditions from memory, then check the text. Compare light-favoured and light-inhibited seeds and explain why sowing, germination and thinning are different things.

agr-nursery.title: Raising seedlings and transplanting
agr-nursery.objective: Explain the sequence of raising and transplanting seedlings, and compare machine and hand planting.

paragraphTitles.agr-nursery-p4: Time spent in the main field

paragraphs.agr-nursery-p1: Raising seedlings means growing plants from seed in a place separate from the field where they will later grow. The place used is a nursery bed. Distinguish where seeds are sown from where the crop will subsequently be grown.
paragraphs.agr-nursery-p2: A nursery makes it easier to protect seedlings from changes in weather, such as rain and wind, and from diseases and pests. It does not guarantee that pests or disease can never occur.
paragraphs.agr-nursery-p3: An advantage is being able to raise healthy, uniformly developed seedlings efficiently in a relatively small area. It is also necessary to observe differences in their size and growth.
paragraphs.agr-nursery-p4: Growing seedlings elsewhere shortens the period for which that crop occupies the main field. Relate this to field use, such as growing another crop there in the meantime.
paragraphs.agr-nursery-p5: Transplanting means planting the raised seedlings into the field. Suitable seedling development and the spacing between individual plants differ by crop.
paragraphs.agr-nursery-p6: A transplanter can cover a large area quickly, but requires techniques such as preparing uniformly developed seedlings. Hand planting allows careful placement of each plant but takes time and labour. Do not generalize that hand planting has no costs, including labour.

agr-nursery.activity: Draw the movement from the nursery bed to the field and label seedling raising and transplanting. Compare machine and hand planting by speed, seedling uniformity, and time and labour.

agr-crop-types.title: Classifying crops by their uses
agr-crop-types.objective: Organize food, feed, green-manure, industrial and horticultural crops by their uses and the parts used.

paragraphs.agr-crop-types-p1: A crop is a plant cultivated by people. The material distinguishes field crops and horticultural crops. When reading its classification diagram, distinguish the higher-level categories from their subcategories.
paragraphs.agr-crop-types-p2: Rice, wheat or barley, and maize are examples of food crops eaten as staples. This is a classification by use, rather than the names of organs such as leaves and roots.
paragraphs.agr-crop-types-p3: Feed crops are used as livestock feed. Green-manure crops, by contrast, are grown to be incorporated into the soil as fertilizer. Distinguish feeding animals from returning material to the soil.
paragraphs.agr-crop-types-p4: Rapeseed, sesame and cotton are examples of industrial crops supplying materials such as oil and fibre. Do not interpret the Japanese term 工芸 as referring only to finished handicrafts.
paragraphs.agr-crop-types-p5: Horticultural crops include fruit crops, vegetables and ornamental plants. Their uses include not only eating but also enjoying the appearance of flowers, cacti and other plants.
paragraphs.agr-crop-types-p6: The material describes a tendency for field crops to be grown on larger areas with mechanization, while horticulture often includes hard-to-mechanize work and cultivation on smaller areas. These are not absolute boundaries applying to every farm.

agr-crop-types.activity: Make four columns for food, feed, green manure and industrial uses, and draw a separate diagram for the three horticultural categories. Check that use and cultivation scale are not treated as the same classification criterion.

agr-plant-responses.title: Light intensity and water regulation
agr-plant-responses.objective: Explain the limit called the light saturation point and water responses in hot conditions and dry soil.

paragraphTitles.agr-plant-responses-p1: More light is not always better

paragraphs.agr-plant-responses-p1: The level-2 material says that photosynthesis increases with light intensity until the light saturation point is reached. It is important to retain the limiting phrase “until that point is reached”.
paragraphs.agr-plant-responses-p2: This explanation does not mean that increasing light without limit also increases photosynthesis without limit. Recognize that the benefit from increasing light intensity has a limit.
paragraphs.agr-plant-responses-p3: When air temperatures are high or direct sunlight makes plants hot, crops release excess water to prevent their internal temperature from rising too far. Distinguish this release from water uptake by roots.
paragraphs.agr-plant-responses-p4: Transpiration is the release of water vapour through leaf stomata. It is not the name of the work of pouring liquid water onto soil or applying fertilizer.
paragraphs.agr-plant-responses-p5: When dry conditions persist and soil contains little water, plants try to retain water internally. Do not apply the explanation about releasing water in hot conditions to every situation.
paragraphs.agr-plant-responses-p6: The text lets you organize relationships between conditions and responses. It does not determine the optimal illuminance, temperature or irrigation volume for a particular crop. Do not add universal settings where no figures are given.

agr-plant-responses.activity: Use “up to the light saturation point”, “when hot” and “when soil water is scarce” as three headings and describe each response separately. Keep settings not determined by the text in a separate, unresolved category.

agr-sowing-design.title: Sowing patterns and plant and row spacing
agr-sowing-design.objective: Distinguish broadcast, row and spot sowing, the reasons for direct sowing, and plant and row spacing.

paragraphs.agr-sowing-design-p1: Broadcast sowing distributes seed across the whole bed; the material gives onion seedling raising as an example. Keep the stated area of the bed in mind rather than interpreting this as scattering seed randomly anywhere.
paragraphs.agr-sowing-design-p2: Row sowing places seeds in a line along the bed. Carrots are one example given. Draw the arrangement to show that the seed positions form a line.
paragraphs.agr-sowing-design-p3: Spot sowing places several seeds at each location; daikon is an example in the material. It does not mean there must always be exactly one seed at each location.
paragraphs.agr-sowing-design-p4: Taproot crops have roots that grow straight down and can suffer root damage or delayed growth when transplanted, so they are direct-sown. The material gives daikon, carrots, okra and sunflowers as examples.
paragraphs.agr-sowing-design-p5: The material also says short-duration leafy vegetables are often direct-sown. Do not confuse spinach and komatsuna in this group with a classification based solely on having taproots.
paragraphs.agr-sowing-design-p6: A planted line of crops is a row, and row spacing is the distance between rows. Plant spacing is the distance between individual plants. Do not determine crop-specific distances simply by looking at the diagram.

agr-sowing-design.activity: Draw broadcast, row and spot sowing separately using dots and lines. Then draw two rows of seedlings and mark plant spacing and row spacing in different colours to explain the difference.

agr-water-decision.title: Deciding when to irrigate
agr-water-decision.objective: Judge irrigation needs by observing crops and soil, and explain seasonal guidance on timing.

paragraphs.agr-water-decision-p1: Irrigation does not mean applying the same amount simply because a scheduled time has arrived. Observe crop growth and soil conditions, then consider how much water is needed at that time.
paragraphs.agr-water-decision-p2: Water requirements vary with temperature and humidity. Even for the same crop, different environmental conditions change the decision; avoid assuming the amount must always be identical.
paragraphs.agr-water-decision-p3: Excessive watering can cause roots to rot. Even when the aim is healthy growth, increasing the amount of water is not always better.
paragraphs.agr-water-decision-p4: Both materials describe summer irrigation mainly in the morning and evening. Level 1 says during the morning, while Level 2 says early morning. Do not turn this guidance into a fixed time for the whole country.
paragraphs.agr-water-decision-p5: For winter, the guidance is during the morning; Level 2 specifies a warm morning. Retain both the seasonal guidance and the need to judge from the crop and soil.
paragraphs.agr-water-decision-p6: Record crop appearance, soil conditions, temperature and humidity, and irrigation time separately. Explaining the reason for the chosen amount helps avoid decisions based only on the clock.

agr-water-decision.activity: Make separate summer and winter records with four fields: crop, soil, temperature and humidity, and time of day. Confirm that the text gives no universal number of liters or fixed clock time.

agr-water-methods.title: Overhead, plant-base and furrow irrigation
agr-water-methods.objective: Match watering locations with equipment and distinguish three irrigation methods.

paragraphs.agr-water-methods-p1: Organize irrigation methods by where water is applied: above the crop, at its base, or between raised beds. Besides learning equipment names, check where each method delivers water.
paragraphs.agr-water-methods-p2: Overhead irrigation applies water from above the crop. Hoses, sprinkler roses, sprinklers and irrigation tubes are used. Distinguish it from watering only at the plant base.
paragraphs.agr-water-methods-p3: Plant-base irrigation delivers water to the base of the crop. One method uses drip irrigation tubes; the materials explain that this can save water.
paragraphs.agr-water-methods-p4: Furrow irrigation sends water between raised beds. Remember that it requires a large amount of water, rather than confusing it with a method needing only a small amount.
paragraphs.agr-water-methods-p5: Irrigation tubes and drip irrigation tubes have similar names. Check the photographs and labels in the materials to distinguish spraying water from supplying small amounts by dripping.
paragraphs.agr-water-methods-p6: Match a sprinkler photograph with the overhead irrigation explanation, and a drip tube with plant-base irrigation. Use photographs to recognize equipment, without assuming every worksite has the same layout.

agr-water-methods.activity: For each of the three methods, write the watering location, equipment examples in the text and water-use characteristics. Draw a simple location diagram so that plant bases and the spaces between beds are not reversed.

agr-soil-texture.title: Soil texture, nutrient retention and drainage
agr-soil-texture.objective: Explain five clay-content texture classes and differences in nutrient retention and drainage.

paragraphs.agr-soil-texture-p1: The materials divide soil texture into five classes according to the proportion of clay. Do not assume these categories are determined by soil color alone.
paragraphs.agr-soil-texture-p2: From the clay-rich end, the names are clay soil (埴土), clay loam (埴壌土), loam (壌土), sandy loam (砂壌土) and sandy soil (砂土). Read the similar Japanese names while keeping the direction of clay content clear.
paragraphs.agr-soil-texture-p3: Nutrient retention is the ability to hold fertilizer nutrients. The table rates clay soil, clay loam and loam as good, sandy loam as somewhat poor, and sandy soil as poor.
paragraphs.agr-soil-texture-p4: The same table rates drainage as poor for clay soil, somewhat poor for clay loam, and good for loam, sandy loam and sandy soil. High nutrient retention does not necessarily mean good drainage.
paragraphs.agr-soil-texture-p5: Loam and clay loam, containing a suitable combination of sand and clay, are listed as suitable for many crops. Do not change “many” into “necessarily optimal for every crop.”
paragraphs.agr-soil-texture-p6: The materials also show a simple observation: soil that will not hold together when squeezed, soil that holds slightly but cracks, and soil that holds together. This is a rough classification clue, not a precise clay-content measurement.

agr-soil-texture.activity: Arrange the five textures from higher to lower clay content, with separate columns for nutrient retention and drainage. Treat squeezing as an observational guide, distinct from determining exact percentage boundaries.

agr-soil-groups.title: Landforms and major soil groups
agr-soil-groups.objective: Match four soil groups with their distribution, colors and uses in the materials.

paragraphs.agr-soil-groups-p1: For soil groups, focus on distribution by landform and soil-layer characteristics. Keep this information separate from the five texture classes based on clay proportion.
paragraphs.agr-soil-groups-p2: Black volcanic-ash soil (黒ボク土) is described as a black soil layer mainly derived from volcanic ash and rich in humus. Connect these features with its distribution on plateaus and hills.
paragraphs.agr-soil-groups-p3: Brown lowland soil (褐色低地土) is shown on natural levees and similar features of alluvial lowlands, with a yellowish-brown soil layer. Relate this to the example of use as upland fields.
paragraphs.agr-soil-groups-p4: Gray lowland soil (灰色低地土) is described with alluvial fans and plains, a gray soil layer, and use as paddy fields. Sharing “lowland” in the name does not make its features identical to other lowland soils.
paragraphs.agr-soil-groups-p5: Organize gley soil (グライ土) as a combination of depressions in alluvial land, a blue-gray layer and paddy-field use. Do not confuse it with the yellowish-brown of brown lowland soil.
paragraphs.agr-soil-groups-p6: Make a comparison using color, landform and examples of use. These descriptions are learning clues; do not record a field soil as definitively identified from just one color feature.

paragraphTitles.agr-soil-groups-p1: A different view from soil texture

agr-soil-groups.activity: Create rows for black volcanic-ash, brown lowland, gray lowland and gley soils, with columns for landform, color and use. Explain which clues in the materials distinguish them.

agr-soil-structure.title: Soil aggregates and the three soil phases
agr-soil-structure.objective: Distinguish aggregates and the solid, liquid and gas phases without imposing one uniform ratio.

paragraphs.agr-soil-structure-p1: An aggregate is a granular unit formed when several soil particles gather together. Understand this structure separately from the classification called soil texture.
paragraphs.agr-soil-structure-p2: The materials explain that soil rich in aggregates has spaces and properties of aeration, water retention and nutrient retention. Consider retained water together with spaces through which water and air move.
paragraphs.agr-soil-structure-p3: The comparison diagram shows tightly packed particles versus spaces between clusters. Check what is being compared, rather than deciding actual field conditions from a soil name alone.
paragraphs.agr-soil-structure-p4: Soil particles and organic matter form the solid phase, moisture the liquid phase, and air the gas phase. Soil consists of these three, not just solid material.
paragraphs.agr-soil-structure-p5: The balance of the phases affects crop growth. The materials also show differing distributions in black volcanic-ash soil and paddies with high groundwater; they do not say every soil should have identical proportions.
paragraphs.agr-soil-structure-p6: The two materials give different ranges for general reference proportions. In this shared course, learn the phases and soil differences; do not merge conflicting ranges into one prescribed setting.

agr-soil-structure.activity: Group soil particles, organic matter, water and air into the three phases. Draw aggregates and the spaces between them, noting that proportions differ between soils and between the materials.

agr-soil-building.title: Soil productivity and three approaches to improvement
agr-soil-building.objective: Understand soil productivity beyond nutrients, distinguishing tillage, acidity improvement and organic matter replenishment.

paragraphs.agr-soil-building-p1: Soil productivity describes the overall productive capacity arising from soil properties. Do not limit it to containing much fertilizer; consider the combined conditions supporting crop growth.
paragraphs.agr-soil-building-p2: The materials list a thick, soft soil layer, aeration and water retention, appropriate nutrients and acidity, organic matter, and microbial activity. Avoid assuming more of just one factor is sufficient.
paragraphs.agr-soil-building-p3: Tillage turns over soil and helps admit air and soften it. Deep tillage means tilling more deeply. This explanation does not establish one universal depth.
paragraphs.agr-soil-building-p4: Improving acidity to suit the crop is another approach. The materials mention lime and similar materials, but retain the condition of an appropriate amount; do not prescribe the same amount for every field.
paragraphs.agr-soil-building-p5: Supplying compost, organic matter and other soil amendments can improve conditions related to soil microbes and humus. Record physical tillage separately from adding organic matter.
paragraphs.agr-soil-building-p6: Use fields for soil softness, water and air conditions, nutrients and acidity, and organic matter and biological activity. Before choosing an improvement method, identify which property needs attention.

agr-soil-building.activity: Create separate fields for tillage, acidity improvement and organic matter replenishment, and write the soil properties each concerns. Explain without adding depths or application rates the text does not set.

agr-soil-ph-measure.title: Crop-appropriate pH and acidity measurement
agr-soil-ph-measure.objective: Distinguish crop pH guidance, instrument types and the materials’ example of simple measurement.

paragraphs.agr-soil-ph-measure-p1: pH indicates soil acidity. Checking a crop-appropriate range differs from investigating clay proportion. A texture name alone does not determine the pH value.
paragraphs.agr-soil-ph-measure-p2: Both materials’ tables give spinach a reference range of pH6.5–7.0, and tea and blueberry 4.5–5.5. Since ranges differ even within one table, do not apply a single target to all crops.
paragraphs.agr-soil-ph-measure-p3: pH instruments include color-comparison types, soil-insertion types and digital-display types. Despite differences in display or construction, check what the instrument measures.
paragraphs.agr-soil-ph-measure-p4: For the simple instrument in the materials, moisten the soil thoroughly, then insert it so the metal electrode is buried and in close contact with soil. Learn preparation and insertion as separate steps.
paragraphs.agr-soil-ph-measure-p5: The same example says to wait about one minute and read after the value stabilizes. This is an example for the featured simple instrument, not one waiting time prescribed for all models.
paragraphs.agr-soil-ph-measure-p6: Record instrument type, soil preparation and the reading. Since the materials differ in how category thresholds such as acidic soil are expressed, shared-course questions do not treat disputed boundaries as one correct answer.

agr-soil-ph-measure.activity: Write the materials’ pH ranges for spinach and blueberry separately. Then organize the direct-insertion example as “moisten → ensure electrode contact → wait for stability → read.”

agr-soil-rotation.title: Continuous-cropping problems and countermeasure options
agr-soil-rotation.objective: Distinguish continuous-cropping problems, their multiple causes and countermeasures such as crop rotation.

paragraphs.agr-soil-rotation-p1: Growing the same crop continuously in the same field may increase pests and diseases or affect growth and yield. These issues are studied as continuous-cropping problems.
paragraphs.agr-soil-rotation-p2: The materials list increases in soil pathogens and pests such as nematodes, nutrient imbalance and accumulating growth-inhibiting substances. Do not assume the cause is always one particular disease.
paragraphs.agr-soil-rotation-p3: Crop rotation means growing different types of crops in a cycle. Distinguish this from repeatedly planting only the same crop in the same field next year; consider crop types and their sequence together.
paragraphs.agr-soil-rotation-p4: Other measures include using grafted seedlings and disease-resistant cultivars. These concern plant selection and are different from rotation, which changes crops in sequence.
paragraphs.agr-soil-rotation-p5: Soil improvement with compost and soil disinfection are also listed. Do not determine chemicals, amounts or specific operating conditions for disinfection from this introductory explanation alone.
paragraphs.agr-soil-rotation-p6: Practice recording what was grown in each field and when, along with observed growth, pests and diseases. Do not identify a cause from one symptom or guarantee that one measure will solve the problem.

agr-soil-rotation.activity: Create your own example field cropping record and show the difference between continuous cropping and rotation. Separate causes from countermeasures, comparing cultivar selection with soil-directed measures.

agr-water-equipment-2.title: Irrigation equipment and midsummer water temperature
agr-water-equipment-2.objective: Distinguish watering roses, sprinkling tubes and drip tubes by their structure, and explain water-temperature precautions in midsummer.

paragraphs.agr-water-equipment-2-p1: When distinguishing equipment, look beyond its overall colour or length to where and how the water comes out. Match the names in photographs to the mechanisms described.
paragraphs.agr-water-equipment-2-p2: A watering rose has small holes that soften the water flow into a shower. It is described as an attachment for the outlet of a watering can or hose.
paragraphs.agr-water-equipment-2-p3: The irrigation tube in the material has many holes and sprinkles water when water flows through it. Do not assume that every hose carrying water uses the same sprinkling mechanism.
paragraphs.agr-water-equipment-2-p4: A drip-irrigation tube releases drops through drip outlets to supply small amounts evenly. Distinguish water sprinkled through many holes from drops delivered through drip outlets.
paragraphs.agr-water-equipment-2-p5: On midsummer days, water inside hoses or tanks may become hot. The point is to consider the actual water being used, as well as the outside air temperature.
paragraphs.agr-water-equipment-2-p6: For watering roses, sprinkling tubes and drip tubes, explain the installation position together with the way water emerges. Do not add a universal flow rate or safe water temperature that the material does not provide.

paragraphTitles.agr-water-equipment-2-p1: Look at where water comes out
paragraphTitles.agr-water-equipment-2-p6: Link each feature to its equipment

agr-water-equipment-2.activity: Hide the equipment names and identify each item from its water-delivery description alone. Use the conditions in the text to explain why hose and tank water should also be checked in midsummer.

agr-soil-biological-2.title: Physical, chemical and biological factors in soil fertility
agr-soil-biological-2.objective: Organize soil fertility into three factors and distinguish examples of soil microorganisms from soil animals.

paragraphs.agr-soil-biological-2-p1: The Level 2 material divides factors related to soil fertility into physical, chemical and biological factors. Do not explain the soil’s overall productive capacity from just one good or bad property.
paragraphs.agr-soil-biological-2-p2: Difficulty of tillage, drainage and water retention are examples of physical factors. Organize soil softness and the movement of water and air as points to observe.
paragraphs.agr-soil-biological-2-p3: Nutrient-holding capacity, pH and oxidation-reduction potential are listed as chemical factors. Avoid confusing them, for example by treating drainage as another name for pH.
paragraphs.agr-soil-biological-2-p4: Soil microorganisms and soil animals are involved in organic-matter decomposition and nitrogen fixation. Biological factors are not judged simply from soil being dark in colour.
paragraphs.agr-soil-biological-2-p5: The material lists bacteria, actinomycetes, filamentous fungi and algae as soil microorganisms, and nematodes and earthworms as soil animals. Do not give all these different groups of organisms the same name.
paragraphs.agr-soil-biological-2-p6: Microorganisms may antagonize one another or live symbiotically. The material explains that maintaining diversity tends to support a favourable soil environment. Do not simplify this to a guarantee that increasing just one organism always improves fertility.

agr-soil-biological-2.activity: Make a table of the three factors and place water retention, pH and organic-matter decomposition in the appropriate columns. Separate the microorganism and soil-animal examples, and explain why no single organism should be treated as a universal solution.

agr-fertilizer-nutrients.title: The three major fertilizer nutrients and their roles
agr-fertilizer-nutrients.objective: Explain nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium functions without treating nutrient deficiency and excess as the same thing.

paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-nutrients-p1: Soil nutrients alone may not meet the quantity a crop needs. Harvesting also removes nutrients from the field. Consider fertilizers in terms of supplementing shortages.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-nutrients-p2: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are treated as the three major fertilizer nutrients. Bag labels list nitrogen, phosphate and potash in that order, so distinguish element names in plants from the component names used on labels.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-nutrients-p3: Nitrogen is involved in stem and leaf growth, leaf colour, and the formation of substances such as proteins. Wanting more stem and leaf growth does not justify increasing nitrogen without limit.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-nutrients-p4: Excess nitrogen tends to produce weak, soft growth. For deficiency, the Level 1 material mentions yellowing from lower leaves, while Level 2 includes pale leaf colour. These examples alone do not establish a single cause for symptoms in front of you.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-nutrients-p5: Phosphorus is involved in plant activities such as nucleic-acid structure and energy transfer. Organize its roles separately rather than replacing them with nitrogen’s role in stem and leaf growth.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-nutrients-p6: Potassium helps promote reactions within plants and regulate transpiration and osmotic pressure. The three nutrients are not different names for the same thing; each has distinct roles.

agr-fertilizer-nutrients.activity: Make three columns for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium and record the roles confirmed in the text. Put nitrogen deficiency and excess in separate columns, and explain why symptom examples are not the same as a definite diagnosis of their cause.

agr-fertilizer-types.title: Classifying fertilizers by materials, nutrients and state
agr-fertilizer-types.objective: Explain chemical and organic fertilizers, compost, single-nutrient and compound fertilizers, and liquid fertilizers using their respective classification criteria.

paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-types-p1: Chemically synthesized fertilizers are called chemical fertilizers, also termed inorganic fertilizers. Many act quickly, but their name alone does not mean that they all act at the same speed.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-types-p2: A single-nutrient fertilizer contains one of the three major nutrients; a compound fertilizer contains two or more. Count the types among those three nutrients, not every substance written on the bag.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-types-p3: Compound fertilizers include chemically manufactured compound fertilizers and blended fertilizers. The material describes blends as mainly mixtures of single-nutrient fertilizers. Keep the explanation of mixing materials separate from classification by the number of major nutrients.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-types-p4: Organic fertilizers are made from organic materials of animal or plant origin. Examples include fish meal or residues, rapeseed cake and bone meal. This classification concerns raw materials, rather than physical forms such as liquid or granules.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-types-p5: Compost can be made by piling and fermenting livestock manure, fallen leaves or rice straw. It has both soil-improvement and fertilizer effects; do not consider only one of these roles.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-types-p6: Liquid fertilizer is in liquid form when applied. This includes not just products originally sold as liquids, but powders or granules dissolved into liquid. Distinguish the original form from the state at application.

agr-fertilizer-types.activity: Head a classification table “raw materials,” “types of major nutrients” and “state at application.” Check that one fertilizer can be described using several terms based on different criteria.

agr-fertilizer-release.title: When fertilizer starts working and how long it lasts
agr-fertilizer-release.objective: Distinguish quick-acting, slow-release and delayed-acting fertilizers by the onset and duration of their effects.

paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-release-p1: When comparing fertilizers, distinguish time until effects begin from how long those effects continue. Similar materials or forms do not necessarily mean the same pattern of action.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-release-p2: Quick-acting fertilizer shows effects soon after application. The material describes a short duration of effect and gives liquid fertilizers and chemically manufactured compound fertilizers as examples, but individual product characteristics must also be checked.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-release-p3: Slow-release fertilizers have long-lasting effects. Examples include coated fertilizers and products with controlled nutrient dissolution. This does not mean every product lasts for the same period.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-release-p4: Delayed-acting fertilizers take time after application before effects appear. They include organic fertilizers that undergo microbial decomposition, with rapeseed cake and bone meal given as examples.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-release-p5: Powder, granules, pellets and liquid describe appearance or the state at application. Do not decide action from form alone, such as assuming granules are always slow-release or powder always delayed-acting.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-release-p6: Compare quick-acting, slow-release and delayed-acting fertilizers using separate columns for onset, duration and examples in the material. Do not memorize the years given for one long-lasting product as a period common to all fertilizers.

paragraphTitles.agr-fertilizer-release-p5: Form and action are separate information

agr-fertilizer-release.activity: Create a comparison table for the three fertilizer types, with separate columns for onset and duration. Also list the four form descriptions and explain how their classification criteria differ from those based on action.

agr-fertilizer-timing.title: Basal fertilizer, top-dressing and excessive application
agr-fertilizer-timing.objective: Distinguish basal and additional fertilizer timing, and explain why seed or root contact and high salt concentrations require attention.

paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-timing-p1: Fertilizer application means giving fertilizer to crops. Consider not only the product but also the crop, growth stage, timing and quantity together.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-timing-p2: Fertilizer applied before planting is basal fertilizer, called motogoe or kihi in Japanese. The material describes mainly using slow-release products. “Basal” itself does not describe fertilizer form.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-timing-p3: Top-dressing is additional fertilizer applied according to crop growth and other conditions. Quick-acting products such as compound and liquid fertilizers are examples in the material. Applying basal fertilizer does not mean every crop will never need additional fertilizer.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-timing-p4: The material warns against direct fertilizer contact with seeds or roots because plants may die. Do not generalize this into placing fertilizer in a heap over seeds without checking components or the application method.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-timing-p5: Excessive fertilizer can raise salt concentration in soil and harm crop growth. Applying more than required does not always improve growth.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-timing-p6: Fertilizer quantities follow crop-specific application standards. Electrical conductivity, or EC, is a clue to soil salt conditions. One value alone cannot determine the same quantity regardless of crop or measurement conditions.

agr-fertilizer-timing.activity: Place basal fertilizer and top-dressing on a cultivation timeline. Below it, separately list seed/root contact, excess fertilizer, EC and crop-specific standards, and explain the problem with simply increasing the amount.

agr-fertilizer-label.title: Fertilizer-bag percentages and nutrient weights
agr-fertilizer-label.objective: Use component order, percentages and bag weight to calculate nutrient weights in a hypothetical example.

paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-label-p1: Read the three fertilizer-bag figures as percentages of nitrogen, phosphate and potash, in that order. They are component percentages, not those same numbers of kilograms contained in the bag.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-label-p2: For calculation practice, assume a fertilizer labelled “12-6-6” in a 25kg bag. These conditions are invented for the exercise and are not instructions to apply one bag to a particular crop.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-label-p3: To find a component’s weight, multiply the total fertilizer weight by its percentage divided by 100. In this example, nitrogen is 25 × 12 ÷ 100 = 3kg.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-label-p4: In the same hypothetical example, phosphate is 25 × 6 ÷ 100 = 1.5kg, and potash is also 25 × 6 ÷ 100 = 1.5kg. Calculate each using its own percentage without confusing the components.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-label-p5: The material classifies chemically manufactured compound fertilizers containing at least two major nutrients with a combined total of 30% or more as high-analysis, and below 30% as ordinary. The example totals 24%, so under these conditions it is ordinary.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-label-p6: Record percentages as % and component weights as kg. Changing bag weight changes component weight even at the same percentage, but does not make the percentage itself change with bag size.

paragraphTitles.agr-fertilizer-label-p4: Calculate other nutrients the same way

agr-fertilizer-label.activity: Calculate the three component weights from the learning example “12-6-6, 25kg.” Then change the assumed bag weight to 50kg and check how weights change while percentages stay the same.

agr-fertilizer-quantity.title: Finding fertilizer quantity from a required nutrient quantity
agr-fertilizer-quantity.objective: Calculate total fertilizer weight from required nutrient weight and nutrient percentage while preserving area and units.

paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-quantity-p1: The kilograms of nutrient required and the kilograms of total fertilizer to apply are different quantities. Link them using the percentage of that component in the fertilizer.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-quantity-p2: Find the required fertilizer quantity by dividing the required nutrient quantity by the component percentage and multiplying by 100. Do not mix entering a percentage number with entering its decimal equivalent.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-quantity-p3: As a calculation-only example, assume a given area needs 4kg of a component and that the fertilizer contains 16% of it. Fertilizer quantity is 4 ÷ 16 × 100 = 25kg. These figures are not actual crop application standards.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-quantity-p4: The 25kg of fertilizer contains 16% of the component, so 25 × 16 ÷ 100 = 4kg. Checking that the reverse calculation returns the original requirement helps detect errors such as forgetting the factor of 100.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-quantity-p5: If an application standard is stated per specified area, the calculated quantity also applies to that area. Do not copy it unchanged as the quantity for a different area.
paragraphs.agr-fertilizer-quantity-p6: When fertilizer contains several components, calculating one does not resolve shortages or excesses of the others. Distinguish calculated quantity from an application decision suited to crop and soil conditions.

agr-fertilizer-quantity.activity: Use the hypothetical requirement of 4kg and content of 16% to calculate fertilizer quantity, then reverse the calculation. Include a reference-area field and record nutrient quantity, fertilizer quantity and area separately.

agr-drainage-foundations.title: Drainage using open ditches and raised beds
agr-drainage-foundations.objective: Distinguish the roles of open ditches and beds, when beds are formed, and conditions for high beds.

paragraphs.agr-drainage-foundations-p1: Consider separately drainage near the field surface and methods that make water move more easily within the soil. Identifying where the water being addressed is located helps distinguish methods.
paragraphs.agr-drainage-foundations-p2: Open-ditch drainage places grooves or channels on the field surface to carry excess water away. They are laid out with water flow in mind; this does not mean digging an identical groove anywhere will work.
paragraphs.agr-drainage-foundations-p3: A raised bed is a growing bed formed by mounding soil. It aims to improve drainage and aeration; do not treat mounding itself as the objective and ignore water movement around it.
paragraphs.agr-drainage-foundations-p4: Bed formation is done before sowing or planting seedlings. The material describes high beds for fields with a high groundwater level, but gives no one height that applies to all fields.
paragraphs.agr-drainage-foundations-p5: Ridge width, ridge height, spacing between ridges and bed width refer to different dimensions. In a diagram, separate horizontal width, vertical height and the gap between neighbouring ridges.
paragraphs.agr-drainage-foundations-p6: Hand work uses tools such as hoes, while machine work attaches bed-forming equipment to tractors or cultivators. This describes different methods and does not permit omitting machine-specific operating procedures or safety checks.

agr-drainage-foundations.activity: Draw open ditches on a simple field plan and high and flat beds in a separate cross-section. Colour-code bed width, height and spacing, using the drawing to explain terms rather than prescribe construction dimensions.

agr-drainage-comparison.title: Drainage methods, field workability and installation
agr-drainage-comparison.objective: Compare where open ditches, subsurface drains, subsoil breaking and orchard mounding act and the constraints of each.

paragraphs.agr-drainage-comparison-p1: Open ditches improve drainage near the surface but create grooves between crops. The Level 2 material notes that, while improving water flow, they may reduce ease of field work.
paragraphs.agr-drainage-comparison-p2: Subsurface drainage uses pipes buried in soil. The material describes protecting pipes with well-draining material before backfilling. Understand their structural difference from an open surface ditch.
paragraphs.agr-drainage-comparison-p3: The Level 2 material compares subsurface drains as making surface work easier while costing more to install. Organize field use and installation burdens as separate aspects, alongside drainage effect.
paragraphs.agr-drainage-comparison-p4: Subsoil breaking uses machinery to fracture hardpan or subsoil so water can move more easily. Burying drainpipes and fracturing a soil layer are different operations.
paragraphs.agr-drainage-comparison-p5: For fruit trees, the material describes ridgelike soil mounds with water flowing between them, or planting on raised soil around the tree base. The area improved may be limited, so do not assume the same effect as improving drainage across the entire field.
paragraphs.agr-drainage-comparison-p6: In a comparison table, separately record whether a method acts at the surface or underground, its workability, installation burden and extent of improvement. Do not turn the depth in an installation example into a design value for every field.

agr-drainage-comparison.activity: List the four drainage methods in a table and record location, workability, installation burden and area improved. Leave depths and dimensions blank when the text does not determine them, and distinguish learning comparisons from actual construction design.

agr-management-shoots.title: Distinguishing pinching, side-shoot removal and leaf removal
agr-management-shoots.objective: Distinguish their purposes by identifying the part removed.

paragraphTitles.agr-management-shoots-p6: Match the work to the part

paragraphs.agr-management-shoots-p1: Pinching removes the tip of a stem. It is one way to shape the crop and distribute nutrients to leaves and fruit. Distinguish cutting the tip from removing leaves along the stem.
paragraphs.agr-management-shoots-p2: A side shoot emerges at the base of a leaf. Side-shoot removal means removing that shoot. The main stem tip and a shoot at a leaf base are in different positions.
paragraphs.agr-management-shoots-p3: Removing side shoots helps prevent excessive foliage and too many fruit, and improves light exposure. It does not mean removing every bud regardless of its position.
paragraphs.agr-management-shoots-p4: Leaf removal may target diseased or overcrowded leaves. Reducing leaf numbers is not the goal in itself; relate the work to improved ventilation and light.
paragraphs.agr-management-shoots-p5: A well-shaped crop is easier to care for and harvest. Be able to explain both what is removed and why it makes management easier.
paragraphs.agr-management-shoots-p6: Pinching mainly targets the tip, side-shoot removal targets side shoots, and leaf removal targets leaves. Locate the part on the plant or diagram before matching the work name. This introduction does not specify crop-specific cutting points or leaf numbers.

agr-management-shoots.activity: Draw a stem and leaves and mark the stem tip, leaf bases and crowded leaves. Match the three work names, explaining the removal location separately from its purpose.

agr-management-thinning.title: Bud, flower and fruit thinning
agr-management-thinning.objective: Distinguish buds, flowers and fruit by development stage, and explain how thinning affects retained fruit.

paragraphs.agr-management-thinning-p1: Removing buds is bud thinning, removing flowers is flower thinning, and removing fruit is fruit thinning. All involve removal, but target different developmental stages.
paragraphs.agr-management-thinning-p2: When too many buds, flowers or fruit develop, their numbers are adjusted. Do not assume that greater numbers always produce the desired quality.
paragraphs.agr-management-thinning-p3: Fruit affected by disease or pests, or with abnormal shape, may also be removed during thinning. Understand the work as judging each fruit’s condition, not only counting them.
paragraphs.agr-management-thinning-p4: Adjusting fruit numbers helps concentrate nutrients and water in the fruit retained. Relate this to the goal of producing good-quality fruit.
paragraphs.agr-management-thinning-p5: Fruit thinning is common in fruit trees but also used in vegetables such as watermelon, melon and tomato. It also concerns vegetables harvested for their fruit.
paragraphs.agr-management-thinning-p6: This general explanation cannot set one number of fruit to retain or one work date for every crop. First organize the target, condition and purpose, then proceed to crop-specific management.

agr-management-thinning.activity: Draw buds, open flowers and fruit as three stages, and label the corresponding thinning operations. Explain fruit removal in terms of nutrients and water for the fruit retained.

agr-management-pollination.title: Pollination and assisted pollination
agr-management-pollination.objective: Identify where pollen lands and explain examples of hand pollination and flower-visiting insects.

paragraphs.agr-management-pollination-p1: Pollination occurs when pollen reaches the stigma of the pistil. Do not confuse this location with a leaf or stem surface.
paragraphs.agr-management-pollination-p2: Where natural pollination is difficult, people apply pollen by hand. Organize the process by following where the pollen moves from and to.
paragraphs.agr-management-pollination-p3: In greenhouses, insects such as honeybees and bumblebees may be used. Distinguish direct application by a person from using insect activity.
paragraphs.agr-management-pollination-p4: The material says honeybees are mainly used to pollinate strawberries. Do not extend this example into a claim that the same insect suits every crop under identical conditions.
paragraphs.agr-management-pollination-p5: The material gives watermelon, melon and squash as examples where hand pollination is used to support reliable fruit set. Learn the crop examples together with this purpose.
paragraphs.agr-management-pollination-p6: A record that hand pollination was performed differs from observing fruit formation afterwards. This introduction neither applies one procedure or time to every flower nor guarantees that every flower will set fruit.

agr-management-pollination.activity: Draw the pistil’s stigma and pollen movement. Make separate columns for hand pollination and insect use, and match the crop examples in the material.

agr-management-training.title: Arranging branches through pruning and training
agr-management-training.objective: Distinguish arranging branch numbers and positions from guiding branches.

paragraphs.agr-management-training-p1: Pruning and shaping arrange branch numbers and positions according to crop growth, flowering and characteristics. They do not mean cutting every branch into the same form.
paragraphs.agr-management-training-p2: Well-arranged branches make care and harvesting easier. This management considers whether the form suits crop growth as well as whether work is convenient.
paragraphs.agr-management-training-p3: Training guides branches toward suitable positions. It is not only removing branches; it also concerns how the branches retained are supported.
paragraphs.agr-management-training-p4: Training helps prevent plants falling over and branches crowding, improving light and ease of care. Observe both supports and branch directions.
paragraphs.agr-management-training-p5: For tomatoes, eggplants and cucumbers, main and side branches are tied to supports or tape. In the material’s fastening example, string forms a figure eight between support and stem.
paragraphs.agr-management-training-p6: The number of branches retained and where they are guided depend on crop characteristics. Here, distinguish pruning/shaping from training rather than applying one form to every crop.

agr-management-training.activity: Draw one diagram changing branch numbers and positions, and another guiding a retained branch toward a support. Label pruning/shaping and training and note their effects on light and care.

agr-management-harvest.title: Harvest maturity and precooling
agr-management-harvest.objective: Distinguish crop-specific harvest indicators and explain precooling as cooling to retain freshness.

paragraphs.agr-management-harvest-p1: Harvesting means collecting a crop that has been grown. The appropriate stage must be recognized; not all crops are judged by identical appearance or size.
paragraphs.agr-management-harvest-p2: The material’s examples use colouring for tomatoes, plant height for spinach, and fruit length for cucumbers. Organize each indicator with its crop.
paragraphs.agr-management-harvest-p3: Vegetables, flowers and fruit crops are often harvested by hand, while mechanization has advanced for crops such as carrots and potatoes. Tools and machines vary with the crop and produce.
paragraphs.agr-management-harvest-p4: Precooling is cooling harvested vegetables and fruit. Its purpose is retaining freshness; it is a different stage from deciding harvest maturity.
paragraphs.agr-management-harvest-p5: Early-morning harvesting is related to cooling produce. Do not assume it has the same conditions as harvesting at hot midday; relate heat at harvest to subsequent cooling.
paragraphs.agr-management-harvest-p6: Precooling methods include using air and using a vacuum. The text gives no single cooling temperature or duration, so do not prescribe identical values for every crop.

agr-management-harvest.activity: Match tomato, spinach and cucumber with their harvest indicators. Arrange harvesting and precooling in order and explain their different purposes.

agr-cover-methods.title: Low tunnels and floating covers
agr-cover-methods.objective: Distinguish tunnel-shaped covering from material placed directly on or just above the crop.

paragraphs.agr-cover-methods-p1: Covering methods differ in position and support. Besides material names, observe where the cover lies relative to crops and beds.
paragraphs.agr-cover-methods-p2: Low tunnels use supports and covering material to form a tunnel over a bed. Relate the structure to retaining warmth and protection against wind, rain and pests.
paragraphs.agr-cover-methods-p3: Tunnel materials include film, nonwoven fabric, shade cloth and insect netting. They do not all work identically; organize them by purposes such as warmth retention or pest protection.
paragraphs.agr-cover-methods-p4: Floating covers touch the crop directly or sit only slightly above it. Their position differs from material raised by supports into a tunnel.
paragraphs.agr-cover-methods-p5: Floating covers can stabilize germination and improve early growth. They also relate to protection from wind, rain and pests; nonwoven fabric and shade cloth are examples.
paragraphs.agr-cover-methods-p6: Covering does not mean every pest is excluded or all management becomes unnecessary in every weather condition. Distinguish method, material and purpose, and relate them to managing each crop.

agr-cover-methods.activity: Draw beds, crops and covers as lines and compare tunnel and floating-cover positions. Record material examples and purposes in separate columns.

agr-cover-mulch.title: Mulch materials and colours
agr-cover-mulch.objective: Organize ground-covering mulch and colour differences affecting soil temperature and weed control.

paragraphTitles.agr-cover-mulch-p6: Material names do not decide disposal

paragraphs.agr-cover-mulch-p1: Mulching covers the soil surface with materials such as rice straw or plastic film. Unlike a floating cover above the crop, it covers a different target.
paragraphs.agr-cover-mulch-p2: Mulch can regulate soil temperature and reduce losses of water and fertilizer. It also relates to keeping soil soft and managing weeds, disease and pests.
paragraphs.agr-cover-mulch-p3: In the material’s comparison, clear film strongly raises soil temperature, while green film has properties intermediate between clear and black. Different colours should not be treated as identical.
paragraphs.agr-cover-mulch-p4: White film is associated with suppressing soil-temperature rises, and black film with suppressing weeds. Distinguish the purpose of warming soil from weed control.
paragraphs.agr-cover-mulch-p5: Silver film uses light reflection. White/black two-layer films and perforated films with planting holes also exist, so both colour and structure matter when selecting materials.
paragraphs.agr-cover-mulch-p6: Biodegradability can reduce disposal work after use, but does not mean material may be left anywhere. Check actual disposal procedures and applicable rules separately from this property.

agr-cover-mulch.activity: Draw where soil is covered and tabulate the purposes of clear, white, black and silver films. Treat material properties and disposal after use as separate checks.

agr-pest-foundation.title: Management that discourages pests and disease
agr-pest-foundation.objective: Explain prevention, early detection and differences between non-pesticide control methods.

paragraphs.agr-pest-foundation-p1: Pest and disease management starts with making conditions less favourable, not only treating problems after they appear. Connect observing the growing environment with checking damage.
paragraphs.agr-pest-foundation-p2: Detecting and responding before pests and disease spread is important. Do not decide the cause from one visual sign alone; also organize where it occurs and how it spreads.
paragraphs.agr-pest-foundation-p3: Methods include using crop characteristics and growing conditions, such as choosing disease-resistant varieties. Do not extend a stated effect of a particular plant to every pest or field.
paragraphs.agr-pest-foundation-p4: Some methods use insects or microorganisms that prey on pests or kill them through parasitism. Distinguish organisms harming crops from their natural enemies.
paragraphs.agr-pest-foundation-p5: Reflective materials, sticky materials and insect nets are other methods. Excluding pests differs in mechanism from attracting and trapping them.
paragraphs.agr-pest-foundation-p6: Fungicides used to prevent or control disease target something different from insecticides for insect pests. Understanding these categories alone does not determine the product, concentration or application frequency.

agr-pest-foundation.activity: Make five columns: prevention, early detection, varieties, natural enemies and materials. Explain each method’s target and mechanism within the text’s scope.

agr-pest-weeds.title: Weed seeds and weed-control methods
agr-pest-weeds.objective: Distinguish preventing seed increase, blocking light, inter-row cultivation, earthing up and tillage.

paragraphs.agr-pest-weeds-p1: A basic principle is preventing weed seeds from entering fields. Consider seeds that cause later emergence as well as removing existing weeds.
paragraphs.agr-pest-weeds-p2: Cut or pull weeds early, before they shed seed. Relate the work not just to visible weeds but to reducing later emergence.
paragraphs.agr-pest-weeds-p3: Mulching with material that blocks light is one weed-control method. Do not assume all covers, including transparent materials, provide the same light-blocking effect.
paragraphs.agr-pest-weeds-p4: Inter-row cultivation works the soil between beds; earthing up moves soil toward the plant base. Both involve soil, but differ in where and how it is moved.
paragraphs.agr-pest-weeds-p5: The material also describes tillage in a field without a crop. Do not apply the same operation where crops are growing without checking that condition.
paragraphs.agr-pest-weeds-p6: Chemicals used for weeds are herbicides. Methods using brush cutters or mowers also exist. Knowing method names is different from learning product conditions or machine operation.

agr-pest-weeds.activity: Group methods into preventing seed increase, blocking light and moving soil. Draw inter-row cultivation and earthing up separately, showing where the soil moves.

agr-pest-ipm.title: Combining methods in IPM
agr-pest-ipm.objective: Distinguish IPM’s purpose and cultural, physical, biological and chemical approaches.

paragraphs.agr-pest-ipm-p1: IPM combines suitable options from available control techniques to suppress increases in pests, disease and weeds. It does not mean continually using one method in every situation.
paragraphs.agr-pest-ipm-p2: The material aims to reduce chemical pesticide amounts while limiting economic losses. The aim is not simply never using any pesticide or reducing every organism to zero.
paragraphs.agr-pest-ipm-p3: Varieties, cultivation methods and field conditions can be adjusted to discourage disease and pests. Relate crop rotation, resistant varieties and clearing dead branches or fallen leaves to this approach.
paragraphs.agr-pest-ipm-p4: Physical approaches use light, heat, tools and materials. For reflective or sticky materials and insect netting, distinguish what is used and how it acts on pests.
paragraphs.agr-pest-ipm-p5: Biological approaches include natural-enemy insects or microorganisms and sex pheromones. Mating disruption uses artificial sex pheromones to interfere with mating and reduce the next pest generation.
paragraphs.agr-pest-ipm-p6: Pesticide use is positioned separately from other approaches. Identify differences between disease, insect and weed targets, and then check each product’s conditions of use separately.

agr-pest-ipm.activity: Make a table of four approaches and classify rotation, insect nets, natural enemies and pesticides. Explain how choosing one method all the time differs from combining methods in IPM.

agr-safety-machine-preparation.title: Checks before using a machine
agr-safety-machine-preparation.objective: Explain checks of starting, stopping and braking as preparation for work, including fatigue and clothing.

paragraphTitles.agr-safety-machine-preparation-p2: Check more than how to start
paragraphTitles.agr-safety-machine-preparation-p3: Do not transfer procedures to another machine
paragraphTitles.agr-safety-machine-preparation-p5: Clothing that is less likely to become caught

paragraphs.agr-safety-machine-preparation-p1: Do not learn to operate an unfamiliar agricultural machine by running it. Before starting work, understand how to operate that machine by reading its instruction manual and other relevant instructions.
paragraphs.agr-safety-machine-preparation-p2: Check not only how to start the engine but also how to operate the brake and stop the engine. Treat being able to start moving and being able to stop safely as a pair.
paragraphs.agr-safety-machine-preparation-p3: The source gives examples of cultivators and brush cutters, but machines that look alike do not necessarily have identical controls or procedures. Do not use this course as a starting procedure that applies to every model.
paragraphs.agr-safety-machine-preparation-p4: Fatigue makes it harder to maintain attention and increases the danger of machine work. Avoid operating machinery when tired and take appropriate breaks. Do not operate machinery after drinking alcohol.
paragraphs.agr-safety-machine-preparation-p5: Choose clothing suitable for the work so that it does not become caught in machinery or belts. Check that protective equipment suits the task and machine; do not recommend the gloves in an illustration indiscriminately for work with all rotating machinery.
paragraphs.agr-safety-machine-preparation-p6: Use separate checklist fields for understanding the controls, stopping, physical condition and clothing. Do not assume that getting the machine to run once makes everything safe while some controls remain unclear. Confirm instructions and guidance appropriate to that machine.

agr-safety-machine-preparation.activity: For a machine you plan to learn to use, make checklist fields for starting, braking, stopping, physical condition and clothing. Leave model-specific operations not determined by the text as items to check in the instruction manual.

agr-safety-inspection-stop.title: Daily inspections and tasks performed with the engine stopped
agr-safety-inspection-stop.objective: Distinguish inspections before, during and after operation from stopping the engine to clear blockages or interrupt work.

paragraphTitles.agr-safety-inspection-stop-p4: Stop even for a temporary interruption

paragraphs.agr-safety-inspection-stop-p1: Daily inspections help maintain machine performance, extend its service life and prevent agricultural accidents. They are not something to do only after a breakdown has stopped the machine.
