paragraphs.agr-safety-inspection-stop-p2: The source describes checking for abnormalities before, during and after operation. Keep these situations separate and record what was checked and when.
paragraphs.agr-safety-inspection-stop-p3: The source explains that the engine must be stopped for inspections other than operational checks while running. Do not interpret this as permission to approach a moving machine and put a hand inside to check it.
paragraphs.agr-safety-inspection-stop-p4: Stop the engine even when interrupting machine work temporarily. Do not omit the stopping check just because you expect to return immediately.
paragraphs.agr-safety-inspection-stop-p5: The engine must also be stopped before clearing a blockage in a machine. Do not extend the exception for operational checks while running to this clearing task.
paragraphs.agr-safety-inspection-stop-p6: Use separate checklist fields for types of inspection, clearing blockages and interrupting work. Saying that the machine has stopped does not mean all its hazards have disappeared; check the instruction manual for its specific safety requirements.

agr-safety-inspection-stop.activity: Separate cards for inspection before operation, operational checks while running, clearing blockages and temporary interruptions. Explain when stopping is required and why the operational-check exception does not extend to clearing material by hand.

agr-safety-pesticide-clothing.title: Clothing and protective equipment for pesticide work
agr-safety-pesticide-clothing.objective: Explain how to prevent pesticides reaching the body or getting inside clothing, and how to check protective equipment suitable for the task.

paragraphTitles.agr-safety-pesticide-clothing-p2: Match equipment to the body part
paragraphTitles.agr-safety-pesticide-clothing-p3: Protection begins with measuring and preparation

paragraphs.agr-safety-pesticide-clothing-p1: Pesticide work requires clothing that prevents the chemical from reaching the skin and other parts of the body. Do not assume that ordinary fieldwork clothing is suitable for every chemical.
paragraphs.agr-safety-pesticide-clothing-p2: Examples in the source include a hat, protective clothing for pesticide work, boots, a mask, goggles and gloves. Match them to the head, body, feet, breathing area, eyes and hands they protect.
paragraphs.agr-safety-pesticide-clothing-p3: The source illustrations show masks being worn during measuring and preparation as well as spraying. In actual work, choose protective equipment that matches the pesticide label; do not prepare it only at the moment spraying begins.
paragraphs.agr-safety-pesticide-clothing-p4: The source shows sleeves of protective clothing worn over gloves and trouser legs over boots. Connect the overlap shown in the illustration with its purpose: keeping pesticide liquid out of clothing and footwear.
paragraphs.agr-safety-pesticide-clothing-p5: The explanation of pesticide work says not to use cotton work gloves that become wet. However, the name rubber gloves alone does not guarantee suitability for all chemicals. Check that gloves match the product label and working conditions.
paragraphs.agr-safety-pesticide-clothing-p6: Protective equipment for pesticides addresses different hazards from clothing intended to prevent entanglement in agricultural machinery. Do not assume equipment used for one task can be transferred unconditionally to another.

agr-safety-pesticide-clothing.activity: Match protective equipment to body parts and check both measuring/preparation and spraying stages. Draw how sleeves and trouser legs overlap the gloves and boots, and explain how this helps keep pesticide liquid out.

agr-safety-pesticide-label.title: Checking the label before use and keeping use records
agr-safety-pesticide-label.objective: Check pesticide concentration, quantity, timing and number of applications together, and distinguish use records from storage checks.

paragraphs.agr-safety-pesticide-label-p1: Before using a pesticide, check the label of the product you will use. Remembering its name alone does not establish that the crop and conditions of use are the same.
paragraphs.agr-safety-pesticide-label-p2: Both the concentration used and the quantity applied must be checked. Do not alter the specified conditions because you think a stronger mixture will work better or because you have some left over.
paragraphs.agr-safety-pesticide-label-p3: Check the timing of use and the permitted number of applications too. Having used the product once before does not mean the conditions for subsequent use have already been checked.
paragraphs.agr-safety-pesticide-label-p4: This material does not replace a product’s current registration details or specify its conditions of use. When using a particular product, check the labeling that applies to that product and crop.
paragraphs.agr-safety-pesticide-label-p5: The source describes entries in a pesticide use log. Reading the conditions before use and recording what was actually used are separate checks; do not do only one of them.
paragraphs.agr-safety-pesticide-label-p6: The source describes storing pesticides in a dedicated place that can be locked. This introduction does not set uniform legal requirements for categories, signs or facilities. Organize use-record checks separately from storage checks.

agr-safety-pesticide-label.activity: Make a sample checklist with fields for concentration, quantity, timing, number of applications, use records and storage location. Without entering actual product names or values, explain which fields must be checked against the real label.

agr-safety-spray-check.title: Spraying equipment, drift and cleanup
agr-safety-spray-check.objective: Check equipment connections and weather, and organize precautions against drift and the work needed after spraying.

paragraphs.agr-safety-spray-check-p1: Check sprayer connections, including the nozzle and nozzle pipe. In addition to looseness, distinguish abnormalities in the illustrated gaskets and damage to the fastening bands as separate inspection items.
paragraphs.agr-safety-spray-check-p2: Drift means sprayed pesticide moving into surrounding areas. Even when aiming at the crop, you must still consider the possibility of pesticide spreading beyond it.
paragraphs.agr-safety-spray-check-p3: The source says to work on days with light wind and stop when the wind is strong. Do not assume the wind always comes from the same direction; check conditions where you are working.
paragraphs.agr-safety-spray-check-p4: Do not spray during rain or immediately before or after rainfall. The source recommends working in the cool morning or evening where possible. Do not turn this into a universal waiting interval or fixed time of day for every pesticide.
paragraphs.agr-safety-spray-check-p5: The source explains washing the equipment after spraying and cleaning up, including washing hands. The specific disposal method for leftover spray and wash water must be checked for the product and worksite; this is not permission to discharge them into waterways.
paragraphs.agr-safety-spray-check-p6: Take appropriate breaks during long periods of work. If you feel dizziness, nausea or other abnormalities during or after spraying, stop working and promptly seek examination by a doctor. Do not spray more than the label permits to reduce leftover liquid; check the disposal method separately.

agr-safety-spray-check.activity: Make separate fields for sprayer connections, wind, rain and equipment after work, and write what to check. Explain why spraying beyond the label limits or discharging liquid into waterways is not a solution.

agr-safety-power-fuel.title: Avoiding assumptions about power and fuel
agr-safety-power-fuel.objective: Check compatibility of power supplies and fuels, and distinguish hazards such as wet hands, ignition sources and running engines during refueling.

paragraphTitles.agr-safety-power-fuel-p2: Do not handle with wet hands
paragraphTitles.agr-safety-power-fuel-p6: Check legal and model requirements separately

paragraphs.agr-safety-power-fuel-p1: The source gives 100-volt alternating current and 200-volt three-phase alternating current as examples of agricultural power supplies. Seeing an example voltage or shape is different from confirming compatibility with the machine in front of you.
paragraphs.agr-safety-power-fuel-p2: Handling an electrical plug with wet hands can cause electric shock. Touching distribution boards or incoming power lines with bare hands is also identified as dangerous. Do not test whether they can be used by touching them.
paragraphs.agr-safety-power-fuel-p3: Machines use different fuels, such as gasoline, diesel, kerosene and premixed fuel. Do not put in the same fuel merely because the machine resembles one you have seen before.
paragraphs.agr-safety-power-fuel-p4: Refuel with the engine stopped. Do not add an exception allowing the engine to keep running for a quick top-up.
paragraphs.agr-safety-power-fuel-p5: During refueling, check that there are no ignition sources nearby, and take care not to spill fuel or overflow the tank. Checking the fuel type and checking the refueling location are separate items.
paragraphs.agr-safety-power-fuel-p6: Do not use this general introduction alone to decide container capacity or material, premix ratios or storage procedures for individual machines. Treat product specifications, model instructions and current applicable requirements as separate checks.

agr-safety-power-fuel.activity: Make fields for supply compatibility and wet conditions for electricity, and fuel type, stopping, ignition sources and spills for fuel. Keep mixing ratios and legal storage-container conditions that the text does not determine as separate checks.

agr-safety-maintenance-tools.title: Distinguishing maintenance tools by shape and use
agr-safety-maintenance-tools.objective: Distinguish maintenance tools by name and construction, and explain inspection, care and storage as a connected sequence of work.

paragraphTitles.agr-safety-maintenance-tools-p3: Double open-ended spanner and ring spanner

paragraphs.agr-safety-maintenance-tools-p1: Consider tool inspection before use, care after use and storage together. Even if tools look alike, check whether their construction fits the bolt or screw being worked on.
paragraphs.agr-safety-maintenance-tools-p2: The socket and handle are separate, allowing a socket suited to the fastener to be fitted. Distinguish this from an adjustable wrench, whose jaw opening can be changed.
paragraphs.agr-safety-maintenance-tools-p3: A double open-ended spanner has an open jaw at each end; a ring spanner is shown as having a ring-shaped end. Look at the shape of the part that contacts the fastener, not just the tool’s name.
paragraphs.agr-safety-maintenance-tools-p4: An adjustable wrench lets you change the jaw opening to match the size of a bolt or nut. Distinguish this construction from choosing a replaceable socket.
paragraphs.agr-safety-maintenance-tools-p5: A hex key is used for fasteners such as hex-socket bolts. Distinguish tools that grip the outside from tools whose working end is inserted into a matching hole.
paragraphs.agr-safety-maintenance-tools-p6: A screwdriver is used for small screws with cross-shaped or straight slots in their heads. Knowing tool names does not establish safe tightening force or maintenance procedures; check methods appropriate to the machine and task separately.

agr-safety-maintenance-tools.activity: Compare the six tool names using clues such as replaceable sockets, ring-shaped ends, adjustable jaws, hexagonal sockets and screw slots. Without reproducing tool photographs, organize the features using descriptions and your own simple drawings.

agr-safety-stepladder.title: Inspecting a stepladder and using it stably
agr-safety-stepladder.objective: Explain stepladder damage, placement and spreader locks, and the dangers of the top cap and leaning sideways.

paragraphTitles.agr-safety-stepladder-p4: Choose the correct place to stand

paragraphs.agr-safety-stepladder-p1: Before using a stepladder, check for cracks, breaks, bends and similar damage. Do not skip today’s inspection just because it was usable yesterday.
paragraphs.agr-safety-stepladder-p2: A stepladder must be positioned stably. Checking that the equipment itself is undamaged and checking that it is stable where placed are separate tasks.
paragraphs.agr-safety-stepladder-p3: Securely engage the chain, clasp or other spreader restraint. Simply opening the legs so that the ladder appears to stand does not complete this check.
paragraphs.agr-safety-stepladder-p4: The source shows standing on or straddling the top cap as dangerous examples. Distinguish the top cap from the steps and check standing positions in the diagram.
paragraphs.agr-safety-stepladder-p5: Illustrations in both sources show the danger of leaning the body beyond the side rails. The level 2 text also mentions sideways instability. Being able to reach something is not enough to establish that your posture is safe.
paragraphs.agr-safety-stepladder-p6: Use separate fields for damage, placement, spreader restraints, standing position and posture. One satisfactory item does not allow you to skip the others; carry out checks appropriate to the stepladder being used.

agr-safety-stepladder.activity: Separate checks before use from checks during use, organizing five items: damage, placement, spreader restraints, the top cap and leaning out. Explain why being able to reach and having a safe posture are different judgments.

agr-safety-workload-2.title: Planning work around health, posture and footing
agr-safety-workload-2.objective: Organize daily health habits, prolonged posture, footing and cleanup as separate parts of work planning.

paragraphTitles.agr-safety-workload-2-p4: Fine work that strains the eyes

paragraphs.agr-safety-workload-2-p1: The level 2 source includes daily habits such as sleep and meals in preparation for work. Read this together with the instruction not to use agricultural machinery or spray pesticides when fatigued.
paragraphs.agr-safety-workload-2-p2: Consider strain on the body when lifting or moving loads. Do not treat posture examples in the text as a guarantee of a lifting method suitable for every weight and physical condition.
paragraphs.agr-safety-workload-2-p3: For work involving prolonged bending and similar postures, the source suggests changing position from time to time. Do not treat remaining in one position as inevitable and omit breaks or divisions between tasks.
paragraphs.agr-safety-workload-2-p4: For detailed work that heavily uses the eyes, examples include resting the eyes and making time to look into the distance. The text gives no universal medical interval that is safe for everyone.
paragraphs.agr-safety-workload-2-p5: Secure your footing when using a brush cutter or cultivator, and check stability and posture when using a stepladder. Include the working location in the plan, not only tool operation.
paragraphs.agr-safety-workload-2-p6: Level 2 also lists cleanup tasks: cleaning machines, drying after washing, maintenance, storage and records. Include the work before starting and after finishing, not just the time when the operation is in progress.

agr-safety-workload-2.activity: Use three columns—before, during and after work—to sort physical condition, posture, footing, eye-rest time, cleaning and records. Do not turn this into a table prescribing individual treatment or permissible lifting weights.

agr-safety-label-fields-2.title: Reading separate fields on a pesticide label
agr-safety-label-fields-2.objective: Distinguish crop, target, dilution, quantity, timing, number of applications and method, and confirm what the labeling means.

paragraphs.agr-safety-label-fields-2-p1: The level 2 source contains a table for reading pesticide-label fields. Check the name, net contents, active ingredients and precautions as separate information; one number alone does not determine every aspect of safe use.
paragraphs.agr-safety-label-fields-2-p2: Check the permitted crop name together with the target pest or disease. Do not replace current product labeling with the assumption that similarly named crops must have identical conditions of use.
paragraphs.agr-safety-label-fields-2-p3: The dilution factor describes how the product is diluted. Application quantity and spray-liquid volume describe how much is used for the target. Reading the dilution factor alone does not establish how much to apply.
paragraphs.agr-safety-label-fields-2-p4: Distinguish conditions on application timing before harvest from methods such as soil treatment and foliar spraying. Do not copy numbers or methods from the source examples into current instructions for another actual product.
paragraphs.agr-safety-label-fields-2-p5: The source distinguishes the number of applications of this product from the total number of applications of pesticides containing the same active ingredient. Changing the trade name does not automatically make applications of the same ingredient unrelated.
paragraphs.agr-safety-label-fields-2-p6: The final expiry date and lot number are different information. The date helps check the period of use; the lot number helps investigate a problem. This explanation of label fields does not complete checks of actual registration or legal applicability.

agr-safety-label-fields-2.activity: Make a label checklist without product names or specific dilution factors. Use separate fields for crop, target, dilution, quantity, timing, method, application counts and expiry; explain why the trade name alone is insufficient.

agr-ricework-seed.title: Seed-rice structure and seed preparation
agr-ricework-seed.objective: Distinguish the positions and roles of the embryo, endosperm and hull, and explain seed disinfection as management during preparation.

paragraphTitles.agr-ricework-seed-p1: Look at the parts of seed rice
paragraphTitles.agr-ricework-seed-p5: Measures against seed-borne pests and diseases

paragraphs.agr-ricework-seed-p1: Seed rice used to prepare for rice cultivation consists of a hull and the brown rice inside it. In addition to learning the names of processed food rice, examine the internal structure as a seed that will germinate.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-seed-p2: The embryo inside the brown rice contains organs that become leaves and roots after germination. Although it is a small part of the seed, it has a role that leads to the later plant body.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-seed-p3: The endosperm stores nutrients needed for growth after germination. Do not confuse the role of the embryo, which contains the organs that become leaves and roots, with that of the endosperm, which stores nutrients.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-seed-p4: The hull protects the brown rice inside. In a structural diagram, show the internal relationship of the embryo and endosperm separately from the outside covering provided by the hull.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-seed-p5: The source lists seed disinfection as a measure against pests and diseases carried on seed rice. It is also important not to group the rice white-tip nematode and diseases such as bakanae together as though they were all the same type of pathogen.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-seed-p6: Understanding the task called seed disinfection is different from choosing a method or a product’s conditions of use. This introduction reviews seed structure and the purpose of preparation without prescribing one chemical concentration or treatment duration for every case.

agr-ricework-seed.activity: Draw your own cross-section of seed rice and label the roles of the embryo, endosperm and hull. Then use separate columns for the purpose of seed preparation and the specific disinfection conditions that need checking.

agr-ricework-soaking.title: Understand seed soaking and pre-germination in sequence
agr-ricework-soaking.objective: Distinguish soaking to absorb water from pre-germination before sowing, and read the source’s indications of seed condition.

paragraphTitles.agr-ricework-soaking-p2: The stated water temperature and duration
paragraphTitles.agr-ricework-soaking-p5: Compare insufficient, suitable and excessive sprouting

paragraphs.agr-ricework-soaking-p1: Seed soaking is the stage of immersing seed rice in water so that it absorbs enough water. Do not treat putting seeds in water and the state of having sprouted as the same thing.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-soaking-p2: The source diagram gives soaking guidelines of a water temperature of 10–15℃ and a duration of 7–10 days. These figures belong to the conditions in the diagram; they do not mean that all seed rice is soaked for the same number of days regardless of water temperature.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-soaking-p3: Pre-germination is the stage of warming soaked seed rice before sowing to start sprouting. The source example describes warming it to 30–32℃ on the day before sowing. Do not confuse the soaking water temperature with the pre-germination temperature.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-soaking-p4: The source calls a state with a sprout about 1 mm long “pigeon-breast” (ハト胸). Read this as an observation guide for sprout condition, rather than assuming that longer sprouts are always better.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-soaking-p5: The pre-germination diagram shows insufficient, suitable and excessive states. Check the condition of the seed rice as well as the number of working days.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-soaking-p6: Record the purposes separately: water absorption during soaking, and sprouting before sowing during pre-germination. Keep stated temperatures and durations together with their source conditions; do not transfer them unconditionally into a specific work plan.

agr-ricework-soaking.activity: Make separate columns for soaking and pre-germination, recording the purpose, the temperature stated in the source and the condition to observe. Check that you have not assigned a temperature or sprout length to the wrong stage.

agr-ricework-nursery.title: Raise seedlings for a rice transplanter
agr-ricework-nursery.objective: Explain in sequence nursery-tray preparation, management after emergence, and the source’s distinction between young and intermediate seedlings.

paragraphTitles.agr-ricework-nursery-p6: Guidelines for young and intermediate seedlings

paragraphs.agr-ricework-nursery-p1: Raise seedlings in nursery trays for planting in the paddy with a rice transplanter. Compared with sowing directly into the paddy, the place where seedlings grow and the work before transplanting are different.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-nursery-p2: The source gives an example of filling a nursery tray measuring 60 cm × 30 cm and 3 cm thick with growing medium. The medium contains fertilizer; water it, sow the seeds and cover them with soil. Record the dimensions as a source example.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-nursery-p3: After covering the seeds with soil, use insulating materials and similar measures in a germination unit or greenhouse to promote emergence. Distinguish pre-germination before sowing from seedling emergence after sowing.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-nursery-p4: The source shows emerged trays being arranged in a greenhouse and covered until the seedlings turn green. This does not mean continuing the same covering indefinitely even after the work stage changes.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-nursery-p5: While raising seedlings, water them while monitoring the greenhouse temperature. Do not leave them unattended after sowing; manage seedling growth together with the nursery environment.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-nursery-p6: The source gives examples of young seedlings raised for 20–25 days and intermediate seedlings raised for 30–35 days. Compare these durations while also checking the seedling diagrams and growth condition; do not assume that days alone determine the category under all conditions.

agr-ricework-nursery.activity: Make sequencing cards from tray preparation through management after emergence. For young and intermediate seedlings, put the source’s example durations and the seedling conditions in separate columns, distinguishing them from instructions for a fixed schedule.

agr-ricework-field.title: Prepare the main paddy and transplant rice
agr-ricework-field.objective: Organize tillage, puddling and transplanting, and distinguish whole-field fertilization from side-row fertilization, and row spacing from hill spacing.

paragraphTitles.agr-ricework-field-p3: When and where to apply fertilizer

paragraphs.agr-ricework-field-p1: In the paddy where seedlings will be planted, use a tractor or similar equipment to till the soil and level the ground. Preparing the main field to receive seedlings is necessary in addition to preparing nursery trays.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-field-p2: Puddling means stirring the soil of a flooded paddy to make it soft. Neither adding water alone nor tilling dry soil alone describes the same operation.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-field-p3: The source lists spreading fertilizer over the entire paddy before puddling and applying fertilizer beside the rows during transplanting. Do not assume that every method applies fertilizer at the same time and in the same place.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-field-p4: In transplant cultivation, raised seedlings are planted with a rice transplanter. The machine’s row count relates to how many rows it plants in one pass; it is different information from the number of seedlings or the crop variety.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-field-p5: Row spacing is the distance between rows; hill spacing is the distance between planted hills. The source gives an example of 30 cm row spacing and states that hill spacing is adjusted on the transplanter. The descriptions of hill spacing differ between the level 1 and level 2 sources, so do not treat them as one universal setting for all paddies.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-field-p6: Summarize main-field preparation, puddling and transplanting separately from settings that depend on machinery and growing conditions. Understanding the preparation sequence does not mean that you have mastered adjusting or operating a real rice transplanter.

agr-ricework-field.activity: Place tillage, water admission, puddling and transplanting on a main-field preparation timeline. Draw the two fertilization examples on separate lines, and distinguish row and hill spacing in a plan view.

agr-ricework-water.title: Water management and growth after transplanting
agr-ricework-water.objective: Match the purposes of water admission immediately after transplanting, shallow water and tillering, and midseason drainage with plant growth.

paragraphTitles.agr-ricework-water-p2: Check for new roots and leaves

paragraphs.agr-ricework-water-p1: Adding water after rice transplanting is called water admission (入水). The source states that its purpose is to protect the transplanted seedlings. Understand the task name separately from any specific water-depth setting.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-water-p2: The source explains that once new roots and leaves develop, management moves to shallow water and a stage of increasing new stems. Link water management to changes in growth, not just to calendar dates.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-water-p3: Tillering means an increase in rice stems. It is not the same as an increase in plant height or sowing new seeds. In explanations of water management, check which type of growth is involved.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-water-p4: Midseason drainage means draining the water and drying the paddy surface according to growth. This differs from keeping the field continuously flooded. Do not set one specific timing or duration based only on this shared introduction.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-water-p5: Adding water, maintaining shallow water and draining water serve different growth stages. Retain the source condition “according to growth”; do not conclude that draining at any time is acceptable.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-water-p6: It is important not to confuse water management suited to rice growth with product-specific water requirements when pesticides are used. This introduction does not prescribe a flooded period or drainage method common to all pesticides.

agr-ricework-water.activity: Match “protect seedlings,” “increase new stems” and “dry the paddy surface according to growth” to the task names in the text. Keep a separate column for conditions to check before deciding numerical settings.

agr-ricework-harvest.title: From heading to harvest
agr-ricework-harvest.objective: Distinguish panicle differentiation, heading and harvest, and explain that a combine brings together cutting and threshing.

paragraphTitles.agr-ricework-harvest-p3: A guideline for time to harvest

paragraphs.agr-ricework-harvest-p1: As rice enters reproductive growth, panicles differentiate. The source calls this the young-panicle differentiation stage. Distinguish the formation of a still-small panicle from the state in which it has emerged outside.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-harvest-p2: Heading means that a developed panicle emerges outside. The source describes approximately 30 days from young-panicle differentiation, but this duration must not become a fixed schedule for all cultivation.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-harvest-p3: The source gives a guideline of about 30–60 days from heading to harvest. Do not replace this range with a single number; in an actual cultivation plan, treat it separately from checking the variety and growth conditions.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-harvest-p4: In harvesting, distinguish cutting the rice plant from threshing, which removes paddy grains from the panicle. These are different stages from hulling, which removes the hull to obtain brown rice.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-harvest-p5: A combine combines the functions of a reaper and a thresher in one machine. The source cites the head-feed combine as an example commonly used in Japan.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-harvest-p6: Drying, hulling and grading still follow cutting and threshing. Do not record “harvested with a combine” and “ready for shipment” as the same state.

agr-ricework-harvest.activity: Put young-panicle differentiation, heading and harvest in sequence, and add the source’s time ranges. Draw a work diagram separating cutting and threshing by the combine from later hulling.

agr-ricework-processing.title: Drying, grading, shipping and the field after harvest
agr-ricework-processing.objective: Explain separately the sequence from drying paddy rice to shipping and the handling of stubble and straw after harvest.

paragraphs.agr-ricework-processing-p1: The source describes freshly harvested paddy rice as having a high moisture content of 20–27%. Do not confuse this moisture percentage with fertilizer nutrient percentages or dryer temperature.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-processing-p2: Dry the harvested paddy rice; the source gives an example of reducing moisture to 14–15%. This figure describes the moisture in paddy rice, not a prescribed temperature setting or drying duration for every machine.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-processing-p3: Hulling removes the hull from dried paddy rice to obtain brown rice. Grading then removes undersized or defective rice from the brown rice. These two processes remove different things.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-processing-p4: The source gives examples of shipping in 30 kg rice bags or flexible bulk bags. Record container capacity and packaging information separately from brown-rice composition or moisture percentage.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-processing-p5: For the field after harvest, the source describes tilling to incorporate stubble, straw and similar residues into the soil. Consider preparing the harvested crop separately from managing what remains in the field.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-processing-p6: Completing the processes through shipment is different from completing paddy management. Organize the purpose of incorporating stubble and straw by tillage, and do not equate understanding a machine operation with being able to perform it safely.

agr-ricework-processing.activity: Draw separate boxes for drying paddy rice, hulling, removing defective rice and shipping. Use a separate flow for stubble and straw left in the field; classify numerical information as moisture %, container kg or machine conditions.

agr-ricework-lowcost.title: Compare direct seeding and wider-spacing transplanting
agr-ricework-lowcost.objective: Distinguish what direct seeding and wider-spacing transplanting omit or change, and explain flooded-paddy versus dry-paddy direct seeding.

paragraphTitles.agr-ricework-lowcost-p1: Direct seeding omits nursery raising and transplanting
paragraphTitles.agr-ricework-lowcost-p2: Direct seeding in a flooded paddy
paragraphTitles.agr-ricework-lowcost-p3: Direct seeding in a dry paddy

paragraphs.agr-ricework-lowcost-p1: Direct seeding means sowing seed directly into the paddy instead of raising seedlings and transplanting them. The source gives reduced nursery work and materials as the reason it saves labor.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-lowcost-p2: This method sows seeds in or on the soil after tillage and puddling. The source also gives examples of seed coatings for emergence, but this introduction does not prescribe specific treatments for chemicals or products.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-lowcost-p3: This method sows into a dry paddy, grows the plants under upland-field-like conditions for a while after emergence, and adds water later. The initial water condition at sowing is not the same as in flooded-paddy seeding.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-lowcost-p4: Wider-spacing transplanting means increasing hill spacing on the rice transplanter to lower planting density. Unlike direct seeding, it changes spacing within a method that plants raised seedlings.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-lowcost-p5: For an example with 30 cm between rows, the source says that increasing hill spacing from 15 cm to 28 cm reduces the required number of nursery trays by 40% or more. Do not turn this conditional example into a guarantee of the same cost reduction in every field.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-lowcost-p6: Direct seeding and wider-spacing transplanting are ways to reduce work or materials. However, they do not eliminate management after sowing or transplanting. Compare them by identifying the particular steps they change.

agr-ricework-lowcost.activity: Make columns for transplant cultivation, direct seeding and wider-spacing transplanting, comparing nursery raising, transplanting and hill spacing. Subdivide direct seeding into two types and diagram the paddy condition at sowing and the later admission of water.

agr-ricework-feed.title: Distinguish feed rice from whole-crop rice silage
agr-ricework-feed.objective: Distinguish feed rice using grains from rice WCS using panicles, stems and leaves as well, and explain production suited to the intended use.

paragraphTitles.agr-ricework-feed-p2: Rice WCS as a feed form
paragraphTitles.agr-ricework-feed-p3: An example of the harvest stage

paragraphs.agr-ricework-feed-p1: Rice used as livestock feed includes feed rice that uses the grains and rice WCS, in which panicles, stems and leaves are harvested and used together. The parts used differ.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-feed-p2: Rice WCS is roughage harvested before the grain is fully ripe and made into silage. Separate the flow that ships only rice grains from the flow that also uses panicles, stems and leaves.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-feed-p3: The source cites around the yellow-ripe stage as a harvest stage related to rice WCS quality. Do not apply the harvest timing for rice grown as a staple food as though it meant the same thing.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-feed-p4: Feed rice can be produced using paddies and rice-growing machinery. Existing varieties as well as varieties developed for feed are used, and the characteristics to check vary with the intended use.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-feed-p5: The source says that many feed varieties have characteristics such as high yield, resistance to lodging and disease resistance. Do not read this as a guarantee that every variety always has the same characteristics.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-feed-p6: The source also mentions cooperation between rice and livestock farmers and ways to reduce production costs. Here we study the relationship between crop production and its users; we do not prescribe livestock-specific feed amounts or feed mixtures.

agr-ricework-feed.activity: Compare feed rice and rice WCS by the parts used, processed form and harvest stage. Organize crop cultivation planning and livestock feeding planning as separate tasks.

agr-ricework-stages.title: Growth stages and observation guides
agr-ricework-stages.objective: Distinguish tillering, young-panicle formation, booting, heading and maturity, and explain the limits of applying a cropping-calendar diagram.

paragraphs.agr-ricework-stages-p1: The level 2 source’s diagram uses an early-maturing cropping season as an example to show the relationship between growth and work. Its months cannot be turned directly into a nationwide schedule for all regions and varieties.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-stages-p2: Tillering means an increase in stems. The level 2 source also mentions nonproductive tillers that do not form panicles. Do not infer that the number of panicles has increased by the same amount simply because stem number has risen.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-stages-p3: As tillering progresses, rice moves from young-panicle formation into reproductive growth. Observe separately the growth that increases leaves and stems and the stage in which panicles are formed.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-stages-p4: Booting is the stage when the panicle grows and the leaf sheath swells. It does not refer only to the state after a panicle has emerged; also observe the changes before emergence.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-stages-p5: The level 2 source defines heading time as when approximately half the productive stems have headed. Distinguish seeing one panicle emerge from a guide describing the stage of the whole field.
paragraphs.agr-ricework-stages-p6: Maturity is described as the stage when grains have hardened and the endosperm has become transparent throughout. Organize this in relation to grain condition, not only the number of days after sowing.

agr-ricework-stages.activity: Place the growth stages on a timeline and match them to stem number, leaf-sheath swelling, panicle emergence and grain condition. Record the months in the cropping-calendar diagram separately from the growth stages to observe.

agr-vegwork-grains.title: Cereal grains, pulses and the use of edamame
agr-vegwork-grains.objective: Identify examples of cereal grains and pulses, and distinguish the use of immature soybeans as edamame.

paragraphTitles.agr-vegwork-grains-p6: Direct sowing and the harvested part

paragraphs.agr-vegwork-grains-p1: This chapter covers cereal crops and pulses as examples of grains grown in upland fields. Connect this with the classification by use studied earlier, matching each crop name with the stage at which it is used.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-grains-p2: The materials list wheat, barley, rye and oats. These are different crops within the cereal group; do not combine the four names as if they were alternative names for one crop.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-grains-p3: Soybeans and adzuki beans are examples of pulses. The plant grouping called pulses can be recorded separately from uses such as food, livestock feed or processing.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-grains-p4: When soybeans are harvested immature and eaten as edamame, they are treated as vegetables. Rather than assuming that different names mean entirely unrelated crops, check the stage at which the crop is used.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-grains-p5: After a peanut flower above ground is fertilized, an elongated gynophore, or peg, enters the soil and a pod develops at its tip. Identify where the harvested part is located, rather than imagining pods attached above the leaves.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-grains-p6: Peanut seeds are sown directly into the field, and the pods are dug out of the soil at harvest. Link direct sowing with the earlier sowing lesson; here, focus on the crop characteristics and the part harvested.

agr-vegwork-grains.activity: List the four cereals and examples of pulses. Draw and explain the stage of use for soybeans and edamame, and the positions of flowers and pods for peanuts.

agr-vegwork-families.title: Vegetable families and their member crops
agr-vegwork-families.objective: Match common vegetables to their botanical families without confusing this with classification by the part eaten.

paragraphs.agr-vegwork-families-p1: Alongside the earlier classification by the part used, this chapter introduces botanical classification by family through examples. Vegetables with the same edible part do not necessarily belong to the same family, and members of one family need not have the same edible part.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-families-p2: Cucumber, melon, watermelon and pumpkin are examples of the gourd family, Cucurbitaceae. Group them by their botanical relationship rather than by their usual way of eating or sweetness.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-families-p3: Eggplant, tomato, sweet pepper and potato belong to the nightshade family, Solanaceae. Treating potato as a root vegetable by its utilized part is compatible with classifying it botanically in Solanaceae.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-families-p4: Cabbage, Chinese cabbage and daikon belong to the cabbage family, Brassicaceae. Notice that the same family includes crops grown for leaves and crops grown for underground parts.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-families-p5: Both materials list lettuce, burdock and crown daisy in Asteraceae, the daisy family, and onion and Japanese bunching onion in Amaryllidaceae, the amaryllis family. Check familiar vegetable names together with their families.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-families-p6: The materials also match carrot with Apiaceae, maize with Poaceae, sweet potato with Convolvulaceae and strawberry with Rosaceae. As well as memorizing the matches, check that you have not confused similar names.

agr-vegwork-families.activity: Arrange crop-name cards by family, then classify the same cards by the part used. Explain the difference between the two classifications, especially for potato, daikon and cabbage.

agr-vegwork-leafy.title: Differences in growing leafy and stem vegetables
agr-vegwork-leafy.objective: Compare typical leafy and stem vegetables in terms of climate, form and growing methods.

paragraphs.agr-vegwork-leafy-p1: Cabbage is introduced as a transplanted vegetable suited to a cool climate. Refer back to the seedling and transplanting lessons for the basic procedure; here, associate the crop with its preferred climate.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-leafy-p2: Chinese cabbage also grows in cool conditions. Transplanting is common, but direct sowing is also used in some regions. There are heading, semi-heading and non-heading types, so do not expect every plant to form the same shape.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-leafy-p3: Lettuce includes both heading and non-heading forms. It prefers cool conditions; light promotes seed germination, and the crop is sensitive to acidity. Check the meaning of light-promoted germination against the earlier germination lesson.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-leafy-p4: The materials explain flower-bud differentiation in lettuce in response to high temperatures. Distinguish its tendency to grow leaves under cool conditions from the change in growth stage brought about by heat.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-leafy-p5: Spinach is usually direct-sown, although it is sometimes transplanted. The materials give a harvest example of one and a half to two months after sowing, at about 25 centimetres in height. Do not treat those days or sizes as guaranteed for every variety and condition.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-leafy-p6: The round edible bulb of an onion is a part where leaves and stem overlap. Do not identify every rounded underground part as a root solely because of its position and shape; check both the organ description and the classification by use.

agr-vegwork-leafy.activity: Make a comparison table for the five crops showing cool conditions, transplanting or direct sowing, and features of seeds or edible parts. Mark the harvest example as a guideline that varies with conditions.

agr-vegwork-rootvegetables.title: Observing daikon and carrot growth
agr-vegwork-rootvegetables.objective: Explain differences in cropping seasons, flower buds and dryness at germination for daikon and carrot.

paragraphs.agr-vegwork-rootvegetables-p1: Daikon is grown throughout the year: in spring and summer as well as autumn and winter. This does not mean that one field anywhere in Japan can always follow exactly the same schedule.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-rootvegetables-p2: The materials give an example of using tunnels for daikon during cold periods. Connect the covering structure with the earlier covering-materials lesson, and understand this as an application to a crop and season.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-rootvegetables-p3: Daikon is direct-sown, and the materials explain that prolonged low temperatures cause flower-bud differentiation. The temperature needed for germination and the subsequent effects of temperature on flower-bud formation are separate points to observe.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-rootvegetables-p4: Carrots contain abundant carotene and are used in cooking, juice and other products. Record their food-use characteristics separately from information about sowing methods and growing climate.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-rootvegetables-p5: Carrots grow in cool climates, are cultivated in many regions of Japan, and are direct-sown. It is important not to confuse widespread cultivation with a claim that identical management works regardless of climate.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-rootvegetables-p6: Carrots germinate poorly when conditions are dry. Apply the three germination requirements to this crop to understand why moisture after sowing matters. This does not establish a uniform watering volume or frequency.

agr-vegwork-rootvegetables.activity: Use two columns for daikon and carrot to record season, covering, sowing, and conditions affecting germination or flower buds. Add which growth stage each condition concerns.

agr-vegwork-fruitvegetables.title: Managing tomatoes, cucumbers and eggplants
agr-vegwork-fruitvegetables.objective: Organize the stages at which three fruit vegetables are used and examples of grafting, side-shoot removal and pruning.

paragraphTitles.agr-vegwork-fruitvegetables-p3: The stage at which cucumbers are used

paragraphs.agr-vegwork-fruitvegetables-p1: Tomatoes include varieties for processing as well as fresh consumption. Besides differences in fruit appearance and sweetness, consider what use each variety is intended for.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-fruitvegetables-p2: The materials describe transplanting tomatoes and using grafted seedlings. Tomatoes produce many side shoots, which are also removed while small. Connect the location of side-shoot removal studied earlier with this crop example.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-fruitvegetables-p3: Cucumbers are used as green fruit before full ripening. The materials explain that they are cultivated both outdoors and in protected facilities, supporting year-round supply. Do not learn this as harvesting only fully mature fruit.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-fruitvegetables-p4: The materials give a fruit length of about 20 centimetres as a cucumber harvest example. Separate the observation of fruit length from the example value, rather than fixing one harvest length for every variety.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-fruitvegetables-p5: Eggplants have many local varieties and a long growing period, so fertilizer requires attention. Do not replace that statement of need with an instruction specifying a particular fertilizer amount or frequency.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-fruitvegetables-p6: As eggplants develop, the materials describe staking, shoot removal, training and pruning. Refer back to the basics of each operation, and organize them as a combination that changes with growth.

agr-vegwork-fruitvegetables.activity: Make a table for the three crops covering use, maturity stage when used, and examples of seedling or branch management. Note that the fruit-length value is an example from the materials, and explain how the operations differ.

agr-vegwork-industrial.title: Growing and processing tea and konjac
agr-vegwork-industrial.objective: Compare the harvested organs, processing and growing periods of tea and konjac as examples of industrial crops.

paragraphTitles.agr-vegwork-industrial-p4: A form that makes harvesting easier

paragraphs.agr-vegwork-industrial-p1: Industrial crops in this chapter are crops that undergo particular processing before use. Link this with the earlier classification by use, and learn through examples how the cultivated parts are utilized.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-industrial-p2: Tea is made by processing the leaves and stems of the tea plant for use as a drink. The harvested part differs from fruit trees grown for their fruit, so first identify which part of the plant is used.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-industrial-p3: The tea plant is an evergreen shrub that can be harvested for many years after one planting. A field of these plants is a tea field. Distinguish this period of use from crops harvested and replanted within a single year.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-industrial-p4: Tea plants are trained to a height that makes harvesting easier. The materials’ description of roughly waist height is an example relating to ease of management, not a numerical height specified for every worker.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-industrial-p5: Konjac is made by harvesting and processing its underground stem, the konjac corm. It is grown from seed corms and takes several years to harvest, so do not plan it on the same schedule as leafy vegetables harvested quickly.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-industrial-p6: The materials describe konjac cultivation on well-drained flat or sloping land. Interpret suitable sites in terms of drainage as well as whether the land is level or sloping.

agr-vegwork-industrial.activity: Compare tea and konjac by harvested organ, use after processing, growing period, and management of site or plant form. Explain how each fits the earlier classifications of organs and uses.

agr-vegwork-feed.title: Forage crops and the concept of silage
agr-vegwork-feed.objective: Explain examples of forage crops and the differences between fresh forage, hay and silage.

paragraphTitles.agr-vegwork-feed-p4: Harvesting heads, stems and leaves together

paragraphs.agr-vegwork-feed-p1: Forage crops are crops used to feed livestock. In addition to pasture grasses, the materials give examples including rice, maize, sorghum and oats.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-feed-p2: Rice and maize are used for livestock feed as well as human food. Even when the crop name is the same, classify it after checking the intended use and the part harvested.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-feed-p3: The materials describe feeding crops to livestock as fresh forage, hay or silage. The crop species grown and the form used after harvest can be recorded as separate information.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-feed-p4: The explanation of silage includes examples of harvesting pasture grasses, or the heads together with stems and leaves of rice and maize. Distinguish this from extracting only the grain for human food.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-feed-p5: Silage is feed stored under an airtight seal without oxygen and allowed to ferment. It differs from hay, which is simply dried grass. This introduction does not specify procedures for entering equipment or conditions for making silage.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-feed-p6: The materials state that forage crops are harvested when their nutritional value is high. This does not mean one calendar date suits every crop; consider both the intended use and the condition of the crop.

agr-vegwork-feed.activity: Make separate tables of crop names and forms of feed. Explain hay and silage through the distinction between drying and sealing for fermentation.

agr-vegwork-environment.title: Reading temperature, light and moisture conditions for each crop
agr-vegwork-environment.objective: Apply basic growing conditions to crop examples without turning light saturation or moisture readings into universal settings.

paragraphTitles.agr-vegwork-environment-p1: Suitable temperatures vary by crop and stage
paragraphTitles.agr-vegwork-environment-p4: Low light and the limit of light response

paragraphs.agr-vegwork-environment-p1: For field crops and vegetables, consider the suitable growing temperature for the species and growth stage. Do not assume that examples of leafy vegetables preferring cool conditions and fruit vegetables preferring warmth remain identical at every growth stage.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-environment-p2: Choice of varieties and growing methods can expand cultivation regions and seasons. Even crops preferring warmth may be grown in cold regions with facilities or covers, so do not decide suitability solely from a region’s name.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-environment-p3: Tomato, melon, maize and carrot are given as examples requiring strong light. When comparing light conditions, record these separately from examples that grow under weaker light.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-environment-p4: Japanese wild parsley (mitsuba) and Japanese ginger (myoga) are examples that grow under weak light. Both materials also describe the light saturation point in this chapter: above a certain light intensity, photosynthesis stops increasing. Apply the earlier explanation of light to these crop examples.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-environment-p5: Too little soil moisture can cause wilting or nutrient deficiency; too much may deprive roots of oxygen and cause rot. The appropriate judgement is not to keep changing the amount endlessly in just one direction.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-environment-p6: The materials list soil-moisture meters and tensiometers, mentioning percentage and pF displays. Do not treat readings with different units or indicators as one scale, or turn a listed percentage into a target for every field without checking measurement conditions.

agr-vegwork-environment.activity: Organize examples of crops requiring strong or weak light, and the two states of moisture deficiency and excess. State whether you are assessing temperature, light or moisture, and avoid mixing readings with different units.

agr-vegwork-seedstorage.title: Vegetable seed storage and types of seed treatment
agr-vegwork-seedstorage.objective: Read seed longevity as a guideline dependent on storage conditions, and distinguish pelleting, disinfection and seed tapes.

paragraphs.agr-vegwork-seedstorage-p1: Seeds have a limited lifespan that varies with crop species and storage conditions. The storage principles in the materials are low temperature and dryness. Avoid memorizing a number of years without checking how the seeds have been stored.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-seedstorage-p2: The materials’ one-to-two-year group includes Japanese bunching onion, onion, garlic chives, spinach, lettuce, burdock, cabbage and carrot. This is a guideline related to the storage conditions in the materials, not a guarantee of germination throughout that time.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-seedstorage-p3: The two-to-three-year group includes daikon, turnip, Chinese cabbage, pea, common bean, broad bean and watermelon; the three-to-four-year group includes cucumber, pumpkin, eggplant and tomato. Compare the groups while noting that storage conditions affect longevity.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-seedstorage-p4: Pelleted seeds are processed into uniformly round shapes. Do not confuse modifying a seed’s shape to make sowing easier with covering sown seeds with soil.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-seedstorage-p5: Disinfected seeds have received a disinfection treatment for purposes such as disease prevention. Learning this category alone does not determine which chemical to use or in what quantity.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-seedstorage-p6: Seed tape holds seeds at fixed intervals between layers of tape. Distinguish its purpose from pelleting seeds into round shapes or disinfecting them, and connect it with the sowing basics studied earlier.

agr-vegwork-seedstorage.activity: Make three separate tables for storage conditions, longevity groups in the materials and processing methods. Match each method to its purpose: making a round shape, disinfecting or providing spacing.

agr-vegwork-tubers-2.title: Storage organs and growing characteristics of potato and sweet potato
agr-vegwork-tubers-2.objective: Using the level 2 materials, explain differences in utilized organs, planting materials and climate for potato and sweet potato.

paragraphs.agr-vegwork-tubers-2-p1: The level 2 materials describe these crops as storing carbohydrates in enlarged underground stems or roots. It is important not to regard every underground part as the same organ.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-tubers-2-p2: The potato tuber used is an enlarged underground stem. Potatoes are grown by planting seed tubers in the field and are described as preferring a cool climate.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-tubers-2-p3: In the level 2 materials, sweet potato is a crop in Convolvulaceae, the morning-glory family, whose enlarged roots are used. Distinguish roots from stems rather than treating them as the same organ as a potato’s underground stem.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-tubers-2-p4: Sweet potato prefers a warm climate. Stems growing from seed roots are cut to make planting slips. The form of material planted differs from planting potato seed tubers directly.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-tubers-2-p5: Both crops can be raw materials for processing, including starch production, and are also classified as vegetables when used for food. Consider the plant organ separately from classification by intended use.
paragraphs.agr-vegwork-tubers-2-p6: The level 2 materials warn that potatoes with skin that has turned green after harvest contain toxins and should not be used for food or offered for sale. Learn this as a safety precaution; do not estimate toxin amounts or decide on safe treatment from appearance alone.

agr-vegwork-tubers-2.activity: Compare potato and sweet potato by utilized organ, planting material, climate and intended use. Put the caution about green potatoes in a separate column from differences in cultivation methods.

agr-facility-structure-vegetables.title: Distinguishing fruit vegetables grown in protected structures
agr-facility-structure-vegetables.objective: Identify the plant families and parts used in tomatoes, strawberries and cucumbers, and distinguish their cultivation and fruit-setting characteristics.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p1: Separate plant family from the part eaten
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p5: Cucumbers are used as young fruit

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p1: Vegetables grown in protected structures may all be classed as fruit vegetables while belonging to different plant families. Tomatoes belong to Solanaceae, strawberries to Rosaceae and cucumbers to Cucurbitaceae. Keep classification by use as a fruit vegetable separate from classification by plant family.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p2: When growing tomatoes, consider their need for strong light. Simply putting them inside a structure does not establish that the light conditions are adequate. Consider the crop’s characteristics together with conditions inside the structure.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p3: Tomatoes have several cropping schedules that together support cultivation throughout the year. “Year-round” does not mean that a single plant continuously yields the same quantity. Read it as a combination of cultivation schedules for different times of year.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p4: Strawberries are vegetables whose fruit is used, but vegetative propagation is important when explaining how seedlings are multiplied. Classification of the part harvested and the method of producing new plants are different classification items.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p5: Cucumbers are used while the fruit is still young, before it fully matures. Do not confuse the source’s description of young fruit with harvesting after the seeds have fully matured.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p6: Cucumbers have separate male and female flowers, but they can develop fruit without pollination or fertilization. Consider the separation of flowers separately from whether pollination is necessarily required for fruit to set.

agr-facility-structure-vegetables.activity: Make three columns for each crop: plant family, part used and characteristic discussed in the lesson. Keep these explanatory items separate, rather than assuming that differences in family alone determine cultivation temperatures or management methods.

agr-facility-structure-strawberry.title: Strawberry daughter plants and raised benches
agr-facility-structure-strawberry.objective: Explain propagation through runners and the working characteristics of raised benches, and distinguish flower-bud differentiation from flowering.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p3: Daughter plants develop at the ends
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p4: The advantage of a raised growing position
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p5: The stage when flower buds form
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p6: How seedling management relates to forcing

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p1: The strawberry seedling production discussed in the source uses vegetative propagation: new plants develop from part of a parent plant. The mere presence of visible seeds on the fruit is not a reason to describe the propagation method here as sowing.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p2: Runners extending from the parent plant are an important part to observe for propagation. In addition to observing flower- and fruit-bearing parts, check what grows out from the parent plant.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p3: New plants form at the ends of the runners. Explaining the sequence of parent plant, extending runner and daughter plant at its end makes clear which part is used for propagation.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p4: Raised benches allow work in a standing position. “Raised” refers to the height of the growing position, not to the plants themselves being tall.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p5: Flower-bud differentiation is the stage when a bud’s development shifts toward becoming a flower bud. It is separate from the opening of a visible flower, so do not confuse advancing flower-bud differentiation with observing flowering itself.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p6: In strawberries, seedling management that advances flower-bud differentiation is linked to forcing cultivation. Organize daughter-plant production for propagation separately from seedling management intended to control when flowers develop, according to their different purposes.

agr-facility-structure-strawberry.activity: Explain the sequence from parent plant to daughter plant in words. Then separately summarize the benefit of raised benches and the purpose of seedling management that advances flower-bud differentiation, checking that working posture and flowering control have not been confused.

agr-facility-structure-flower-calendar.title: Planning flower shipment schedules
agr-facility-structure-flower-calendar.objective: Explain the short-day response of chrysanthemums and the purpose of supplementary lighting, and distinguish scheduling through combinations of cultivars from low-temperature treatment.

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-calendar-p: Flowers produced in protected structures include cut flowers shipped after their stems are cut, and plants grown and shipped in pots. Check not only the flower’s name but also the form in which the crop is produced for use.
Shipping flowers throughout the year involves combinations of cropping schedules and cultivars. Year-round shipping does not mean that a single cultivar or one plant continues flowering all year.

Autumn chrysanthemums are treated as short-day plants. When considering flowering time, observe the relationship with the lengths of day and night, not just daytime brightness. This does not mean that every chrysanthemum should be managed under the same day-length conditions.
Supplementary lighting of autumn chrysanthemums supplies light at night to delay flowering. Remembering that adding light always brings flowering forward would reverse the purpose of this treatment.

Different groups, including summer, summer–autumn and autumn chrysanthemums, relate to different flowering seasons. Combining these groups and applying supplementary lighting within a crop are separate approaches that support year-round shipments.

Lilies are grown from bulbs, and treatments such as low-temperature treatment are used to adjust shipment schedules. Do not treat day-length control in chrysanthemums and treatment of lily bulbs as the same method.

agr-facility-structure-flower-calendar.activity: Explain autumn-chrysanthemum lighting, combinations of chrysanthemum groups and low-temperature treatment of lily bulbs by separating the crop concerned from the purpose. Do not invent specific lighting hours or treatment temperatures from this lesson.

agr-facility-structure-flower-forms.title: Plant forms and flower arrangements in cut-flower crops
agr-facility-structure-flower-forms.objective: Explain the differences between flowering woody plants, herbaceous perennials and bulb-grown plants, and describe spray-type carnations.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p1: Separate the product from the plant form
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p5: How flowers are borne on carnations
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p6: Distinguish repeat flowering from flower type

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p1: “Cut flower” describes the form in which a product is shipped and used. Cut-flower crops can be flowering woody plants, herbaceous perennials or plants grown from bulbs. Do not learn cut flowers as a single growth form.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p2: Roses are grown in protected structures as cut flowers from flowering woody plants. Understand both the plant form and the product: a plant with woody characteristics is used for its cut stems and flowers.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p3: Chrysanthemums are classified as herbaceous perennials, and shoot cuttings are given as a main propagation method. Distinguish harvesting flowers from the work of multiplying plants.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p4: Lilies are cut-flower crops grown from bulbs. Easter lilies (Lilium longiflorum), Asiatic hybrids and Oriental hybrids are among the groups. Separate the shared use of bulbs from the differences among these groups.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p5: Carnations are herbaceous perennial cut-flower crops. Spray types bear multiple flowers on one stem. When describing flower numbers, observe a single stem as the unit of comparison.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p6: Carnations include standard types as well as spray types. Organize the ability to flower in different seasons separately from types classified by how flowers are borne.

agr-facility-structure-flower-forms.activity: For the four flowers, summarize plant form and the propagation or flower arrangement described in the lesson. When explaining spray types, make clear what is being compared on one stem rather than counting all flowers on an entire plant.

agr-facility-structure-house-types.title: Covering materials and rain shelters
agr-facility-structure-house-types.objective: Compare glasshouses, plastic houses and rain shelters by their covering materials and the area covered.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p4: Do not combine cost and service life into one measure
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p5: A structure covered only at the roof

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p1: When examining types of protected structures, first look at the material covering the exterior. The main categories are glasshouses and plastic houses. This classifies structures from a different perspective than roof shape.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p2: Glasshouses transmit light well and are durable enough for long use. However, their construction costs are comparatively higher than structures covered with plastic. Consider durability separately from the initial expense.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p3: Compared with glass, plastic materials are light and easy to handle. Nevertheless, the name “plastic” does not mean identical durability: distinguish flexible films from rigid materials.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p4: Low construction cost and the ability to use the same material for a long time are separate advantages. Compare glass and plastic in separate columns for cost, weight, handling and durability.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p5: Rain shelters have film covering the roof. Do not assume that the word “structure” means the sides are completely enclosed; check exactly which areas are covered.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p6: Rain shelters are described as preventing rain from falling directly on crops and helping prevent fruit cracking and pest or disease problems. Do not confuse this rain-sheltering mechanism with a guarantee that pests and diseases will never occur.

agr-facility-structure-house-types.activity: Create a comparison sheet with separate entries for covering material, area covered, cost and durability. Check that a structure with only the roof covered has not been incorrectly described as completely enclosed.

agr-facility-structure-roof-types.title: Single-span and multi-span structures and roof shapes
agr-facility-structure-roof-types.objective: Distinguish the arrangement of spans from roof shape, and match the main shape names to observable features.

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-roof-types-p1: A single-span structure is based on one roof. The source lists ventilation, sunlight and resistance to wind and snow among its characteristics, but the name alone does not establish the actual wind or snow resistance of the structure being used.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-roof-types-p2: Multi-span structures connect several single spans. They offer a spacious interior, easier working conditions and improved heating efficiency, but less light reaches areas near the connections. Check spaciousness and brightness separately.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-roof-types-p3: A gable roof slopes on both sides. Identify the name by examining the roof’s cross-section, separately from whether there is one span or several. Gable roofs occur in both single-span and multi-span structures.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-roof-types-p4: A curved roof has a rounded outline. This name describes roof shape; the rounded outline alone does not establish that covering materials and all necessary weather precautions are the same.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-roof-types-p5: In a three-quarter roof, the two roof surfaces are not equally wide. The presence of slopes on both sides does not mean their widths are equal; distinguish the wider surface from the narrower one.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-roof-types-p6: The Venlo type is a Dutch-style structure characterized by high eaves. Do not equate roof-peak height with eaves height; identify the part whose height is being described.

agr-facility-structure-roof-types.activity: Explain names using the number of spans, roof outline, widths on each side and position of the eaves. Do not infer wind-resistance ratings or safe snow loads from shape names.

agr-facility-structure-outer-covers.title: Strengths and weaknesses of exterior covering materials
agr-facility-structure-outer-covers.objective: Compare glass, agricultural PVC, agricultural PO films and rigid films in terms of light, weight, soiling and durability.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p3: Heat retention and weight of agricultural PVC
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p6: Do not arbitrarily fix replacement intervals

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p1: Exterior covering materials cover the outside of a protected structure. Even materials that look equally transparent differ in weight, ease of handling, heat retention and durability. Do not use apparent transparency as the only basis for comparison.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p2: Sheet glass used for exterior covering transmits light well. Light transmission matters, but it alone cannot determine material costs, handling or management of the whole structure.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p3: Agricultural PVC film transmits light and retains heat well. However, its weight, stickiness, tendency to collect dirt and susceptibility to tearing require attention. The Level 1 source also warns that burning it produces toxic gas. Recognize this hazard as well as its benefits, and do not independently choose burning as a disposal method.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p4: Special agricultural polyolefin (PO) films are lighter and less sticky and collect less dirt than agricultural PVC. Even within the film category, agricultural PVC and PO films should not be treated as having the same properties.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p5: Rigid films, including agricultural fluoropolymer films, are also used for exterior covering. Both sources mention durability of ten years or more, but this lesson uses that statement to explain material characteristics, not to guarantee the same service life for every product.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p6: Replacement guidelines differ by material. The two sources also give different ranges of years for agricultural PVC. This lesson does not combine them into one number: learn material characteristics separately from deciding when to replace a product.

agr-facility-structure-outer-covers.activity: Compare agricultural PVC and PO films for weight, stickiness and tendency to collect dirt. Check that statements about durability have not been turned into a guarantee fixing one replacement interval for actual products.

agr-facility-structure-inner-covers.title: Interior covers and what passes through them
agr-facility-structure-inner-covers.objective: Compare transparent films, nonwoven fabric and shade cloth for heat retention and the passage of light, moisture and air.

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-inner-covers-p1: An interior cover is a covering used inside the structure. Even when a film has the same name as an exterior-cover film, distinguish its position and purpose. Interior-cover films are normally thinner than exterior-cover films.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-inner-covers-p2: Transparent films for interior covering include agricultural PVC, PO, polyethylene and EVA films. Their shared transparency does not mean that their heat retention or handling characteristics are identical.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-inner-covers-p3: Agricultural polyethylene film has poorer heat retention than the other flexible films discussed here. When explaining material selection, consider price and transparency separately from resistance to heat loss.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-inner-covers-p4: Nonwoven fabric is used as a heat-retaining curtain. It transmits less light than transparent film but allows water vapor and water to pass through. Lower light transmission does not mean that nothing can pass through it.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-inner-covers-p5: Shade cloth blocks some light while allowing air through. Understand its shading function together with its breathability; do not describe it as functioning like a sealing transparent film.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-inner-covers-p6: When comparing heat-retaining materials, separately consider which of light, water vapor, water and air can pass through. Explain the several properties shown in the lesson rather than linking a material’s name to just one advantage.

agr-facility-structure-inner-covers.activity: Explain how light, moisture and air pass through nonwoven fabric and shade cloth. Check that heat retention, shading and sealing have not been described as the same function.

agr-facility-structure-heating.title: Heating methods and unheated structures
agr-facility-structure-heating.objective: Explain hot-air heating, hot-water heating and unheated structures, without confusing savings on heating fuel with total costs.

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-heating-p1: Protected structures can be heated using hot air or hot water. Classify how heat is supplied separately from the names of fuels.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-heating-p2: Hot-air heating is described as easy to install and widely used. Ease of installation alone does not show that it is the least expensive or always the most efficient method for every structure.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-heating-p3: The sources describe heaters using electricity, gas and wood pellets as well as heavy oil and kerosene. Do not restrict the term “heating equipment” to equipment that uses only one kind of fuel.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-heating-p4: Solar-heat use and heat pumps are also listed in relation to heating protected structures. Distinguish learning the names of methods from checking the procedures for installing, connecting and operating individual machines.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-heating-p5: Unheated houses do not use heaters and are described as suitable for cold-tolerant crops. Avoiding heating-fuel costs is an advantage, but it does not mean that all cultivation costs become zero.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-heating-p6: Even an unheated house may use an additional tunnel cover to improve heat retention at night. Distinguish reducing heat loss from adding heat with a heater, and do not assume that a particular minimum temperature is guaranteed.

agr-facility-structure-heating.activity: Divide a structure’s description into heating method, energy used and measures for retaining heat. When explaining the advantage of an unheated structure, identify exactly which type of cost is avoided.

agr-facility-structure-cover-functions-2.title: Covering functions and their cultivation context
agr-facility-structure-cover-functions-2.objective: Distinguish light diffusion, heat shielding and UV filtering, and explain their effects on pollinating insects and storage conditions as well as their benefits.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-cover-functions-2: Consider water on the covering too
Storage conditions for agricultural EVA film

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-cover-functions-2: The Level 2 source lists light diffusion, which distributes light evenly inside the structure, as a criterion for selecting materials. Distinguish the amount of light transmitted from how incoming light spreads.

Water attached to a covering can block light or be associated with disease. Check functions affecting how droplets form as well. A material’s transparency alone does not mean that the effects of water can be ignored.
