Do not stop at “it clumped”; also record whether there are cracks. Compare this as the intermediate example between soil that will not hold together and soil that retains a firm clump.
paragraphs.agr-par11-soil-handtest-profile-p3: The texture name for the example that retains its clump after squeezing is clay soil. Do not group the small, cracked clump with this same clay-soil example. These are simple distinctions based on the published diagram, separate from precise measurement of clay percentage.
paragraphs.agr-par11-soil-handtest-profile-p4: Brown lowland soil is described not only by its yellowish-brown color, but also by that color extending through all or almost all of the soil layers. Distinguish a record of one yellowish-brown patch at the surface from a description of the entire profile. The source gives natural levees in alluvial lowlands as distribution examples and also mentions use as upland fields.
paragraphs.agr-par11-soil-handtest-profile-p5: The distribution description of gray lowland soil combines places— alluvial fans and plains—with the condition of good drainage. Read this alongside the description of gray soil layers and paddy-field use. This distribution statement alone does not establish that the particular paddy in front of you also drains well.
paragraphs.agr-par11-soil-handtest-profile-p6: For example, a report saying “it clumped slightly when squeezed and had cracks” corresponds to loam through clay loam in the simple test. In contrast, “the entire soil profile was yellowish brown” is information to compare with the brown lowland soil description. Do not replace the hand-test result with a color record or assume yellowish brown determines a hand-test group. Keep texture by feel separate from layers and landform.

agr-par11-management-film-effects.title: Reading film color, structure and functions
agr-par11-management-film-effects.objective: Distinguish the effects of mulch films on soil temperature, weeds and reflection, and how the presence of holes affects rainwater passage.
agr-par11-management-film-effects.activity: For transparent, green, silver and black-and-white two-layer films, record temperature effects and additional purposes separately. Then add the necessary structural condition to a rainwater-entry comparison, and distinguish installation procedures that the sources do not establish.

paragraphTitles.agr-par11-management-film-effects-p1: State the scope of the comparison
paragraphTitles.agr-par11-management-film-effects-p4: Read the two-layer structure of black-and-white film

paragraphs.agr-par11-management-film-effects-p1: In both sources’ color comparison, transparent film ranks highest for raising soil temperature. Read this as its rank within the table, rather than merely an impression of a “high” effect. Do not extend it to a result covering every material and weather condition, or infer the temperature increase or suitable growing temperature from the ranking.
paragraphs.agr-par11-management-film-effects-p2: Green film is described as having a soil-warming effect between transparent and black film, as well as suppressing weeds. Recording temperature alone would omit the other purpose. “Between” compares the soil-temperature effect; it does not assign the same ranking to weed-suppression strength.
paragraphs.agr-par11-management-film-effects-p3: The silver entry lists three functions: limiting soil-temperature rise, pest and disease control, and fruit coloration. Relate these to light reflection, while keeping soil temperature, pests and diseases, and fruit color as separate observations. This entry alone does not guarantee equal effects against all pests and diseases or complete prevention of damage.
paragraphs.agr-par11-management-film-effects-p4: The sources list film with combined white and black layers as limiting soil-temperature rise. Do not judge it from one color alone as “only weed control because it contains black.” Explain the two-layer structure together with the stated purpose. This description does not give installation instructions about which side faces upward.
paragraphs.agr-par11-management-film-effects-p5: Film with planting holes is called perforated film. The sources explain that films other than perforated ones hinder rainwater from infiltrating the soil. Retain the condition of whether holes are present rather than saying rain enters the soil equally through all films. Perforation does not by itself establish that the required water will always be sufficient.
paragraphs.agr-par11-management-film-effects-p6: In film comparison records, separate soil warming or limiting temperature rise, weed suppression and use of reflection. For rainwater, also note whether there are holes. For example, retain both temperature and weeds for green film, and all three stated purposes for silver film. Do not choose a material on one advantage alone; suitability for actual growing conditions needs a separate check.

agr-par11-management-physical-controls.title: Differences between control using light, adhesion and heat
agr-par11-management-physical-controls.objective: Distinguish the actions and targets of reflection, lighting, attraction and trapping, heat, and perimeter planting in the level-2 source’s physical-control examples.
agr-par11-management-physical-controls.activity: Classify reflective tape, yellow lamps, yellow and blue sticky materials, solar heat and warm water, and barrier plants by target and action. Use concrete examples to correct the statement “they are the same method because both are yellow.”

paragraphTitles.agr-par11-management-physical-controls-p: Yellow lamps are not trapping materials
Barrier plants grown around the crop
Control methods work in different ways

paragraphs.agr-par11-management-physical-controls-p: The level-2 source describes using insects’ tendency to approach or avoid light, and gives reflective tape for aphid suppression. Level 1 also pairs aphids with reflective tape. Remember this as a light-reflecting material, separate from trapping insects on an adhesive surface. This example does not determine installation height or spacing.

Level 1 lists yellow lamps as a pest-prevention method, while level 2 gives examples of suppressing nocturnal moths such as the cotton bollworm and common cutworm. Switching on a lamp differs from sticking insects to an adhesive surface. Do not transfer the targets and action of yellow lamps directly to yellow sticky materials just because their color is the same.

Sticky tape is used to attract and capture pests. The level-2 examples pair yellow with greenhouse whiteflies and similar pests, and blue with thrips and similar pests. Distinguish the color–target combinations; do not assume all insects respond identically to the same color. These are examples for organizing targets, not thresholds for pest abundance or installation density.

The level-2 source lists solar heat and warm water separately as physical means of suppressing pests and diseases. Distinguish these heat-based examples from reflection and adhesive capture. Do not merge them into one procedure or infer required temperatures and treatment times. This explanation does not authorize starting treatment without checking specific conditions.

Level 2 gives an example in upland cropping: planting wheat or other small-grain cereals and forage grasses around the field or crop reduces aphid occurrence. It calls these barrier plants. Distinguish this from capturing insects on sticky surfaces or using reflective tape. Do not generalize it to mean that any surrounding plants prevent every pest.

When explaining an example, combine “what is used,” “which target is stated,” and “how it is suppressed.” Pairing aphids with reflective tape, nocturnal moths with yellow lamps, and greenhouse whiteflies with yellow sticky materials helps prevent confusion based on visible color alone. Understanding targets and action does not mean installation or product-use conditions have been checked.

agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details.title: Comparing feed-rice variety traits and costs
agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details.objective: Separate the variety traits emphasized for whole-crop rice silage and feed rice, and explain the sources’ price comparison and concrete cost-reduction examples.
agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details.activity: Make separate columns for WCS and feed rice. Match them with stem-and-leaf volume, eating quality and brown-rice quality, and large grains. Divide cost-reduction measures into growing methods and material use, and note what current information is missing from the price comparison.

paragraphTitles.agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details-p1: WCS varieties also emphasize stems and leaves
paragraphTitles.agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details-p2: A different view of quality from table rice
paragraphTitles.agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details-p3: Large grains as a stated tendency
paragraphTitles.agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details-p4: Unit selling price and production cost
paragraphTitles.agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details-p5: Livestock farmers’ compost as one measure
paragraphTitles.agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details-p6: Compare traits in relation to their use

paragraphs.agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details-p1: Whole-crop rice silage (WCS) uses stems and leaves as well as panicles, so stem-and-leaf volume appears in descriptions of dedicated varieties. Both sources say varieties with abundant stems and leaves have been developed. Describing only a large-grain trait does not fully explain a WCS variety.
paragraphs.agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details-p2: The feed-rice variety description says selection is not governed by cooked-rice eating quality or brown-rice quality. Rice eaten as a staple and rice used as feed are evaluated with different priorities. Do not extend this to mean that no quality checks at all are needed for feed.
paragraphs.agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details-p3: The sources also note that many feed-rice varieties have large grains. This describes a tendency within a variety group. It does not justify identifying rice as feed rice from large grains alone or assuming every feed variety has the same grain size.
paragraphs.agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details-p4: Both sources explain that feed rice needs low-cost production because its unit selling price is lower than table rice. The lesson here is how selling price relates to production cost. No date of price confirmation or amount is provided, so do not treat this statement as current trading prices.
paragraphs.agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details-p5: Cost-reduction examples include using compost from livestock farmers, alongside direct seeding and sparse planting. Separate changes to planting methods from measures concerning materials used. The sources do not say that compost always reduces costs or makes checking fertilizer application rates unnecessary.
paragraphs.agr-par11-riceveg-feed-details-p6: When considering cooperation between rice and livestock farmers, distinguish the emphasis on stem-and-leaf volume for WCS from the emphasis on criteria other than eating quality, together with grain traits, for feed rice. Then compare ways of limiting production cost relative to the unit selling price. This organization does not prescribe a particular variety, feeding amount or compost application rate.

agr-par11-riceveg-organ-examples.title: Finding the utilized-organ category from vegetable names
agr-par11-riceveg-organ-examples.objective: Match the vegetables listed in the sources to leaf-and-stem, root and fruit vegetable categories, and distinguish utilized-organ classification from botanical families.
agr-par11-riceveg-organ-examples.activity: Place labels for spinach, lettuce, asparagus, broccoli, daikon, carrot, lotus, cucumber, tomato, eggplant, sweet pepper and edamame in the three utilized-organ columns. Explain how this differs from a task asking for botanical family names.

paragraphTitles.agr-par11-riceveg-organ-examples-p2: Lettuce is also in the leaf-and-stem column
paragraphTitles.agr-par11-riceveg-organ-examples-p3: Check crops used for stems or flowers too
paragraphTitles.agr-par11-riceveg-organ-examples-p4: Root vegetables also include an underground stem
paragraphTitles.agr-par11-riceveg-organ-examples-p6: Edamame is an example used for its seeds

paragraphs.agr-par11-riceveg-organ-examples-p1: The utilized-organ table lists spinach, Chinese cabbage and cabbage in the leaf-and-stem category. Practice matching each name to that column. This grouping focuses on the part used; it does not mean the three vegetables belong to the same botanical family.
paragraphs.agr-par11-riceveg-organ-examples-p2: Both sources also list lettuce among leaf-and-stem vegetables. Match the name to the source’s column rather than classifying it only by resemblance to cabbage. This category alone does not determine lettuce variety or whether it forms a head.
paragraphs.agr-par11-riceveg-organ-examples-p3: The sources also place asparagus and broccoli in the leaf-and-stem column. Do not move them out merely because the category name contains “leaf.” The aim here is to learn the sources’ classification by utilized organ, not to assume that every crop is eaten for exactly the same organ.
paragraphs.agr-par11-riceveg-organ-examples-p4: Daikon and carrot are examples of root vegetables, and lotus appears in the same column. The lotus illustration is labeled lotus rhizome (renkon). This category is not limited to roots alone: the sources group crops used for roots or underground stems together. Do not equate their individual organ structures solely on the basis of this classification.
paragraphs.agr-par11-riceveg-organ-examples-p5: Both sources place cucumber, tomato, eggplant and sweet pepper in the fruit-vegetable column. Practice finding this utilized-organ category from each crop name. Do not replace a grouping based on use with a botanical family name or a single growing method.
paragraphs.agr-par11-riceveg-organ-examples-p6: Both sources also list edamame in the fruit-vegetable column. This column includes crops eaten for seeds as well as fruits, so do not switch to another classification axis simply because the name refers to beans. Levels 1 and 2 present crops such as strawberry differently, but this lesson covers the crop correspondences common to both.

agr-par11-facility-heat-cover-installati.title: Organizing heat retention by material, layers and installation
agr-par11-facility-heat-cover-installati.objective: Compare covering insulation by layer count and material, and distinguish airtightness, fixed inner linings, movable curtains and tunnels inside greenhouses.
agr-par11-facility-heat-cover-installati.activity: Arrange written labels for the outer covering, fixed inner lining, movable curtain and tunnel inside a greenhouse. Explain comparisons of layer count for the same material separately from comparisons of different materials, and include a check for gaps.

paragraphTitles.agr-par11-facility-heat-cover-installati: Compare layer count and material separately
Position of a fixed inner lining

paragraphs.agr-par11-facility-heat-cover-installati: The level-1 source explains that cooling equipment may be used to lower temperatures during hot summer conditions. In contrast, insulation retains heat through coverings and similar means. Do not group ventilation and cooling with insulating covers as methods that change temperature in the same direction.

The insulating effect of coverings depends on the material type and the number of layers. The source states that more layers of the same material provide greater heat retention. Do not extend this into judging different materials by layer count alone.

Even when a covering is installed, the presence of gaps is a separate check. The source also says preventing gaps and improving airtightness helps retain heat. Alongside fields for material names and layer count, a field checking gaps separates the conditions affecting insulation.

One inner-lining method fixes insulating material a short distance inside the outer covering. This means understanding the positions of outer cover and inner lining, rather than adding more covering on the outside. The source does not determine an exact gap dimension or a universal installation method for every facility.

Another inner-lining method uses movable curtains that can open and close. Compared with a fixed lining, its distinguishing feature is this opening-and-closing structure. Record the curtain system separately from material types such as nonwoven fabric; do not infer the material from the equipment name alone.

The source also shows single or double tunnels inside a greenhouse. The outer covering over the whole greenhouse, inner curtains and tunnels around plants occupy different positions. When describing the number of layers, specify which part is being counted. Do not turn this into a universal prescription for required layers or temperature settings.

agr-par11-facility-plant-condition-signs.title: Reading seedling and crop abnormalities by part and condition
agr-par11-facility-plant-condition-signs.objective: Separate observations of cotyledons, stem tips, roots, fruit, leaf color and internodes in the level-1 disorder examples, without identifying a cause from appearance alone.
agr-par11-facility-plant-condition-signs.activity: Make columns for stem tips, leaves, roots and fruit, and place the examples of water shortage, excess moisture, calcium deficiency, excess nitrogen and insufficient light in them. State observed conditions separately from suspected causes, and do not decide fertilizer or irrigation quantities from appearance.

paragraphTitles.agr-par11-facility-plant-condition-signs: Two visible signs of water shortage
From excess moisture to root damage
Do not judge excess nitrogen by color alone
Observe stems and leaves together under insufficient light

paragraphs.agr-par11-facility-plant-condition-signs: Missing cotyledons are among the stated features of unhealthy seedlings. Observe whether cotyledons are present separately from counting true leaves. Other features, such as leggy growth and lesions, also matter, so do not use cotyledons as the sole health criterion. Record which plant part was inspected.

In the source’s water-shortage example, the stem tip droops and leaves wilt. Recording the direction of the stem tip separately from leaf condition conveys observations more clearly than simply saying the plant “looks weak.” These appearances alone do not establish the cause or required irrigation amount.

The excess-moisture explanation starts with too much water causing insufficient air in the soil. It describes damage such as root rot, necrosis and root lignification, which may ultimately lead to plant death. Read this as an example relating water and air around roots, not a claim that moist soil always causes death in the same sequence.

The fertilizer-deficiency section gives blossom-end rot as an example of a physiological disorder caused by calcium deficiency, with a tomato-fruit photograph. Organize leaf-yellowing examples separately from disorders appearing on fruit. Do not use the photograph’s appearance alone to identify a cause or decide fertilizer quantities.

The excess-nitrogen example includes dark-green leaves, excessive vegetative growth and greater susceptibility to lodging. Dark green alone does not prove healthy growth. Separate leaf color, density of growth and tendency to fall over, and do not confuse these with the example of lower leaves turning yellow under nitrogen deficiency.

The insufficient-sunlight example describes thin stems, long internodes and thin, large leaves. Do not judge growth as good from height alone; observe stem thickness, internode length, and leaf thickness and size together. These are related examples in the source, not diagnostic criteria that establish insufficient light without checking other conditions.

agr-par11-flower-surface-methods.title: Four methods of managing orchard ground
agr-par11-flower-surface-methods.objective: Distinguish clean cultivation, mulching, sod culture and combined management, and explain advantages and cautions when grass is retained.
agr-par11-flower-surface-methods.activity: Match three ground records—bare soil, laid cut grass, and living forage grass—to their management methods. For sod culture, make three columns for water and nutrients, pests and diseases, and natural enemies. Briefly state what to check before judging.

paragraphTitles.agr-par11-flower-surface-methods-p1: Clean cultivation keeps the ground bare
paragraphTitles.agr-par11-flower-surface-methods-p3: Sod culture covers the surface with growing grass
paragraphTitles.agr-par11-flower-surface-methods-p5: Consider pests and natural enemies together

paragraphs.agr-par11-flower-surface-methods-p1: Clean cultivation is also called the bare-ground method. It maintains an orchard soil surface without grass. It describes the ground condition to maintain, rather than merely a single mowing operation. Uncovered topsoil is more easily washed away by rainwater, so do not assess the absence of grass only as an advantage.
paragraphs.agr-par11-flower-surface-methods-p2: Mulching covers the ground over the area where roots spread with straw, cut grass, polyethylene film or similar materials. The stated effects include preventing soil loss and evaporation of soil moisture. The condition of the surface cover differs from growing live grass. Record the material before identifying the management method.
paragraphs.agr-par11-flower-surface-methods-p3: Sod culture grows grass to cover the orchard ground. The main examples in the source are forage plants in the grass and legume families. Distinguish mulching with cut grass from using grass growing on site in sod culture. Family examples alone do not establish that the same species suits every orchard.
paragraphs.agr-par11-flower-surface-methods-p4: Grass in sod culture also uses nutrients and water and may compete with fruit trees. The visible grass cover alone does not show that trees have enough water or nutrients. Alongside the cover condition, retain a caution in management records that trees and grass use the same resources.
paragraphs.agr-par11-flower-surface-methods-p5: Grass may provide a place for pests and diseases to occur, but may also house beneficial natural enemies. Do not conclude from grass presence alone that only harmful organisms increase or that it always helps control them. Keep both possibilities open, distinguishing checks of actual occurrence from the name of the management method.
paragraphs.agr-par11-flower-surface-methods-p6: Combined management brings these methods together to use their strengths and compensate for weaknesses. Rather than applying one name to every place, explain what is covered and what is retained in the combination. To summarize, distinguish keeping bare ground, covering with materials and growing grass, then consider the purpose of combining them.

agr-par11-flower-soil-profile.title: Connecting surface management with changes within the soil
agr-par11-flower-soil-profile.objective: Use schematic comparisons of clean cultivation, sod culture and mulching to explain differences in organic matter, aggregates and rainwater.
agr-par11-flower-soil-profile.activity: Make four columns for clean cultivation, sod culture, organic mulch and polyethylene film. Record what the text says about changes in organic matter, aggregates and rainwater. Leave unstated depths, percentages and days required for changes blank; do not infer numbers.

paragraphTitles.agr-par11-flower-soil-profile-p1: Compare the surface and subsurface separately
paragraphTitles.agr-par11-flower-soil-profile-p2: Erosion susceptibility shown for clean cultivation
paragraphTitles.agr-par11-flower-soil-profile-p3: Layers and aggregates under sod culture

paragraphs.agr-par11-flower-soil-profile-p1: When comparing ground management, examine not only surface cover but also the organic-matter-containing layers beneath it and the structure of upper soil. The source’s schematic distinguishes areas with high, medium and low organic matter and shows their extent for each method. High, medium and low are comparison labels, not measured depths or content percentages.
paragraphs.agr-par11-flower-soil-profile-p2: The clean-cultivation comparison shows upper soil with little coarse organic matter and poorly developed aggregation. Read the relationship that topsoil in this state is easily washed away by rainwater. Connect the bare surface condition with the internal description of low organic matter and poorly developed soil aggregates.
paragraphs.agr-par11-flower-soil-profile-p3: The sod-culture schematic shows the organic-matter-containing layer extending downward. It depicts abundant coarse organic matter and well-developed aggregates in the upper soil. Treat the spread of the organic layer and the grouping of soil particles as separate observations, so comparison goes beyond simply saying grass is present on the surface.
paragraphs.agr-par11-flower-soil-profile-p4: For mulch made from organic materials such as straw and cut grass, the source describes humification of the material and its effects spreading into lower layers. Its comparison also shows aggregates increasing during this process. Describe the process rather than treating newly laid material and soil after humification as the same state.
paragraphs.agr-par11-flower-soil-profile-p5: In the upper soil under organic mulch, the source shows advanced humification and many water-stable aggregates. The focus is their ability to retain their structure under the action of water. Beyond the description of aggregate development under sod culture, compare organic mulch with attention to this water stability.
paragraphs.agr-par11-flower-soil-profile-p6: Covering with polyethylene film and similar materials is described as limiting rainwater entry into the soil. Even within mulching, do not transfer the explanation of organic matter humifying and spreading into lower layers directly to film. In summary, distinguish runoff on bare ground, organic layers and aggregates under sod, humification and water stability under organic mulch, and rainwater entry under film.

agr-par12-general-rice-classification-de.title: Keep rice regions, grain traits and growing locations as separate classifications
agr-par12-general-rice-classification-de.objective: Explain the level-2 source’s growing regions, grain-shape and stickiness tendencies, the name kome, paddy and upland rice, and distribution in Japan as separate classification axes.
agr-par12-general-rice-classification-de.activity: Add the main regions for Asian and African rice, and compare indica and japonica by shape and stickiness. In separate columns, record the scope of kome, growing locations for paddy and upland rice, and Japan’s predominant type and distribution. Explain without mixing classification axes.

paragraphTitles.agr-par12-general-rice-classification-de: Two rice species and their main growing regions
Pair indica grain traits with its cooked properties
Compare japonica using the same two traits
Distinguish paddy and upland rice by growing location
Read Japan’s predominant type separately from its distribution

paragraphs.agr-par12-general-rice-classification-de: The level-2 source describes Asian rice as grown worldwide, mainly in Asia, and African rice as grown mainly in West Africa. Match these main regions to the two names already learned. “Mainly” does not mean they are entirely absent elsewhere. Record the place name and species classification together.

The indica description gives two tendencies: grains are generally long and slender, and many varieties are not sticky when cooked. Grain shape and properties after cooking are separate observations. Organize them as tendencies stated in the source, not as a shape-only rule identifying every variety or a guarantee that all indica has the same texture.

Japonica is described as generally having short, rounded grains, with many varieties becoming sticky when cooked. Compare both indica and japonica using the same two items: grain shape and cooked stickiness. Learn to explain these traits as well as naming the classification predominant in Japan.

The source calls both brown rice and milled white rice kome. Alongside the previously learned hulling and milling sequence, check the scope of this name. For example, a brown-rice record labeled kome does not establish that it was milled white rice. When distinguishing processing stages, also specify brown or white rice.

Rice grown in paddies is called suito, while rice grown in upland fields is rikuto, also called okabo. This classification corresponds to where it is grown. Do not substitute these two names directly for the indica–japonica classification or the brown–white processing stages.

The next explanation says most rice cultivation in Japan is paddy rice, and rice is grown in every prefecture, from warm Okinawa to cold Hokkaido. “Mainly in what kind of place” differs from “in which regions cultivation exists.” This distribution statement does not establish that the same variety or cropping pattern works at every location.

agr-par12-general-direct-seeding-compari.title: Compare direct seeding’s benefits and conditional drawbacks
agr-par12-general-direct-seeding-compari.objective: Distinguish the level-2 source’s description of direct-seeding adoption, benefits for expansion, climate-, variety- and bird-related drawbacks, and the labor-time example for overall mechanization.
agr-par12-general-direct-seeding-compari.activity: Organize direct seeding into five columns: extent of adoption, lighter work and scale, climate, varieties and bird damage. Put “about 25 hours annually per 10a” in a separate column for overall mechanization. Do not add current adoption percentages or hours saved that the source cannot establish.

paragraphTitles.agr-par12-general-direct-seeding-compari: “Very little” is not an adoption percentage
Link lighter work with farm scale
Climate and unstable emergence or establishment
Record bird damage as a separate drawback
Pair mechanized labor time with area

paragraphs.agr-par12-general-direct-seeding-compari: The level-2 rice introduction says direct seeding, in which seed rice is sown directly into paddy fields, is very limited. This is a qualitative description of adoption at publication. For example, write “very limited according to the source,” without adding an unstated percentage or claiming adoption remains the same today.

The benefits table links reduced nursery and transplanting work to easier expansion of scale. Add this meaning for farm scale to the work-reduction explanation already learned. “Easier to expand” does not guarantee every farm can increase its area. Explain the reason work becomes lighter separately from the possibility of expansion.

One drawback is that climate can make emergence and seedling establishment unstable. Record establishment alongside emergence as a term focusing on seedlings establishing and growing after sowing. Explaining that seeds are directly sown does not verify stable seedling growth. This statement does not specify countermeasure materials or treatment conditions.

The direct-seeding drawbacks table qualifies lodging susceptibility by variety. Simply writing “direct-seeded plants always lodge” loses both the variety condition and degree of possibility. Keep susceptibility together with differences among varieties, without applying identical outcomes or countermeasures to all varieties.

The source also lists susceptibility to bird damage as a drawback of direct seeding, separate from climate-related emergence instability and variety-related lodging. For example, an uneven seedling stand alone does not establish birds as the cause of every loss. Understanding this entry differs from identifying bird species or choosing specific control methods.

The same page describes an established integrated mechanized system and annual labor time of about 25 hours per 10a. Read the area of 10a, annual period and approximation together with the number. This is an example concerning rice mechanization, not time spent only on direct seeding or hours saved after adopting it. Nor is it a current result for every farm.

agr-par12-soil-nutrient-details.title: Separate nutrient functions from deficiency and excess
agr-par12-soil-nutrient-details.objective: Use the level-2 explanations of nitrogen, phosphate and potash to distinguish leaf size, flowering and fruiting, soil conditions, roots and uptake of other elements.
agr-par12-soil-nutrient-details.activity: Make columns for nitrogen, phosphate and potash. Record functions, deficiency/excess examples and soil conditions separately. For potassium deficiency, also note which leaves and parts change, and explain why observation alone cannot determine fertilizer quantities.

paragraphTitles.agr-par12-soil-nutrient-details-p1: Observe leaf size under nitrogen deficiency too
paragraphTitles.agr-par12-soil-nutrient-details-p3: The condition of soil rich in aluminum or iron

paragraphs.agr-par12-soil-nutrient-details-p1: Level 2 lists small leaves as well as pale leaf color in its nitrogen-deficiency examples. Separate color and size records to show which feature was observed. Do not identify nitrogen deficiency or decide extra fertilizer quantities from small leaves alone. Organize leaf size as one observation example in the nitrogen explanation.
paragraphs.agr-par12-soil-nutrient-details-p2: The phosphate entry describes its main influence on flowering and fruiting. This focuses on different growth stages from nitrogen’s leaf color and stem-and-leaf growth. For example, separate flowering and fruit-set columns from leaf color. Do not turn this relationship into an instruction that more phosphate always produces more flowers or fruit.
paragraphs.agr-par12-soil-nutrient-details-p3: The phosphate explanation adds that in soils with abundant aluminum or iron, it becomes less water-soluble and less available to plants. Distinguish a component being present in fertilizer from its availability in soil. Do not estimate soil aluminum or iron amounts from leaf or flower appearance, or record this condition as verified without checking it.
paragraphs.agr-par12-soil-nutrient-details-p4: The level-2 potash entry states that it influences root development. Include underground roots as well as aboveground leaves when organizing nutrient functions. Separate root development from the small-leaf nitrogen-deficiency example to avoid confusing the three nutrients. Root condition alone does not allow calculation of the required potash amount.
paragraphs.agr-par12-soil-nutrient-details-p5: Excess potassium is described as inhibiting uptake of other elements. Simply supplying more to avoid deficiency overlooks uptake of other nutrients. This explains a relationship between nutrients. No universal upper application limit is stated, so do not invent a limit or additional quantity.
paragraphs.agr-par12-soil-nutrient-details-p6: Examples include leaf margins turning brown starting from lower or outer leaves, and spots across the whole leaf. Go beyond “leaf discoloration”: separate locations—lower/outer leaves, margins, whole leaf—from appearances—brown color and spots. These are published deficiency examples, not diagnostic criteria proving potassium is the sole cause whenever spots appear.

agr-par12-soil-application-area-tools.title: Compare application areas and spreader functions
agr-par12-soil-application-area-tools.objective: Distinguish the areas and purposes of whole-field and localized fertilization in level 2, and compare three spreaders by materials and coverage.
agr-par12-soil-application-area-tools.activity: Match methods and purposes to whole-field and root-growth-area columns. For the three spreaders, record granular materials, organic matter such as compost, and powdered or sand-like lime. Separate application quantities and operating conditions that machine names do not establish.

paragraphTitles.agr-par12-soil-application-area-tools-p2: The purpose of spreading roots widely
paragraphTitles.agr-par12-soil-application-area-tools-p6: Material-form conditions for a lime sower

paragraphs.agr-par12-soil-application-area-tools-p1: Whole-field fertilization puts fertilizer across the field; localized fertilization applies it only where roots grow. The distinction is placement area. Keep this separate from timing, such as basal and topdressing, or fertilizer-component classifications. Even within one field record, when and where fertilizer was applied can occupy separate columns.
paragraphs.agr-par12-soil-application-area-tools-p2: The source associates whole-field application with encouraging roots to spread widely. Retain this purpose alongside the coverage description. Do not turn it into a ranking that whole-field application is always best for every crop and soil. “Widely” does not imply that larger application quantities are better.
paragraphs.agr-par12-soil-application-area-tools-p3: Localized application is described as effective when reducing waste. Pair this purpose with application where roots grow. Choosing whole-field or localized application differs from calculating required nutrient amounts. Do not add a uniform percentage saving for all fertilizers or instructions to place fertilizer directly against roots.
paragraphs.agr-par12-soil-application-area-tools-p4: A broadcaster distributes granular fertilizers and soil amendments over a wide area. Record both material state—granular—and coverage—wide. This explains its difference from machines handling organic matter such as compost more clearly than learning names alone. The function alone does not establish actual settings or all compatible products.
paragraphs.agr-par12-soil-application-area-tools-p5: A manure spreader is shown distributing organic matter such as compost across the whole field. Pair compost as a material with whole-field spreading as a function. Compare its stated materials with the broadcaster’s granular fertilizer. Capability for whole-field spreading does not mean that whole-field fertilization must be chosen for that field.
paragraphs.agr-par12-soil-application-area-tools-p6: The lime-sower entry describes spreading powdered or sand-like lime and organic fertilizers. Retain the material-form conditions, not merely the name lime. Compare the three machines using their combinations of granular materials, compost and similar matter, and powdered/sand-like materials. Matching names to uses does not verify compatible products, settings or safe operation.

agr-par12-management-machine-mechanisms.title: Distinguishing sprayers and mowers by mechanism
agr-par12-management-machine-mechanisms.objective: Explain manual pressure, powered pressure and airflow in sprayers, and mower power, cutting mechanisms and ride-on designs.
agr-par12-management-machine-mechanisms.activity: Compare pressure and airflow characteristics of manual sprayers, powered sprayers and SS machines. For three mower types, compare carrying method, cutting mechanism and ride-on capability only within the text’s scope. A photograph does not establish operating competence.

paragraphTitles.agr-par12-management-machine-mechanisms-: An SS with a tank and fan
A mower that chops grass with vertical rotation
Match ride-on design with cutting width

paragraphs.agr-par12-management-machine-mechanisms-: The level-2 shoulder-carried manual sprayer stores pressure manually and sprays a chemical solution as mist onto crops or weeds. Link its name not only to carrying position but also to how pressure is generated. “Manual” is not simply a person holding it; it distinguishes pressurization. Chemical-solution selection and pressure settings are outside this lesson.

The source shows a backpack powered sprayer pressurized by an engine or motor to spray a chemical solution. Separate carrying differences—backpack or shoulder—from pressure-generation differences—manual or powered. Do not assume all backpack equipment is manual.

The speed sprayer, also abbreviated SS, has a large tank and large fan. The source describes a mechanism applying large quantities of chemicals to fruit trees and similar crops at once, reaching high places and wide areas. Separate the tank’s liquid-holding role from use of the fan. This does not guarantee numerical reach or quantities, or absence of drift outside the area.

Brushcutters are also called grass cutters. Carried on the shoulder or back, they use an engine or motor to rotate a cutter and cut weeds. Examples shown include a carbide-tipped saw blade and a nylon-cord cutter. Organize carrying method, rotation power and cutter type separately. This does not say both cutters are interchangeable on every model.

The self-propelled mower description names the hammer-knife mower. Its hammer-knife cutters rotate vertically to chop grass finely. Do not apply the portable brushcutter explanation directly to this cutting mechanism. Learn the rotation mechanism together with the grass-chopping function.

A ride-on mower lets a person ride while mowing. The source describes a wide cutting width suitable for large grounds. Do not equate “self-propelled” with “ride-on”; distinguish machines explicitly described as ridden. This comparison describes machines, not slope limits, operating qualifications or actual-machine procedures.

agr-par12-management-power-fuel-informat.title: Separate power-source classification from fuel checks
agr-par12-management-power-fuel-informat.objective: Distinguish DC/AC and single-/three-phase classifications, foreign-matter risks at connectors, and source cautions about unidentified and long-stored fuel.
agr-par12-management-power-fuel-informat.activity: Use separate classification columns for DC/AC and single-/three-phase, matching the dryer and heater examples. Separately list connector debris, unidentified fuel and deterioration during storage. Report without filling unknown information from appearance.

paragraphTitles.agr-par12-management-power-fuel-informat: Compare power transmission in single and three phases
Dust and debris can also cause accidents
Link long storage with machine trouble

paragraphs.agr-par12-management-power-fuel-informat: Level 2 gives dry cells and batteries as direct-current sources labeled DC. Outlets and similar sources are alternating current, labeled AC. Match examples and abbreviations without swapping AC onto batteries or DC onto outlets. This classification alone does not establish that a machine can be connected.

The source distinguishes single-phase from three-phase, explaining that single-phase transmits less power at once and three-phase more. It then says smaller machines often use single-phase and larger machines three-phase. Retain “often” rather than treating every large-looking machine as three-phase.

Rice dryers and facility heaters are examples of large machines using three-phase AC. Record drying and heating purposes with their names rather than just “large machines.” Seeing these examples differs from checking the power specifications of individual machines on site.

The source warns that inserting an electrical plug with dust or debris trapped between plug and outlet can also cause accidents. Checking wet hands differs from checking foreign matter at the connection. This does not permit use with debris present or describe cleaning while energized.

The source’s checking principle is not to use stored fuel whose type is unknown. Using fuel suited to a machine first requires knowing what it is. Do not replace verified identification with its storage location or appearance. This lesson does not devise identification procedures based on color examples or container appearance.

The source explains that fuel deteriorates during long storage and can cause machine failure, warning against using old fuel. Separate the earlier check of fuel identity from whether its condition has changed in storage. Do not invent a universal storage period for all fuels or mixing procedures to restore old fuel.

agr-par12-riceveg-legume-uses.title: Link legume functions with their uses
agr-par12-riceveg-legume-uses.objective: Distinguish legume-family membership from oil-crop classification, and explain rhizobia, Japan-grown soybeans’ food uses, dedicated varieties and postharvest peanut handling.
agr-par12-riceveg-legume-uses.activity: Place soybean, peanut, azuki and common bean in the family column, and separately mark the two also classed as oil crops. Organize soybeans’ five foods and dedicated varieties. For peanuts, distinguish postharvest steps from uses retaining the shell.

paragraphTitles.agr-par12-riceveg-legume-uses-p1: Match four crops to the legume family
paragraphTitles.agr-par12-riceveg-legume-uses-p2: A separate classification based on oil use

paragraphs.agr-par12-riceveg-legume-uses-p1: Level 2 lists soybean, peanut, azuki and common bean as legumes. Do not stop at soybean and azuki; match peanut and common bean to the same family column too. This botanical grouping does not say they are all processed into the same food.
paragraphs.agr-par12-riceveg-legume-uses-p2: Soybean and peanut are also classified as oil crops among industrial crops because they contain much oil. Botanical legume classification and classification for oil production can coexist. Do not erase food uses when recording “oil crop”; retain the classification focus in the heading.
paragraphs.agr-par12-riceveg-legume-uses-p3: The source explains that nitrogen-fixing rhizobia live symbiotically on legume roots. Read the statement that these crops can be grown with less fertilizer in connection with this relationship. It does not mean crops obtain unlimited quantities of all nutrients themselves. This alone cannot justify zero fertilizer or specific application rates.
paragraphs.agr-par12-riceveg-legume-uses-p4: The source’s main uses for domestically grown soybeans are tofu, natto, simmered beans, miso and soy sauce. Organize all five as food uses connecting one crop to multiple products. The list gives no processing steps or recipes; keep name matching separate from food-manufacturing procedures.
paragraphs.agr-par12-riceveg-legume-uses-p5: Level 2 says soybean and edamame, which is used immature, each have dedicated varieties. Alongside the basic fact that immature soybean is called edamame, check variety distinctions matched to use. Do not reinterpret this as every variety suiting the same uses merely by changing harvest time.
paragraphs.agr-par12-riceveg-legume-uses-p6: For peanuts, the described sequence is digging out underground pods, drying, then shelling. Uses include roasted peanuts in shells, roasted kernels and peanut snacks, as well as boiling and eating them in their pods. Distinguish uses that handle shells differently rather than assuming every food follows the same postharvest sequence.

agr-par12-riceveg-grain-purpose.title: Distinguish small-grain cereals and maize by use
agr-par12-riceveg-grain-purpose.objective: Explain cereal food/feed uses, sweet corn and dent corn, dedicated varieties versus F1, and the stated conditions for a cleaning crop.
agr-par12-riceveg-grain-purpose.activity: Compare wheat with the other three cereals by use. Then separate sweet corn and dent corn by growth stage, purpose and form of use, recording dedicated varieties and F1 separately. For the cleaning-crop example, note which preceding-crop land is used and what is removed.

paragraphTitles.agr-par12-riceveg-grain-purpose-p6: A following crop that absorbs excess nutrients

paragraphs.agr-par12-riceveg-grain-purpose-p1: Level 2 says wheat is used mostly for food, while barley, rye and oats are widely used for feed as well as food. Compare their stated uses rather than memorizing four names alone. Do not turn this contrast into a claim that wheat has no nonfood uses.
paragraphs.agr-par12-riceveg-grain-purpose-p2: Sweet corn is presented as eaten fresh at an immature stage in Japan and classified as a vegetable. Do not restrict maize to mature grain use from its crop name alone; read growth stage together with purpose. This does not prescribe cooking methods or serving quantities.
paragraphs.agr-par12-riceveg-grain-purpose-p3: Dent corn is grown for feed and used as green fodder or made into silage. Its purpose and forms of use differ from using sweet corn’s immature ears. Record green cutting as a utilization method separately from silage as a processed, stored form.
paragraphs.agr-par12-riceveg-grain-purpose-p4: The source says sweet corn and dent corn each have dedicated varieties. “Dedicated” indicates the intended use. Do not assume any maize suits the same use without checking variety; provide a column distinguishing food and feed purposes.
paragraphs.agr-par12-riceveg-grain-purpose-p5: The same explanation says almost all maize varieties are first-generation hybrids, also called F1 or hybrids. Do not drop “almost” and make an exceptionless claim. Dedicated variety describes purpose, while F1 describes crossing origin; they can be recorded separately.
paragraphs.agr-par12-riceveg-grain-purpose-p6: Maize’s strong nutrient uptake is also used after vegetables on land prone to salt accumulation, removing excess nutrients as a cleaning crop, called seiko sakumotsu in the source. Focus on the preceding crop’s land and nutrient uptake. This is not a treatment eliminating all soil diseases or guaranteeing nutrient levels afterward. The example alone cannot determine cropping conditions or duration.

agr-par12-facility-ventilation-condition.title: Ventilation effects and opening conditions in cold weather
agr-par12-facility-ventilation-condition.objective: Explain how level-2 ventilation effects vary with location and environment, mechanically controlled opening order, avoiding direct cold drafts, and shading as an option.
agr-par12-facility-ventilation-condition.activity: Separate fan capacity, installation position, air temperature and humidity. Explain mechanically controlled opening order and two cold-weather responses. Compare forced ventilation with shading when natural ventilation does not lower temperature.

paragraphTitles.agr-par12-facility-ventilation-condition: Capacity alone does not determine effectiveness
The stated scope of tomato facilities
Two options if natural ventilation does not cool enough

paragraphs.agr-par12-facility-ventilation-condition: Forced ventilation uses electrically driven fans, but level 2 lists more than capacity as influences on effectiveness. Installation position, temperature and humidity also matter. Do not assume equal effects from equal-capacity fans alone; check position and environment separately.

The level-2 explanation includes both taking in outside air and pushing hot indoor air out. Distinguish observing an air-moving device from the function of exchanging indoor and outdoor air. This alone does not determine the required airflow or installation location for a particular facility.

Level 2 says forced ventilation is most widespread in protected tomato cultivation. Read this as the source’s crop-specific description, not identical use across all crops. It provides no current adoption percentage or installed-unit count and does not verify today’s adoption.

Begin with natural ventilation. For mechanically controlled systems, level 2 gives the order of opening curtains first, then roof vents. Proceed to side vents if the inside temperature remains high. Retain mechanical control and continuing heat as conditions alongside the opening names.

Opening side vents in cold weather can expose crops directly to cold outdoor air. The source describes narrowing the side-vent opening or keeping side curtains closed. Do not read this as always fully opening curtains. Link both responses to avoiding direct cold drafts.

When natural ventilation fails to lower temperature, level 2 describes forced ventilation or shading to prevent excessive warming. Air exchange and light interception use different mechanisms. Do not invent an instruction always to use both together, shading percentages or operating setpoints; compare them as additional source options.

agr-par12-facility-strawberry-developmen.title: Read strawberry runners and flower buds by their conditions
agr-par12-facility-strawberry-developmen.objective: Distinguish the two runner-development conditions, natural flower-bud differentiation and flowering the next year, promotion conditions and listed nursery-method names.
agr-par12-facility-strawberry-developmen.activity: Use three conditional columns for runner development, flower-bud differentiation from autumn, and flowering/fruiting from the following spring. Separately list promotion conditions and four nursery methods. Do not add unstated temperatures, durations or fertilizer-withholding schedules.

paragraphTitles.agr-par12-facility-strawberry-developmen: Flowering and fruiting from the next spring
Names of cool-highland and night-cooling propagation
Distinguish low-temperature dark and pot methods too

paragraphs.agr-par12-facility-strawberry-developmen: Earlier seedling lessons covered mother plants, runners and daughter plants. Level 2 explains that runners develop after flowering and fruiting end, or when nutrition is excessive. These conditions are not both required simultaneously. A runner alone also does not prove the particular plant has excessive nutrition.

Under natural conditions, flower-bud differentiation occurs from autumn with low temperatures and short days. Read season, temperature and day length together; do not replace this with flowers opening in autumn. This is the bud becoming a flower bud, distinct from observing open flowers or harvested fruit.

In the same natural-condition explanation, higher temperatures and long days from the following spring lead to flowering and fruiting. Preserve the year-to-year connection between autumn’s low-temperature/short-day differentiation and flowering/fruiting in the warmer, longer days of the following year. Do not mix both condition pairs into one stage.

Nursery conditions for earlier flower-bud differentiation include low temperature, short days and withholding fertilizer. Do not select only temperature and day length and imply they are the entire list. This is learning the stated examples, not telling growers when or for how many days to withhold fertilizer from particular seedlings.

Level 2 names cool-highland seedling raising (高冷地育苗) and night-cooling seedling raising (夜冷育苗). Keep them distinct as method names appearing in the source. The page gives no detailed procedures, temperatures or durations, so do not infer and add operating conditions from the names.

The same list includes low-temperature dark seedling raising (低温暗黒育苗) and pot seedling raising (ポット育苗). Do not treat the former name and the container term “pot” as one meaning; record each method separately. Being able to list four names differs from mastering their procedures. Do not claim differentiation is guaranteed under identical conditions for every method.

agr-par12-flower-cultivar-area.title: Compare cultivar-area shares for six fruit crops within the same source year
agr-par12-flower-cultivar-area.objective: Read the published 2017 cultivar-area shares and explain within-crop ranking, sums, different populations and limits on unlisted portions.
agr-par12-flower-cultivar-area.activity: For each crop’s three cultivars, record 2017, cultivated area, cultivar name and percentage. Compare the sums of the two listed grape and Japanese-pear cultivars. Explain why equal 17% shares in different crops do not establish equal actual areas, and what cannot be determined about unlisted peach shares.

paragraphTitles.agr-par12-flower-cultivar-area-p4: Match persimmon cultivars with sweetness or astringency
paragraphTitles.agr-par12-flower-cultivar-area-p5: Add two Japanese-pear cultivars and compare
paragraphTitles.agr-par12-flower-cultivar-area-p6: Do not assign all unlisted peaches to one cultivar

paragraphs.agr-par12-flower-cultivar-area-p1: The source’s 2017 satsuma examples are 宮川早生 at 17%, 青島温州 at 10% and 興津早生 at 9%. Read each as a cultivated-area share. These differ in both year and subject from the same page’s 2014 citrus-shipment explanation. This lesson restricts itself to the 2017 cultivar comparison, not current areas or shipment volumes.
paragraphs.agr-par12-flower-cultivar-area-p2: The listed 2017 apple examples are ふじ 47%, つがる 12% and 王林 7%. Among these three, ふじ has the largest share. This ranking does not reveal individual fruit size or selling price. Record cultivar, cultivated-area measure, year and percentage as a set.
paragraphs.agr-par12-flower-cultivar-area-p3: The same 2017 grape list gives 巨峰 22%, ピオーネ 12% and デラウェア 12%. The latter two have equal published values, so their order in the list does not rank one above the other. Adding 巨峰 and ピオーネ gives 34%. This is a share within grapes, not an area total including other fruit crops.
paragraphs.agr-par12-flower-cultivar-area-p4: The 2017 persimmon examples are 富有 17%, 平核無 12% and 刀根早生 11%. The source identifies 富有 as sweet persimmon and the latter two as astringent, so retain these pairings. Equal 17% values for 富有 and 宮川早生 do not imply equal actual areas: the denominators are persimmon area and satsuma area respectively.
paragraphs.agr-par12-flower-cultivar-area-p5: The 2017 Japanese-pear examples are 幸水 30%, 豊水 21% and 新高 7%. 幸水 plus 豊水 is 51%, larger within that crop than the 34% for 巨峰 plus ピオーネ within grapes. This compares shares in separate crop populations. It neither compares actual pear and grape areas nor calculates a combined area share.
paragraphs.agr-par12-flower-cultivar-area-p6: The 2017 peach examples are あかつき 15%, 白鳳 13% and 川中島白桃 11%. Their simple sum is 39%, leaving a difference of 61 percentage points from 100%. This difference cannot be assigned to one unlisted cultivar. Since rounding of original values is unspecified, do not treat it as a precise residual-area calculation; understand that some portion is unlisted.

agr-par12-flower-group-records.title: Check flower-group records by headings and subcategories
agr-par12-flower-group-records.objective: Match additional flower names to flowering woody plants, orchids, succulents and other headings, and check foliage-plant and herb subcategories and recording errors.
agr-par12-flower-group-records.activity: Create headings for flowering woody plants, orchids, succulents/cacti, foliage plants and herbs, and enter the additional names in the text. Add subcategories where needed. Correct one セッコク entry and explain why the parent heading still matters even when both entries say “woody.”

paragraphTitles.agr-par12-flower-group-records-p1: Additional examples under flowering woody plants
paragraphTitles.agr-par12-flower-group-records-p2: Check the Western-orchid column by name
paragraphTitles.agr-par12-flower-group-records-p6: The same “woody” label can have different parent headings

paragraphs.agr-par12-flower-group-records-p1: The column for flowering woody plants lists アザレア, ツツジ, ツバキ and サザンカ. On receiving these names, first check that horticultural column. Matching the table category does not simultaneously establish botanical family, shipping form or identification of actual plants.
paragraphs.agr-par12-flower-group-records-p2: Additional Western-orchid examples are シンビジューム, デンドロビウム, オンシジューム, バンダ and パフィオペディルム. Do not stop at the broad orchid heading; match the inner Western-orchid column too. Names alone do not determine temperature settings or growing duration.
paragraphs.agr-par12-flower-group-records-p3: カンラン, フウラン and セッコク belong in the Eastern-orchid column. For example, notes classifying シンビジューム as Western, カンラン as Eastern and セッコク as Western require correction of セッコク. Knowing one orchid example differs from checking each received name individually.
paragraphs.agr-par12-flower-group-records-p4: Aloe, シャコバサボテン and Kalanchoe appear under the combined succulents-and-cacti heading. Since the heading combines two terms, do not rename every item there as a cactus. Nor can an item be moved into orchids simply because its flowers are enjoyed. Preserve the table’s grouping.
paragraphs.agr-par12-flower-group-records-p5: Among foliage plants, dracaenas and palms are listed as woody, while ferns, Anthurium and Spathiphyllum are herbaceous. Recording only “foliage plant” loses this inner distinction. Return to the table to check woody or herbaceous, rather than deciding from leaf or pot size alone.
paragraphs.agr-par12-flower-group-records-p6: Among herbs, lemongrass, basil, chamomile and lemon balm are herbaceous; rosemary is woody. Foliage dracaenas and herb rosemary both correspond to “woody,” but their parent headings differ. Recording heading, subcategory and item name in that order prevents mixing separate groups merely because a subcategory name matches.

agr-par22-fertilizer.title: Cross-check fertilizer names, ingredients, form and action
agr-par22-fertilizer.objective: Explain the abbreviations, ingredient tendencies, compost origins, patterns of action and forms described in the Level 2 material as separate pieces of information.
agr-par22-fertilizer.activity: Divide an imaginary delivery note into four columns: “name and classification”, “main materials”, “form”, and “onset and duration of action”. Enter 硝安 and 硝酸アンモニウム as two names for the same fertilizer, and match cattle-, pig- and chicken-manure compost names to their main materials. Then briefly explain pellet shape versus mixed ingredients, the two routes to delayed action, and the slow-release example lasting 1 year or more, without mixing them up. Keep this exercise separate from identifying actual materials or deciding application amounts.

paragraphTitles.agr-par22-fertilizer-p1: Pair the abbreviation with its full name
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-fertilizer-p2: Separate blended-fertilizer examples from ingredient tendencies
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-fertilizer-p3: Trace compost names to their main materials
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-fertilizer-p4: Compare two routes to delayed action
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-fertilizer-p5: Preserve the limits of the long-lasting example
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-fertilizer-p6: Record form and mixed ingredients separately

paragraphs.agr-par22-fertilizer-p1: The nitrogen-fertilizer column in the Level 2 material lists urea and 硝安, with 硝酸アンモニウム (ammonium nitrate) given alongside the latter. For example, if a list you receive says 硝安 and another record says 硝酸アンモニウム, check this correspondence and pair them. Rather than counting the two written names as different fertilizers, retain the link between the name and its classification column.
paragraphs.agr-par22-fertilizer-p2: The Level 2 material gives BB fertilizer and organic-containing blended fertilizer as examples of blended fertilizers. It explains that they are made mainly by mixing straight chemical fertilizers, and that many include organic fertilizers. “Many” describes an ingredient tendency; it does not mean every blended fertilizer contains the same ingredients.
paragraphs.agr-par22-fertilizer-p3: Some compost names come from their main materials. The cattle-manure, pig-manure and chicken-manure composts listed in the Level 2 material are examples whose principal materials are manure from those respective animals. Read them within the explanation of compost made by piling up materials and allowing them to ferment. Do not record them as untreated manure itself merely because of the material name.
paragraphs.agr-par22-fertilizer-p4: For delayed-action fertilizers, the Level 2 material lists not only organic fertilizers but also chemical fertilizers whose components dissolve poorly. With organic fertilizers, focus on the route through microbial decomposition before nutrients become available for absorption; with the other type, focus on components that do not dissolve readily. Classifying all chemical fertilizers as necessarily fast-acting would leave out this second explanation.
paragraphs.agr-par22-fertilizer-p5: The explanation of slow-release fertilizers states that some remain effective for 1 year or more. This means the examples include long-lasting products; it does not guarantee that every slow-release fertilizer acts for the same period. In your records, keep the “slow-release” category separate from the example duration in the material, and do not confuse it with the duration of an actual product.
paragraphs.agr-par22-fertilizer-p6: The Level 2 material describes pellets as a form produced by processing solids into cylinders. The same page also gives examples of fertilizers mixing chemical and organic fertilizers. The former is information about form; the latter concerns ingredients. For example, do not decide the ingredient combination from the observation “it was cylindrical” alone. Cross-check form and ingredients in separate columns.

agr-par22-hormones.title: Compare five plant hormones by what they act on
agr-par22-hormones.objective: Understand what hormones produced within plants are, and organize the actions listed for five types by their targets and the direction of change.
agr-par22-hormones.activity: Write the five names on the left, and separate “part or state affected” from “direction of change listed in the material” on the right. Then explain auxin and cytokinin as a pair in relation to buds, and gibberellin and abscisic acid as a pair in relation to seed dormancy. Finally, briefly explain why knowing how a substance acts is different from determining the conditions for using a chemical product.

paragraphTitles.agr-par22-hormones-p4: Focus on buds and leaves for cytokinin
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-hormones-p6: Organize the state and actions of ethylene

paragraphs.agr-par22-hormones-p1: Plant hormones are substances produced within plants that regulate growth and differentiation in very small amounts. Distinguish the name of a substance made inside the plant from “hormone treatment”, the operation of applying a chemical solution externally to flowers or buds. First create three columns—substance name, target of its action, and direction of change—to make the following five types easier to compare.
paragraphs.agr-par22-hormones-p2: The Level 2 material links auxin with suppressing the growth of axillary buds. This relationship is presented together with the term “apical dominance”. Removing side shoots, which you have already studied, is a physical operation; here the topic is the action of a substance regulating bud growth. Even when both discussions concern side buds, do not put the operation name and substance name in the same column.
paragraphs.agr-par22-hormones-p3: The listed examples of gibberellin action include stem elongation and breaking seed dormancy. Promoting parthenocarpy and fruit enlargement is also listed. Stem length, seed dormancy and fruit development are different observation targets. Rather than writing only “promotes growth”, record each target separately. The previously studied treatment example for seedless grapes is not the whole range of actions listed here.
paragraphs.agr-par22-hormones-p4: The cytokinin column lists increasing lateral buds and suppressing leaf ageing. Although both concern buds, the direction of change described differs from the suppression of side-bud growth in the auxin column. Recording the explanation about bud number separately from the explanation about leaf ageing also helps you organize the multiple targets of one substance.
paragraphs.agr-par22-hormones-p5: For abscisic acid, this lesson covers the relationship with seed dormancy described in the material. Whereas the gibberellin column indicates breaking dormancy, read this one as moving seeds into dormancy. In your comparison notes, pair the substance name with the direction of change relating to dormancy. This correspondence alone cannot determine an amount or treatment method to use on actual seeds.
paragraphs.agr-par22-hormones-p6: Ethylene is introduced in the material as a gas. Its listed actions include both promoting and suppressing flowering, as well as fruit ripening. The name alone therefore does not justify defining it only as “a substance that makes flowers open earlier”. Record flowering and fruit ripening as separate targets, and do not confuse this discussion with the previously studied preservation of cut-flower quality. To summarize, explain the five substance names, their targets, and directions such as promotion or suppression separately.

agr-par22-weeds.title: Two herbicide classifications and separate equipment uses
agr-par22-weeds.objective: Explain separately the plants affected, the routes of component uptake or action, and the purpose of separating equipment by use.
agr-par22-weeds.activity: Organize the range of plants affected and the route of component action in separate columns. Then draw two work notes: one where a previously used chemical remains in equipment, and another where a chemical drifts onto nearby crops. Explain the relevant equipment separation or the purpose of the parts in each case. Finally, summarize in one sentence the weed growth stage that must remain in the explanation of soil-treatment herbicides.

paragraphTitles.agr-par22-weeds-p1: Understand the wider purpose of reducing weeds
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-weeds-p2: Classify by which plants are affected
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-weeds-p4: Components remaining in soil and weed growth stage
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-weeds-p5: Why equipment uses are kept separate
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-weeds-p6: The purpose of equipment for preventing drift

paragraphs.agr-par22-weeds-p1: Weeds can also harbor pests and diseases. The Level 2 material connects reducing weeds with growing healthy, vigorous crops and obtaining a stable supply of good-quality produce. Rather than counting only the amount of weeds, consider the field environment, including crops, pests and diseases.
paragraphs.agr-par22-weeds-p2: The material describes selective herbicides as controlling weeds without affecting the crop being grown, and non-selective herbicides as affecting all plants in the sprayed area. This classification focuses on which plants the chemical affects. Do not treat knowing the category name as having checked whether a particular product may be used on an individual crop.
paragraphs.agr-par22-weeds-p3: Foliar-treatment herbicides act after their components are absorbed through stems and leaves. This is a different classification axis from selective versus non-selective, which concerns the plants affected. When noting category names, separate the range of target plants from the part through which components enter, so that the two explanations are not confused.
paragraphs.agr-par22-weeds-p4: For soil-treatment herbicides, the material explains that components sprayed onto soil remain there and suppress weed emergence and growth. It also specifies that effectiveness declines on weeds that have already grown large. When comparing them with foliar-treatment herbicides, retain not just where the components are, but also the weeds’ growth stage.
paragraphs.agr-par22-weeds-p5: The Level 2 material states that equipment used to spray herbicides is not to be shared with pest-and-disease control. Another passage explains that crop injury can occur if a previously used chemical has not been sufficiently removed. Keep separating equipment by use distinct from the cleanup record for washing it, rather than combining them into one checklist item.
paragraphs.agr-par22-weeds-p6: Where other crops are nearby, dedicated nozzles and covers are listed for the purpose of preventing spray drift onto surrounding crops. This is a different route of chemical movement from crop injury caused by chemicals remaining inside equipment. In work notes, separate residues within equipment from drift into the surroundings, and record what each check is intended to prevent.

agr-par22-vegetables.title: Read leafy and stem vegetables by form, region and cultivation method
agr-par22-vegetables.objective: Explain the additional information about leafy and stem vegetables using separate perspectives: form, season and region, uses, cultivation method and breeding improvements.
agr-par22-vegetables.activity: Create columns for “form”, “season and region”, “examples of use” and “cultivation method” for the five vegetables, and enter only what this lesson has confirmed. Pair the three cabbage types with their shape and heading characteristics, and separately explain in one sentence the improvement linked to year-round spinach cultivation. Leave unspecified columns unfilled rather than guessing, and note what information still needs checking.

paragraphTitles.agr-par22-vegetables-p1: Separate nationwide cultivation from summer production areas
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-vegetables-p2: Compare cabbage types by shape and heading
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-vegetables-p3: Read Chinese-cabbage uses and its seasonal introduction
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-vegetables-p4: Put lettuce leaf form and cultivation method in separate columns
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-vegetables-p5: Year-round spinach cultivation and breeding improvements
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-vegetables-p6: Separate the edible part of onions from seedling handling

paragraphs.agr-par22-vegetables-p1: The Level 2 material explains that cabbage is grown throughout Japan and that cool plateaus and high-elevation areas are used in summer. “Throughout Japan” describes the extent of cultivation, while “summer plateaus and high-elevation areas” combines a season and location. These statements are not contradictory; retain the season in notes checking summer production areas.
paragraphs.agr-par22-vegetables-p2: The material lists winter-type cabbage (寒玉) as flattened and tightly headed, and spring-type cabbage (春玉) as soft and loosely headed. Round-type cabbage (丸玉) is spherical. When comparing the three, record shape and heading characteristics separately from the type names. In this lesson, learn the correspondence of the listed characteristics rather than inferring cultivation schedules or the properties of every variety from a type name.
paragraphs.agr-par22-vegetables-p3: Examples of Chinese-cabbage use include pickles and hot-pot dishes, and the Level 2 material introduces it as an autumn vegetable. The dishes it is used in and the cultivation schedule are different information. For example, separating “uses: pickles and hot-pot dishes” from “seasonal introduction: autumn vegetable” helps prevent turning “autumn” alone into nationally fixed sowing or harvest dates.
paragraphs.agr-par22-vegetables-p4: The lettuce forms listed include leaves that form a round head, those that do not, and those with curled leaves. The Level 2 material also describes lettuce as an example of transplant cultivation. Leaf heading and curling describe form; transplanting describes the method of moving seedlings to grow them elsewhere. Checking one column does not mean the other has also been verified.
paragraphs.agr-par22-vegetables-p5: The Level 2 material links breeding improvements in spinach with progress toward year-round cultivation. This differs from the use of cool plateaus and high-elevation areas for summer cabbage. Do not read “year-round” as continuously harvesting from one plant throughout the year; organize the relationship described in the material, in which breeding improvements have advanced year-round cultivation.
paragraphs.agr-par22-vegetables-p6: The Level 2 material states that onions are transplanted. This describes moving seedlings to grow them in the field, which is separate from describing the organs making up the edible bulb. Keep the edible part and cultivation method in separate columns in onion notes. A round bulb underground alone does not justify placing onions in the same direct-sowing column as daikon.

agr-par22-facility.title: Read protected tomato and strawberry production by indicator and region
agr-par22-facility.objective: Organize production quantities, main production areas and growth of protected tomatoes and strawberries while preserving the material’s years and indicators.
agr-par22-facility.activity: Make two rows, one for tomatoes and one for strawberries, and record protected-production quantity in 2018, its unit, and the main production areas listed. In separate columns, note the two types of tomato growth and the two strawberry trends—area and yield per 10a. Explain aloud the distinction between quantity, area and quantity per unit area.

paragraphTitles.agr-par22-facility-p1: Separate production quantity from cultivated area
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-facility-p2: Link tomato production areas with cropping schedules
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-facility-p3: Two types of tomato growth overlap
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-facility-p4: Strawberries mainly under protection, and the 2018 quantity
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-facility-p6: Compare the direction of area and yield per 10a

paragraphs.agr-par22-facility-p1: The Level 2 material gives Japan’s protected tomato production in 2018 as about 562,000 tonnes. This refers to tomatoes grown under protection, not total tomato production including open-field cultivation. The same section also describes tomatoes as having the largest cultivated area in Japan’s protected cultivation. Recording the weight figure separately from the area ranking makes clear what is being compared.
paragraphs.agr-par22-facility-p2: Examples of major tomato production areas include Kumamoto, Aichi and Hokkaido. The material explains that each area has suitable cropping schedules and that a relay between production areas enables year-round shipments. In a planning exercise, separate the production-area name from the shipment-period column. Do not turn these three examples into a production-volume ranking or an exhaustive list of places where tomatoes can be grown.
paragraphs.agr-par22-facility-p3: Tomatoes are described as growing through vegetative and reproductive growth in parallel. Do not regard the growth of leaves and stems and the formation of flowers and fruit simply as a sequence in which one must finish completely before the other starts. Recording both stems and leaves and flowers and fruit in observations from the same period provides practice in comparing how the two progress.
paragraphs.agr-par22-facility-p4: For strawberries, the material indicates that protected cultivation is the main approach. The listed national production of protected strawberries in 2018 is about 135,000 tonnes. For example, a record reading “2018 / protected strawberries / about 135,000 tonnes” preserves the year, subject, quantity and unit together. Do not rewrite it as a current quantity or as total strawberry production irrespective of cultivation method.
paragraphs.agr-par22-facility-p5: The main strawberry production areas listed are Tochigi, Fukuoka and Kumamoto. Kumamoto also appears in the tomato column, but the other examples differ. For example, when making an assignment sheet for both crops, check the crop name and prefecture as a pair to avoid transferring Aichi and Hokkaido from the tomato examples directly into the strawberry column. This compares major production-area examples in the material; it is not a current ranking.
paragraphs.agr-par22-facility-p6: The strawberry trends described in the material combine decreasing planted area with increasing yield per 10a. Total growing area and quantity obtained from a fixed area are different indicators, so do not confuse them when their directions differ. This description gives no specific comparison years or rates of change. It cannot be combined with the preceding 2018 quantity and rewritten as a figure for that year’s rate of increase or decrease.
