agr-par22-fruit.title: Purposes of fruit-growing materials and types of transport machinery
agr-par22-fruit.objective: Organize four examples of purposes affecting growth and the descriptions of transport machinery separately by crop, change and type.
agr-par22-fruit.activity: Match the person-in-charge’s notes—“Unshu mandarin rind”, “pears before harvest”, “fruit ripening”, and “apple roots and branches”—with the four purposes listed in the material. Then organize the two monorail types and the two terms describing the illustrated carrier in separate columns. Finally, explain separately what can be read from the list and what must be checked for each actual machine or product.

paragraphTitles.agr-par22-fruit-p1: The purpose of preventing loose rind
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-fruit-p2: Retain both the crop and pre-harvest fruit drop
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-fruit-p3: An example acting on the pace of ripening
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-fruit-p4: An example promoting root and branch formation
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-fruit-p5: There are two types of monorail
paragraphTitles.agr-par22-fruit-p6: Read the two descriptors of the listed carrier

paragraphs.agr-par22-fruit-p1: In its list of plant-growth-regulator purposes, the Level 2 material gives an example for Unshu mandarins (ウンシュウミカン): preventing the fruit rind from becoming loose. This concerns the state of the rind and should be recorded separately from enlarging fruit or improving coloration. What can be read here is the correspondence between a crop and the change targeted by the stated purpose.
paragraphs.agr-par22-fruit-p2: For apples, pears and similar crops, the purpose listed is preventing fruit from falling before harvest. Do not shorten this to “prevent fruit drop” alone; preserve both the timing—before harvest—and the crop name. The list says ナシ (pear). That line alone does not justify applying the same treatment to all pears or to a particular cultivar.
paragraphs.agr-par22-fruit-p3: The same list also includes the purpose of bringing ripening forward in many fruit trees. This targets a different change from suppressing fruit drop. Preserve the scope of “many”, rather than reading it as bringing harvest forward by the same amount for every fruit tree. The purpose column alone does not determine a specific treatment date or how many days earlier ripening will occur.
paragraphs.agr-par22-fruit-p4: For apples and similar crops, a purpose listed is promoting the formation of roots and branches. This shows that the material’s list includes organ formation in roots and branches, not only fruit condition. Cuttings and grafting are names of propagation methods; this column describes which growth change is targeted. It is not a table for deciding product names, quantities or application methods.
paragraphs.agr-par22-fruit-p5: Among the listed transport-machine examples, the agricultural monorail is also called a single-rail carrier, and both non-ride-on and ride-on types are described. “Transport” is its use; “ride-on or non-ride-on” is information about type. Identifying something as a monorail alone does not establish which type it is. Do not transfer riding conditions from another machine you have seen.
paragraphs.agr-par22-fruit-p6: Another transport example is described as a crawler-type self-propelled carrier. Organize “crawler type” and “self-propelled” as two pieces of information alongside the carrier name. “Self-propelled” alone does not establish that it is a ride-on type. Distinguish reading the example in the material from checking an actual machine’s riding permission, load capacity and operating method.

agr-s27-climate-detail.title: Japan’s location, maritime climate and seasonal conditions
agr-s27-climate-detail.objective: Organize the material’s explanations of geography, precipitation and seasons while retaining regional differences and the range of times described.
agr-s27-climate-detail.activity: Record Japan’s location and main climate zone, its maritime character and annual precipitation, and its four seasons and typhoon season in separate columns. Prepare a handover that distinguishes tendencies described in the material from observations made on the day.

paragraphTitles.agr-s27-climate-detail-p1: The East Asian coast and the main climate zone
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-climate-detail-p5: Background and scope of extreme rainfall
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-climate-detail-p6: Explain the place and time together

paragraphs.agr-s27-climate-detail-p1: The Level 2 material describes Japan as a country on the coast of East Asia and identifies its main climate zone as temperate. Organize its location and main climate zone alongside the differences between Okinawa and Hokkaido studied earlier. “Mainly temperate” does not mean that every location in Japan has the same climate.
paragraphs.agr-s27-climate-detail-p2: The material connects Japan’s maritime climate with abundant precipitation over the year as a whole. An annual characteristic and whether it rains on a particular day are different information. In farm records, distinguish the column describing national characteristics from the column for weather observed locally.
paragraphs.agr-s27-climate-detail-p3: The material distinguishes four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. Arrange rising spring temperatures and plant growth, prolonged rain during the rainy season, and the hot, humid summer that follows in seasonal order. This is not a timetable specifying exact starting dates for each region or work dates common to all crops.
paragraphs.agr-s27-climate-detail-p4: The material describes typhoons passing through Japan from July onward. Read this as a seasonal tendency presented in the material. Retain the range of time described; do not turn it into a claim that typhoons can never occur before July or pass through on the same date every July.
paragraphs.agr-s27-climate-detail-p5: The material explains that localized heavy rain and bands of successive heavy rainfall have become more likely, particularly in western Japan, under the influence of global warming and other factors. This describes a background and regional tendency. This sentence alone does not establish the cause of an individual rainfall event or justify concluding that such events cannot occur outside western Japan.
paragraphs.agr-s27-climate-detail-p6: For example, in an imaginary handover, communicate the background statement “Japan is mainly temperate and has maritime characteristics” separately from the observation “We recorded rain during the rainy season on this farm.” Today’s task is to keep the main climate zone, annual precipitation, seasonal order and stated typhoon period distinct rather than treating them as the same kind of information.

agr-s27-production-2019.title: Read 2019 agricultural output value by product, amount and share
agr-s27-production-2019.objective: Match the 2019 total and the values and shares of four crop categories, and compare them without mixing indicators.
agr-s27-production-2019.activity: Copy the four 2019 categories into four columns: year, product category, 100 million yen, and share. Read the amount and share columns aloud to check them. Also explain why the sum of these four categories does not represent all agriculture.

paragraphTitles.agr-s27-production-2019-p5: Read the flowers and ornamental plants row
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-production-2019-p6: Four categories are not the whole total

paragraphs.agr-s27-production-2019-p1: The Level 2 material gives Japan’s agricultural output value for 2019 as 89,387 units of 100 million yen. Record “2019”, “agricultural output value” and “100 million yen” together with the number. This is a monetary indicator for that year; it does not give the current output value, planted area or harvest weight.
paragraphs.agr-s27-production-2019-p2: For vegetables in 2019, the material lists an output value of 21,515 units of 100 million yen and a share of 24%. These are different columns for the same category. Include the column headings when copying the figures, so that, for example, 21,515 is not recorded as weight and 24% is not treated as vegetables’ share of planted area.
paragraphs.agr-s27-production-2019-p3: In the same 2019 table, rice is listed at 17,484 units of 100 million yen and 20%. When comparing rice with vegetables, keep the year and monetary unit the same. The 20% is a share of agricultural output value, not the self-sufficiency rate of rice eaten in Japan.
paragraphs.agr-s27-production-2019-p4: The 2019 fruit entry is 8,399 units of 100 million yen and 9%. Retain the category name “fruit”; do not silently replace it with a figure for fruit trees from another year. The basic approach is to put values from different years or coverage scopes in separate columns before comparing them.
paragraphs.agr-s27-production-2019-p5: The material gives flowers and ornamental plants in 2019 as 3,264 units of 100 million yen and 4%. This 4% is their share of total agricultural output value. Its denominator differs from the shares of cut flowers or potted plants within this category, so do not present them as the same ratio.
paragraphs.agr-s27-production-2019-p6: The vegetables, rice, fruit, and flowers and ornamental plants selected for this exercise do not include every agricultural product category. Do not add their amounts together and describe the result as the same total as 89,387 units of 100 million yen. In the handover list, retain the four columns—year, product category, amount and share—and match only information actually shown in the table.

agr-s27-self-supply-2019.title: Cross-check the 2019 self-sufficiency rates by weight
agr-s27-self-supply-2019.objective: Match five product categories with their self-sufficiency rates by weight, and distinguish these from the calorie-based explanation.
agr-s27-self-supply-2019.activity: Make a 2019 record matching rice, wheat, soybeans, vegetables and fruit with their values. Correct an imaginary note that swaps wheat and soybeans, and explain how these figures differ from the approximately 40% calorie-based figure.

paragraphTitles.agr-s27-self-supply-2019-p3: Do not swap wheat and soybeans

paragraphs.agr-s27-self-supply-2019-p1: The Level 2 material contains both an explanation that food self-sufficiency is around 40% on a calorie basis and a 2019 table by product category on a weight basis. These use different indicators. Do not compare the overall figure of about 40% with the individual weight-based entries as if they had the same denominator.
paragraphs.agr-s27-self-supply-2019-p2: The 2019 weight-based table gives rice as 97%. Although the text emphasizes rice self-sufficiency, do not round the specific table value to 100% when copying it. Retain the combination “2019—weight basis—rice—97%”.
paragraphs.agr-s27-self-supply-2019-p3: The same table gives wheat as 16% and soybeans as 6%. The material explains that these two have low self-sufficiency rates and depend heavily on imports. Check the category name and value together rather than relying on memory and reversing the two percentages.
paragraphs.agr-s27-self-supply-2019-p4: The 2019 weight-based self-sufficiency rate for vegetables is shown as 79%. Although the year is the same, this differs from vegetables’ 24% share of agricultural output value. Do not move 79% into the monetary-share column or 24% into the weight-based self-sufficiency column.
paragraphs.agr-s27-self-supply-2019-p5: The fruit entry is 38% on a weight basis for 2019. To compare it with vegetables’ 79%, stay within the same table of product categories, year and weight basis. This historical table alone does not establish that the current self-sufficiency rate for fruit is 38%.
paragraphs.agr-s27-self-supply-2019-p6: If an imaginary record says “rice 97%, wheat 6%, soybeans 16%”, check each product category against the original table and identify the swap between wheat and soybeans. Also check the year and weight-basis label. Learn to check each row against its heading, rather than memorizing numbers alone.

agr-s27-rice-history.title: Keep historical rice value, variety area and consumption figures distinct
agr-s27-rice-history.objective: Retain the material’s years, indicators and units for rice, and distinguish output value, area by variety and annual consumption.
agr-s27-rice-history.activity: Make separate columns for monetary value, area and annual amount per person, adding the year or the material’s publication-time context. Read the fiscal 1962 and fiscal 2021 values aloud with the correct units.

paragraphTitles.agr-s27-rice-history-p2: The explanation linking dining out and output value
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-rice-history-p3: The area covered by the Koshihikari statement
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-rice-history-p4: The ranking is described up to publication
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-rice-history-p5: Two fiscal years for annual consumption per person
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-rice-history-p6: Do not merge different indicators in one entry

paragraphs.agr-s27-rice-history-p1: The Level 2 material gives rice output value in 2021 as approximately 1.4 trillion yen and its share of agricultural output value as approximately 15%. Both figures are approximate. Record them together as the 2021 amount and share, keeping them separate from the 2019 table.
paragraphs.agr-s27-rice-history-p2: The material explains the background as people increasingly avoiding eating out following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, with rice output value declining. This describes developments at the time covered by the material. Do not treat it as a forecast that the same trend continues today or as proof of reduced income on an individual farm.
paragraphs.agr-s27-rice-history-p3: For Koshihikari, the material states that it accounts for one-third or more of the nationwide planted area. The indicator here is area. Retain the scope described rather than changing it into a claim about one-third or more of rice harvest weight or output value.
paragraphs.agr-s27-rice-history-p4: The explanation of Koshihikari’s planted area also states that it has ranked first continuously since 1979. Treat this as a historical account up to the material’s publication, not a guarantee that it will always rank first in the future. Retain that the ranking concerns planted area.
paragraphs.agr-s27-rice-history-p5: For annual rice consumption per person, the material gives fiscal 1962 as the peak at approximately 118 kg and fiscal 2021 as approximately 50.8 kg. Match each figure with its fiscal year and kg unit when comparing them. Retain the indicator as an annual amount per person, rather than total national consumption.
paragraphs.agr-s27-rice-history-p6: In the handover exercise, put 2021 output value, Koshihikari’s planted area and annual consumption per person in the two fiscal years in separate columns. Explain what each indicator measures; do not infer a decline in a particular variety’s area from a monetary decline or call a per-person quantity a national total.

agr-s27-vegetable-origins.title: Read the listed examples of vegetable output value, origins and introduction
agr-s27-vegetable-origins.objective: Distinguish years, examples and the scope used to count types, and match examples native to Japan with those introduced from abroad.
agr-s27-vegetable-origins.activity: Put the five examples native to Japan and the four introduced from abroad in two columns, and explain how the scopes of approximately 20 types and approximately 160 types differ. Add 2021 and the unit to the monetary-value column.

paragraphTitles.agr-s27-vegetable-origins-p2: Pair each example with Japanese origin
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-vegetable-origins-p3: Retain the other examples of origin
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-vegetable-origins-p4: The difference between about 20 and about 160 types
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-vegetable-origins-p5: Examples of vegetables introduced from abroad
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-vegetable-origins-p6: A handover with separate classification columns

paragraphs.agr-s27-vegetable-origins-p1: The Level 2 material gives vegetable output value in 2021 as approximately 2.1 trillion yen and its share of all agriculture as approximately 24%. This describes a different year from the 2019 vegetable table. Both concern monetary value, but do not omit the years and treat them as the same figure.
paragraphs.agr-s27-vegetable-origins-p2: Examples the material lists as vegetables native to Japan include udo and mitsuba. Match these two names with the Japanese-origin column. This is an exercise in names, not training to identify an actual plant or image with certainty. Also, do not make the list imply that these are the only two vegetables native to Japan.
paragraphs.agr-s27-vegetable-origins-p3: The same Japanese-origin examples also include myoga, fuki and jinenjo. When recording the material’s examples, add these to the same column as udo and mitsuba. Where something is cultivated and the origin category described in the material are not the same information.
paragraphs.agr-s27-vegetable-origins-p4: The material states both that approximately 20 types of vegetables are native to Japan and that approximately 160 types are cultivated in Japan. The first is an origin category; the second covers types cultivated in Japan. Do not read this as saying that all 160 types are native to Japan or that only 20 types are cultivated.
paragraphs.agr-s27-vegetable-origins-p5: The material lists tomatoes, cabbage, Chinese cabbage and onions as examples of vegetables introduced from abroad. Here, match these four names with the category “introduced from abroad”. Being cultivated in Japan and being native to Japan are different information.
paragraphs.agr-s27-vegetable-origins-p6: For example, separate headings for “examples of vegetables cultivated in Japan” and “examples listed as native to Japan” help prevent introduced vegetables such as tomatoes from being moved into the native-origin category. The year and share of output value belong in another column. Organize today’s examples without expanding them into a list claiming to cover every type.

agr-s27-fruit-components.title: Organize fruit-tree output values, component examples and introduced techniques
agr-s27-fruit-components.objective: Explain the material’s fruit-tree output values and examples, fruit components and descriptions of techniques while distinguishing their scope.
agr-s27-fruit-components.activity: Summarize fruit-tree examples, the 2021 monetary value, four component examples and introduced techniques in separate columns. Prepare an explanation that does not turn the description of components into a guarantee of disease prevention or treatment.

paragraphTitles.agr-s27-fruit-components-p1: Listed fruit trees with high output values
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-fruit-components-p3: Read the first two component examples
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-fruit-components-p4: Read the other two component examples
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-fruit-components-p5: Interest in functions is different from a guarantee
paragraphTitles.agr-s27-fruit-components-p6: Examples of new techniques in the material

paragraphs.agr-s27-fruit-components-p1: The Level 2 material lists satsuma mandarins, apples, grapes, pears, peaches and persimmons as fruit trees with high output values. This list is not a table of their individual amounts or exact ranking. Also retain the listed name “pear” without narrowing it to a particular type without evidence.
paragraphs.agr-s27-fruit-components-p2: The material gives fruit-tree output value in 2021 as approximately 9,159 units of 100 million yen and approximately 10% of all agriculture. Read it with “2021”, “fruit trees”, “approximately” and “100 million yen” together. Put it in a separate column from the 2019 fruit-table values of 8,399 units of 100 million yen and 9%, preserving the differences in year and wording.
paragraphs.agr-s27-fruit-components-p3: Vitamins and polyphenols are among the examples the material gives of components abundant in fruit from fruit trees. Record these in the components column. This explanation alone neither guarantees that every fruit contains the same types and amounts nor determines the content of any individual fruit.
paragraphs.agr-s27-fruit-components-p4: The same explanation also lists dietary fiber and minerals. Organize these together with vitamins and polyphenols as the four component examples presented in the material. Keep fruit-tree type names, component names and output values in separate classification columns, identifying what kind of information each is.
paragraphs.agr-s27-fruit-components-p5: The material explains that attention is being paid to the functions of fruit in maintaining health, preventing disease and similar purposes. This describes an area of interest, not a guarantee that eating a particular fruit will prevent or cure disease. Retain the strength of the statement “is attracting attention” in your study notes.
paragraphs.agr-s27-fruit-components-p6: The techniques introduced for fruit trees include protected cultivation and dwarfing cultivation. Retain the scope that these techniques have also been introduced into fruit-tree cultivation; do not turn it into an instruction that the same equipment or methods can be selected for every tree species and region. In your study notes, record examples of fruit-tree types and examples of cultivation techniques in separate columns.

agr-s30-plant-detail.title: Organize additional terms for flower buds, germination and cropping plans by stage
agr-s30-plant-detail.objective: Explain the additional examples and alternative names for flower-bud differentiation and germination in the No. 2 material, and distinguish planting from the cropping-pattern perspective of aiming for economical cultivation.
agr-s30-plant-detail.activity: Make three columns for flower-bud differentiation, germination and cultivation planning, and sort cards containing the examples and alternative names. For daikon, also write the relevant conditions alongside the day-length, low-temperature and germination descriptions. Finally, explain that planting is an action, whereas a cropping pattern organizes cultivation with environmental conditions and economy in mind. Check that you have not added figures for days, covering depth or profit that the material does not give.

paragraphTitles.agr-s30-plant-detail-p1: Buds that become flowers and regular differentiation
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-plant-detail-p3: Keep long-day and low-temperature columns separate
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-plant-detail-p4: Distinguish planting from the purpose of a cropping pattern
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-plant-detail-p5: Light-germinating and light-favoring name the same group

paragraphs.agr-s30-plant-detail-p1: A flower bud is a bud that will later bear a flower. Alongside tomato, the No. 2 material lists eggplant, sweet pepper and cucumber as examples of the type that differentiates flower buds regularly. Group these as the listed examples of differentiation after some growth; this does not mean that they all flower together after a fixed number of days. Record flower-bud formation and flowering as separate stages.
paragraphs.agr-s30-plant-detail-p2: The No. 2 material lists chili pepper, shiso, strawberry, soybean, chrysanthemum and morning glory as short-day plants, focusing on conditions in which the dark period exceeds a certain length. For example, place a soybean card in the column headed “Examples of day-length responses in flower-bud differentiation.” Do not use this list alone to set a dark-period duration or flowering date common to every cultivar.
paragraphs.agr-s30-plant-detail-p3: The examples for conditions in which the dark period is shorter than a certain length include spinach, daikon, wheat, aster and dianthus. The same page also gives daikon among the examples of flower-bud differentiation in response to low temperature. Even when daikon appears in both descriptions, do not merge day length and low temperature into the same environmental condition. Check each listed example together with the condition described by its column.
paragraphs.agr-s30-plant-detail-p4: Planting, or sakutsuke, means cultivating a crop by sowing or transplanting it. In contrast, the No. 2 material describes a cropping pattern as a cropping system for economical cultivation under natural conditions that vary by region and season. When explaining a plan, for example, do not reduce a cropping pattern to the sowing date alone. Retain both its organization in response to the environment and its aim of economical cultivation. This is not a guarantee that the plan will actually make a profit.
paragraphs.agr-s30-plant-detail-p5: Light-germinating seeds, which germinate more readily in light, are also called light-favoring seeds. The examples in the No. 2 material are carrot and lettuce. Treat “light-germinating” and “light-favoring” as corresponding names, rather than counting them as two separate seed groups. The material describes covering them with a thin layer of soil, but the category name alone does not determine a covering depth in millimeters.
paragraphs.agr-s30-plant-detail-p6: Dark-germinating seeds, which germinate less readily in light, are also called light-inhibited seeds. This column in the No. 2 material lists daikon, tomato and watermelon. In the material’s relative comparison, they are covered more thickly with soil. Keep long-day and short-day responses in flower-bud differentiation separate from responses to light during seed germination: these classifications concern different stages.

agr-s30-soil-detail.title: Read irrigation comparisons and nutrient uptake in detail
agr-s30-soil-detail.objective: Compare water, materials and labor separately for furrow irrigation, and explain the listed tubing material and discharge mechanism, the meaning of essential elements, the links between elements, substances and uptake sites, and nitrogen’s role as a constituent.
agr-s30-soil-detail.activity: Make two imaginary comparison notes. The first has three columns for water, materials and labor in furrow irrigation, and two columns for tubing-material examples and water discharge. The second matches carbon and hydrogen/oxygen using “Element / Substance taken up / Plant part.” Explain the meaning of essential elements in one sentence. Finally, separate nitrogen’s visible effects from its role as a constituent. Do not add figures or specifications for actual products.

paragraphTitles.agr-s30-soil-detail-p1: Compare water and materials separately in furrow irrigation
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-soil-detail-p2: Tubing materials and how water is sprayed
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-soil-detail-p4: Link carbon with carbon dioxide and leaves
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-soil-detail-p5: For hydrogen and oxygen, also follow the water-and-root pathway
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-soil-detail-p6: Retain nitrogen’s role as a constituent

paragraphs.agr-s30-soil-detail-p1: The No. 2 description of furrow irrigation contrasts its lack of material and labor requirements with its need for a large amount of water. Concluding that materials and labor must also be high because water use is high would change the material’s explanation. Separate “Water needed,” “Materials” and “Labor” in notes comparing methods. Do not treat this example as a guarantee that no preparation or management is needed in any field.
paragraphs.agr-s30-soil-detail-p2: The listed description of irrigation tubing says that it is made from materials such as vinyl and sprays water through many holes. Read the material example together with the discharge mechanism. Drip-irrigation tubing is described as releasing droplets through drip outlets, so similar names do not establish that the discharge mechanisms are the same. Do not turn “such as vinyl” into a material specification for every product.
paragraphs.agr-s30-soil-detail-p3: Essential elements is the collective term for nutrients indispensable to plant growth. Rather than stopping at the name “three primary fertilizer nutrients,” organize this as a term for nutrients that plants cannot grow without. This lesson does not settle the total number or classification of elements for which differences between the materials still require checking. Also distinguish understanding the term from deciding which fertilizer to add and in what amount.
paragraphs.agr-s30-soil-detail-p4: In the No. 2 explanation of nutrients, carbon is linked to the uptake of carbon dioxide from the air through leaves. Make separate, matching columns for the element “carbon,” the substance taken in, “carbon dioxide,” and the uptake part, “leaves.” This differs from the explanation of nutrients supplied to soil as fertilizer. The name carbon does not justify recording that all of it is taken from soil through roots.
paragraphs.agr-s30-soil-detail-p5: The same No. 2 explanation describes hydrogen and oxygen through the pathway of water absorption by roots. Even when considering the previously learned uptake of oxygen in respiration, retain the water-derived uptake described here. Write “Hydrogen and oxygen / Water / Roots” and compare it with the preceding “Carbon / Carbon dioxide / Leaves.” Do not confuse the element, substance and plant-part columns, or infer individual uptake amounts from this explanation.
paragraphs.agr-s30-soil-detail-p6: The nitrogen section explains not only its relationship with stems, leaves and leaf color, but also its involvement in growth and yield performance as a constituent of proteins and chloroplasts. Do not compress external observations, such as darker or paler leaves, and explanations of what is built inside the plant into a single column. Learning about nitrogen and chloroplasts does not establish the cause from leaf appearance or determine an additional fertilizer amount.

agr-s30-rice-detail.title: Record paddy-weed management, post-harvest work and labor saving
agr-s30-rice-detail.objective: Explain the listed paddy-weed measures, the targets of post-harvest tillage, and machinery sharing and cost categories while retaining the material’s conditions.
agr-s30-rice-detail.activity: Sort paddy-weed measures into field preparation, chemicals, weeders and living organisms. Next, distinguish the targets of post-harvest tillage, and write separately about equipment sharing in dry direct seeding and cost categories in sparse planting.

paragraphTitles.agr-s30-rice-detail-p1: Record weed species and growth stage first
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-rice-detail-p3: Match control categories with how they work
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-rice-detail-p4: Drying methods and machine settings are separate
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-rice-detail-p5: Distinguish the targets of post-harvest tillage
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-rice-detail-p6: Labor saving involving machinery and seedling boxes

paragraphs.agr-s30-rice-detail-p1: Observing weed species and growth stage is important in paddy-weed management. Simply writing “There are weeds” does not retain which species are present or how far they have grown. Record these in separate columns as information for considering control methods. These observations alone do not determine the chemical or amount to use.
paragraphs.agr-s30-rice-detail-p2: The No. 2 material gives autumn tillage, early-spring tillage and careful puddling as examples of cultural control. It links field preparation and cultivation work with reducing weed emergence. Retain the listed seasons when organizing them, but do not treat them as a guarantee that the same schedule suits every paddy.
paragraphs.agr-s30-rice-detail-p3: The material describes herbicide use as chemical control, and mechanical weeding with manual or powered paddy weeders as physical control. Having young aigamo ducks eat weeds is an example of biological control. Match not only the category names but also whether chemicals, machinery or living organisms are doing the work. This explanation does not specify chemical-use conditions, actual machine operation or procedures for introducing aigamo ducks.
paragraphs.agr-s30-rice-detail-p4: For preparing harvested paddy rice, the No. 2 material lists fuel-heated drying. Separate its purpose of reducing moisture from its method of applying heat from fuel. Writing “fuel-heated drying” does not mean that the actual machine temperature or operating time has been checked. Do not reinterpret the moisture percentage of paddy rice as a dryer temperature setting.
paragraphs.agr-s30-rice-detail-p5: The material describes tilling promptly after harvest to promote decomposition of stubble and straw. It also mentions digging up perennial weeds and burying weeds at the surface. Rather than merging residue decomposition, the plants to dig up and the plants to bury into one cleanup column, distinguish what each action targets. This description does not determine actual machine operation or settings for different soil conditions.
paragraphs.agr-s30-rice-detail-p6: The description of dry direct seeding includes examples of sharing seeders and other equipment with the cultivation of upland crops such as wheat. This is an equipment-sharing perspective, separate from omitting nursery raising. In contrast, the explanation of reducing seedling-box requirements through sparse planting links this to costs such as seed and nursery materials, and to labor time. Separate equipment sharing from box-related cost categories. Neither universal machine compatibility nor the same savings in every field are guaranteed.

agr-s30-facility-flower.title: Distinguish protected-flower groups, growing media and bulb treatments
agr-s30-facility-flower.objective: Explain the listed chrysanthemum and rose classifications, the directions of lily-bulb treatments, and the carnation propagation method within the material’s scope.
agr-s30-facility-flower.activity: Make three columns for “Plant / Treatment or classification name / What the explanation concerns.” Organize chrysanthemum groups and flower forms, and rose growing media and groups. Then link each of the two lily-bulb treatments with its effect on dormancy and its cropping pattern.

paragraphTitles.agr-s30-facility-flower-p1: Chrysanthemum groups and the target of flowering control
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-facility-flower-p2: Give chrysanthemum flower forms a separate column
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-facility-flower-p3: The listed growing medium for roses
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-facility-flower-p4: Rose flowering habit and group names
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-facility-flower-p5: The different effects of lily-bulb treatments

paragraphs.agr-s30-facility-flower-p1: A list of chrysanthemum groups includes winter chrysanthemums as well as summer, summer-autumn and autumn chrysanthemums. In the No. 2 material, the groups linked with short-day behavior and flowering control through supplemental lighting are summer-autumn and autumn chrysanthemums. Including winter chrysanthemums in the same list does not establish that the lighting method is shared by every group.
paragraphs.agr-s30-facility-flower-p2: When organizing the same chrysanthemums, make a flower-form column separate from the seasonal-group column. The flower-form names listed in the No. 2 material are rinzaki and spray type. These two names alone do not establish visual identification features or how many flowers to retain on a stem.
paragraphs.agr-s30-facility-flower-p3: For protected rose cultivation, the No. 2 material describes hydroponic cultivation using rockwool as the growing medium as the main method. Link the previously learned hydroponic system with this listed example of roses and its solid-medium name. This is a statement in the material, not a figure establishing the current national adoption rate or equipment specifications suitable for every cultivar.
paragraphs.agr-s30-facility-flower-p4: The roses listed for protected cultivation are the hybrid tea and floribunda groups, which have repeat-flowering characteristics. Record the flowering habit and the two group names as separate pieces of information. This page does not give group-specific branch-training methods or environmental settings, so do not supply working conditions merely from the group names.
paragraphs.agr-s30-facility-flower-p5: The explanation of adjusting lily shipment timing links refrigerated bulb storage with breaking dormancy and places it on the forcing side. In contrast, freezing treatment is described as delaying dormancy and is linked with retarded cultivation. Do not merge both under the single phrase “cold treatment.” Match the treatment name, its effect on dormancy and the cropping pattern in three columns. Do not derive temperatures or treatment durations from this.
paragraphs.agr-s30-facility-flower-p6: The No. 2 material lists shoot cuttings as a method of propagating carnations. Classifying the flowers produced as large-flowered or spray types is separate from classifying how to multiply plants. The point confirmed here is the name of the propagation method. This page alone does not determine cutting length, rooting conditions or how to select mother plants.

agr-s30-fruit-detail.title: Read additional fruit-thinning conditions, orchard weather and regions
agr-s30-fruit-detail.objective: Add condition and position criteria for fruit thinning, and organize weather types and fruit-specific regional examples without confusing them.
agr-s30-fruit-detail.activity: Divide a fruit-thinning checklist into damage, development, shape and position for bagging. Next, make six weather columns and organize the listed examples for citrus, apple, grape and sweet persimmon with the relevant crop, season and region. Finally, reflect on field conditions that regional examples alone cannot determine.

paragraphTitles.agr-s30-fruit-detail-p1: Check condition and position during fruit thinning
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-fruit-detail-p3: Listed preparations against strong winds for citrus
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-fruit-detail-p6: The stated regional scope for sweet persimmons

paragraphs.agr-s30-fruit-detail-p1: When selecting fruit for thinning, the No. 2 material also lists damaged fruit and fruit whose development is delayed. Fruit in positions that make bagging difficult is another target to check. Do not stop at conditions such as damage or deformity; include position for bagging as a separate item. This explanation alone does not determine the number to retain or the thinning date for every tree.
paragraphs.agr-s30-fruit-detail-p2: When organizing weather influences on orchards, the material lists strong winds, cold, heavy rain, drought, heavy snow and hail. Keep abundant rain separate from water shortage, and heavy snow separate from hail. The explanation says that measures are taken in regions susceptible to damage; it is not a procedure saying that identical materials should be installed in every orchard.
paragraphs.agr-s30-fruit-detail-p3: For citrus, the material follows its susceptibility to cold and strong winds with examples of using windbreak trees or wind-protection materials. Preparing for wind around trees differs in management scope from individually bagging fruit. Do not treat the term wind protection as a guarantee that cold, heavy rain, drought and all other weather damage will disappear. Use it to guide checks for each orchard.
paragraphs.agr-s30-fruit-detail-p4: The apple section says that apples are widely cultivated in regions with cold winters. Do not turn this seasonal regional characteristic, “cold in winter,” into an instruction that low temperatures are needed at every growth stage. Descriptions of growing regions and names of operations such as artificial pollination and fruit thinning can be organized as separate information.
paragraphs.agr-s30-fruit-detail-p5: Grapes are introduced as a crop widely grown throughout Japan. The same section also gives examples of protected cultivation because of susceptibility to wind, rain and disease. Having growing areas widely distributed across the country does not mean that management conditions are identical everywhere. Read geographical distribution separately from cultivation methods suited to the orchard environment.
paragraphs.agr-s30-fruit-detail-p6: The No. 2 material introduces sweet persimmon as a fruit characteristic of Japan, giving warm regions from Fukushima southward as examples of where it is cultivated. This explanation concerns sweet persimmon; do not apply the same regional conditions to every type merely because it is called persimmon. The stated “from Fukushima southward” range is not a boundary for deciding individual orchard suitability from place names alone.

agr-s30-label-detail.title: Read pesticide-label names, ingredients and quantity fields separately
agr-s30-label-detail.objective: Explain the No. 2 material’s label table without confusing purpose and name, ingredient name and content, manufacturing location, expiry and purchase quantity, crop-name examples or the two quantity fields.
agr-s30-label-detail.activity: Make an imaginary checklist with fields corresponding to the six paragraphs. Revise a field recording only the trade name, a record with an ingredient name but no ingredient content, and a field mixing original-product quantity with diluted-liquid quantity so that the unchecked information is clear. Do not add directions or quantities for actual products.

paragraphTitles.agr-s30-label-detail-p1: Separate purpose, trade name and type
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-label-detail-p2: Ingredient name and content are two pieces of information
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-label-detail-p3: Keep the manufacturing location’s name and address
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-label-detail-p4: Link expiry information with purchase-quantity planning
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-label-detail-p5: Do not extend the listed crop-name example automatically
paragraphTitles.agr-s30-label-detail-p6: Identify what quantity the use-amount field represents

paragraphs.agr-s30-label-detail-p1: The No. 2 material’s label table separates the use-purpose name, such as fungicidal or insecticidal use, from the pesticide name assigned for sale. It also explains that pesticides with different names can be of the same type. In receiving notes, separate “For what purpose?”, “Under which name?” and “Of which type?” Do not assume that different trade names necessarily mean different types. This is not an exercise in inferring identical directions for separate products from matching names or types.
paragraphs.agr-s30-label-detail-p2: The label table has an item for the names and contents of active ingredients and other ingredients. An ingredient name tells what is present; its content tells how much of that ingredient is present. Product quantity, in contrast, tells how much product is inside the bag or container. For example, a note saying “Ingredient name recorded; content blank” does not mean that the entire ingredient field has been checked. Do not copy ingredient content and total container quantity into the same field, or derive an actual product’s concentration or use amount from this explanation.
paragraphs.agr-s30-label-detail-p3: The No. 2 material lists the manufacturing location’s name and address as an independent label item. Keep that name and address separately from the trade name in notes used to cross-check product information. Similarities in part of a name do not establish an identical manufacturing location. This lesson concerns reading addresses. It does not decide under current rules that manufacturing must be domestic, or guarantee quality or safety from an address alone.
paragraphs.agr-s30-label-detail-p4: The material’s explanation of final expiry links to purchasing only the amount that can be used within that period. Once the expiry information has been recorded, separately reconsider the quantity you intend to buy. This does not authorize increasing application amounts or frequency to use up leftovers. The lesson reads the relationship between purchase planning and the expiry field; it does not decide a particular product’s current expiry or whether use after expiry is permitted.
paragraphs.agr-s30-label-detail-p5: The No. 2 material gives an example in which a listing for tomato is not treated as covering cherry tomato when cherry tomato is not listed. This lesson uses that example to teach checking each listed crop name individually. Instead of assuming “similar names mean it has been checked,” record the crop name actually read. This is a reading example from the teaching material, not the result of determining the current approved uses of a real product.
paragraphs.agr-s30-label-detail-p6: The material’s use-amount and spray-liquid-amount explanation distinguishes pesticides used as supplied from those diluted before use. For the former, read the weight of product used; for the latter, read the quantity of prepared, diluted spray liquid. The shared word “amount” does not make original-product quantity and prepared-liquid quantity the same thing. When checking an imaginary record, first retain which quantity the field represents. Do not supply a specific pesticide’s dilution factor, application amount or treatment area from this comparison.
